o: Their explicit attitudes are definitely false
The task suggests a discrepancy, not that self-reports are lies.
Their implicit attitudes may differ from their explicit attitudes
Correct: reaction-time tasks like the IAT can reveal automatic associations.
Attitudes have no affective component
Automatic associations are partly affective.
Implicit attitudes cannot be measured
Reaction-time tasks are designed to measure them.
questions.x: Explicit attitudes are consciously reported; implicit attitudes are automatic associations measured indirectly, as with reaction times on the Implicit Association Test. Slower pairing of a group with positive words suggests a weaker automatic positive link than self-reports imply. A gap between the two does not prove the person is lying.

questions.q: LaPiere's classic study found that businesses served a traveling couple in person but later said in letters they would refuse such customers. What does this show?
o: Stated attitudes do not always predict actual behavior
Correct: written attitudes and in-person behavior diverged.
Behavior always matches stated attitudes
The study found the opposite.
Attitudes predict behavior only in groups
The study did not compare individual and group contexts.
Cognitive dissonance reduces attitude change
The study did not measure dissonance.
questions.x: In the 1930s, LaPiere traveled with a Chinese couple, who were refused service only once in about 250 establishments, yet most businesses later wrote that they would not serve Chinese guests. The gap shows that stated attitudes, especially general ones measured in the abstract, may not predict actual behavior in real situations.

questions.q: After choosing between two equally appealing job offers, people later rate the chosen job higher and the rejected job lower. What explains this?
o: The overjustification effect
No reward undermined interest here.
Learned helplessness
Helplessness follows uncontrollable outcomes.
Approach–avoidance conflict
The conflict was resolved; this is the attitude shift afterward.
Post-decision dissonance reduction
Correct: spreading the alternatives apart justifies the choice.
questions.x: After a difficult choice between similar options, people experience post-decision dissonance and reduce it by spreading the alternatives: they boost their view of the chosen option and downgrade the rejected one. Approach-approach conflict describes the choice itself, not the attitude change that follows it.

questions.q: According to Zajonc's drive theory, the mere presence of others tends to:
o: Impair performance on every kind of task equally
Presence helps some tasks and hurts others, depending on whether the response is dominant.
Strengthen dominant responses, aiding simple or well-learned tasks
Correct: arousal from others boosts the dominant response, which is usually correct only for easy tasks.
Lower arousal and make people calmer
Drive theory says others raise arousal, not lower it.
Improve performance only on novel, complex tasks
Complex tasks are usually hurt, because the dominant response there tends to be wrong.
questions.note: Easy task + audience = better; hard task + audience = worse.
questions.x: Zajonc proposed that others' presence raises arousal, and arousal strengthens whatever response is dominant, meaning most likely. On easy or well-practiced tasks the dominant response is correct, so performance improves; on hard or new tasks it is often wrong, so performance suffers. That is why the effect is not uniform and not limited to complex tasks.

questions.q: In a study, an audience improved performance on a simple task, but the effect vanished when the audience members were blindfolded. Which explanation does this most support?
o: Evaluation apprehension
Correct: if observers cannot judge the performer, concern about being evaluated drops and so does the effect.
Mere presence theory
Mere presence predicts an effect even from observers who cannot see.
Diffusion of responsibility
That concept explains reduced helping in groups, not task performance.
Social loafing
Loafing occurs when individual effort is pooled and unidentifiable, not when watched.
questions.x: Evaluation apprehension holds that audiences raise arousal because performers worry about being judged. Blindfolded observers cannot judge, so if the effect disappears with them, judgment concern is the active ingredient. Mere presence theory would predict that simply having bodies in the room is enough, which this result contradicts.

questions.q: A theory proposes that an audience raises arousal because the performer's attention is split between the task and the observers. This is known as:
o: Evaluation apprehension theory
That theory centers on fear of being judged, not on divided attention.
Mere presence theory
Mere presence says others raise arousal simply by being there.
Distraction-conflict theory
Correct: the conflict between attending to the task and to others creates arousal.
Deindividuation theory
Deindividuation concerns lost self-awareness in groups, not attentional conflict.
questions.x: Distraction-conflict theory says an audience pulls attention away from the task, and the conflict between attending to the task and to the observers creates arousal. That arousal then produces the usual facilitation or impairment. It differs from evaluation apprehension, which locates the cause in fear of judgment rather than in split attention.

questions.q: The loss of self-awareness and sense of personal responsibility that can occur in large, anonymous groups is called:
o: Social loafing
Loafing is reduced effort on pooled tasks, not loss of self-awareness.
Group polarization
Polarization is the strengthening of initial attitudes through discussion.
Deindividuation
Correct: anonymity and arousal in crowds reduce self-awareness and restraint.
Conformity
Conformity is matching group norms, which can happen with full self-awareness.
questions.x: Deindividuation is a state of reduced self-awareness and personal accountability produced by anonymity, arousal and immersion in a group. People become less guided by internal standards and more by the immediate situation. It differs from social loafing, which is reduced effort on pooled tasks, and from conformity, which can occur with full self-awareness.

questions.q: Participants wearing loose hoods that hid their faces delivered longer noise blasts to a target than participants wearing large name tags. This finding is best explained by:
o: Deindividuation produced by anonymity
Correct: hidden identity lowers accountability and self-monitoring, increasing aggression.
Social facilitation
Facilitation concerns performance changes from an audience, not anonymity.
The bystander effect
The bystander effect concerns failures to help, not increased aggression.
Informational social influence
Nothing in the design involved looking to others for correct information.
questions.x: Anonymity is a key trigger of deindividuation: when identity is hidden, people feel less accountable and monitor their own behavior less, which can release aggression. Name tags make people identifiable and restore restraint. Social facilitation is not the answer because the manipulation was anonymity, not whether an audience was watching.

questions.q: Anonymous participants dressed as hospital staff gave weaker punishments than identifiable controls, while anonymous participants dressed as executioners gave stronger ones. What does this suggest about deindividuation?
o: Anonymity always increases aggression
Here anonymity decreased punishment in the hospital-staff group.
Costumes have no effect once anonymity is controlled
The costume clearly changed behavior in opposite directions.
Deindividuation only occurs in groups larger than ten
Group size was not manipulated, so this cannot be concluded.
It heightens responsiveness to situational cues and norms
Correct: anonymous people follow the norms cued by the situation, prosocial or antisocial.
questions.note: Deindividuation is not automatically antisocial; it amplifies salient norms.
questions.x: Deindividuation does not simply unleash aggression; it makes people more responsive to the norms cued by their situation. Nurse costumes cue caring, so anonymous people punished less, while executioner costumes cue harm, so they punished more. The opposite outcomes rule out the idea that anonymity always increases aggression.

questions.q: A man collapses on a crowded train platform. Each onlooker assumes someone else will call for help, so no one does. Which process is most directly at work?
o: Deindividuation
Deindividuation involves lost self-awareness, typically leading to disinhibited acts.
Pluralistic ignorance
That involves misreading others' calm as a sign of no emergency, not assuming others will act.
Diffusion of responsibility
Correct: with many onlookers, each feels less personally obligated to act.
Group polarization
Polarization concerns attitudes becoming more extreme after discussion.
questions.x: Diffusion of responsibility occurs when the presence of many bystanders makes each feel less personally obligated, because responsibility is spread across everyone. The key clue is that each person assumes someone else will act. Pluralistic ignorance is different: it is misreading others' calm as a sign that there is no emergency at all.

questions.q: A bystander weighs the physical danger of intervening against the guilt and blame she would feel if she did nothing, and helps only when the balance favors it. This reflects the:
o: Arousal: cost-reward model
Correct: people help when the costs of not helping exceed the costs of helping.
Diffusion of responsibility account
That account concerns the number of bystanders, not a cost-benefit calculation.
Kin selection hypothesis
Kin selection explains preferential helping of genetic relatives.
Just-world hypothesis
That is the belief people get what they deserve, which often reduces helping.
questions.x: The arousal: cost-reward model says witnessing an emergency creates unpleasant arousal that people want to reduce, and they choose the response with the best cost-benefit balance. They help when the costs of not helping, such as guilt and blame, outweigh the costs of helping, such as danger. Diffusion of responsibility focuses instead on bystander number.

questions.q: Cyclists perform a simple pedaling task beside co-actors. In condition 1 each rider's output is displayed separately; in condition 2 only the combined output is shown. Which pattern is predicted?
o: Equal effort in both conditions, since co-actors are present in both
Whether output is identifiable determines facilitation versus loafing.
Lower effort in condition 1 and higher effort in condition 2
This reverses the effect of identifiability.
Lower effort in both conditions compared with riding alone
Identifiable output in front of others typically raises effort on a simple task.
Higher effort in condition 1 and lower effort in condition 2
Correct: evaluated individual output yields facilitation; pooled output yields loafing.
questions.note: Others present + individually evaluated = facilitation; pooled = loafing.
questions.x: Whether co-actors produce facilitation or loafing depends on evaluation. When each rider's output is displayed, others' presence raises arousal and evaluation concern, boosting a simple task. When only combined output is shown, individuals can hide in the group and effort drops. Presence alone does not decide the outcome; identifiability does.

questions.q: The tendency for group discussion to strengthen the attitudes members already held is called:
o: Group polarization
Correct: discussion pushes the group further in its initial direction.
Groupthink
Groupthink is about suppressing dissent for harmony, not attitude intensification.
Social loafing
Loafing concerns effort, not attitudes.
Deindividuation
Deindividuation concerns lost self-awareness, not shifts after discussion.
questions.x: Group polarization is the tendency for discussion to push a group's average attitude further in the direction members already leaned. A mildly favorable group becomes strongly favorable. Groupthink is different: it concerns suppressing dissent to preserve harmony, which leads to poor decisions rather than defining attitude intensification.

questions.q: During discussion, group members hear new arguments that support the position most of them already favored, and their views become more extreme. This mechanism of polarization is best described as:
o: Normative social comparison
That mechanism relies on wanting to appear favorable relative to others, not on new arguments.
Persuasive arguments (informational influence)
Correct: exposure to novel supporting arguments shifts members further.
Diffusion of responsibility
That explains reduced helping in groups.
Reduction of cognitive dissonance
Dissonance concerns inconsistency between attitudes and actions.
questions.note: Two polarization mechanisms: informational (new arguments) and normative (social comparison).
questions.x: Polarization has two main explanations. In the informational (persuasive arguments) account, discussion exposes members to new arguments supporting the majority view, which pushes them further. In the normative (social comparison) account, members shift to appear at least as committed as others. New arguments are the hallmark of the informational mechanism.

questions.q: According to Janis, which set of conditions most strongly predisposes a group to groupthink?
o: Low cohesion and frequent turnover of members
Low cohesion reduces pressure for unanimity.
Diverse members and a leader who encourages debate
These conditions protect against groupthink.
Clear decision procedures and access to outside experts
Systematic procedures and outside input reduce groupthink.
High cohesion, a directive leader and insulation from outsiders
Correct: these are Janis's key antecedent conditions.
questions.x: Janis identified antecedents that make groupthink likely: high cohesiveness, directive leadership, insulation from outside opinions, lack of systematic procedures and high stress. The other options describe conditions, such as diversity, encouraged debate and outside experts, that protect against groupthink.

questions.q: In a task matching tones to a reference pitch, participants conformed to a unanimous incorrect majority on 32% of trials. When one confederate gave the correct answer, conformity fell to 7%. What does this show?
o: Majority size is the only factor controlling conformity
Majority size did not change; breaking unanimity did.
A single dissenter who breaks unanimity sharply reduces conformity
Correct: one ally made resisting the majority far easier.
Conformity in this task was purely informational
The design does not isolate informational influence; social support matters for normative pressure.
Conformity becomes permanent once it begins
Conformity fell immediately when the situation changed.
questions.x: A unanimous majority exerts strong pressure, but a single dissenter breaks that unanimity and gives others social support to resist. Here conformity dropped from 32% to 7% even though the incorrect majority was no smaller. This shows unanimity, not just majority size, drives conformity.

questions.q: A new resident starts composting because she admires her neighbors and wants to be like them, though she is not convinced it helps the environment. In Kelman's framework, this is:
o: Identification
Correct: she adopts the behavior to establish a valued relationship with the group.
Internalization
Internalization requires genuinely accepting the belief's merit.
Compliance
Compliance is driven by rewards or punishments, not admiration.
Obedience
No authority figure commanded the behavior.
questions.note: Compliance (reward) < identification (relationship) < internalization (belief).
questions.x: Kelman described three levels of attitude change. Compliance is driven by rewards or punishments, identification by wanting a relationship with or to resemble an admired group, and internalization by genuine belief in the idea. She adopts the behavior to be like her neighbors without believing in it, which is identification, not internalization.

questions.q: After an obedience study, participants explained that they were simply carrying out instructions and that the experimenter bore responsibility. Milgram called this mindset the:
o: Agentic state
Correct: people see themselves as agents executing another's wishes, shifting responsibility.
Foot-in-the-door effect
That describes compliance growing from small to large requests, not shifting responsibility.
Deindividuated state
Deindividuation involves anonymity in crowds, not responsibility shifted to an authority.
Cognitive dissonance
Dissonance is discomfort from inconsistency, which people resolve rather than delegate.
questions.x: Milgram proposed that people under authority can enter an agentic state, viewing themselves as instruments carrying out another's wishes rather than as autonomous actors. Responsibility is shifted to the authority, which allows harmful actions. This differs from deindividuation, which arises from anonymity in a crowd rather than from deferring to an authority.

questions.q: In an obedience study, the shock level rose in small 15-volt steps, so each command was only slightly greater than the one already obeyed. This incremental structure exploits the:
o: Door-in-the-face technique
That starts with a large request that is refused, then a smaller one.
Low-ball technique
Low-balling changes the terms after a commitment is made.
Reciprocity norm
Reciprocity involves returning a favor, which is absent here.
Foot-in-the-door effect
Correct: agreeing to small requests makes larger ones harder to refuse.
questions.x: The foot-in-the-door effect is the tendency to agree to a large request after first agreeing to a small one. Small 15-volt steps meant each new command was only slightly beyond what had already been done, making refusal feel inconsistent. Door-in-the-face works in reverse, starting with a large refused request followed by a smaller one.

questions.q: The process by which an immigrant group's distinctive cultural traits fade as members adopt the dominant culture is called:
o: Assimilation
Correct: the minority group is absorbed into the majority culture.
Multiculturalism
Multiculturalism preserves distinct cultures side by side.
Cultural diffusion
Diffusion is the spread of a cultural trait from one group to another, not absorption of a group.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is judging a culture by its own standards.
questions.x: Assimilation is the process by which a minority group's distinct traits fade as members adopt the dominant culture's language, customs and identity. Multiculturalism keeps distinct cultures alive side by side. Cultural diffusion is the spread of individual traits between groups, not the absorption of an entire group.

questions.q: A city funds heritage festivals and offers public services in several languages so immigrant communities can keep their traditions while participating fully in civic life. This policy reflects:
o: Assimilation
Assimilation expects minority traits to fade, not be preserved.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation blends cultures into a new single 'melting pot' culture.
Segregation
Segregation separates groups physically and socially, not integrates them.
Multiculturalism
Correct: distinct cultures are valued and maintained within one society.
questions.note: Multiculturalism = salad bowl; amalgamation = melting pot.
questions.x: Multiculturalism, often called the salad bowl model, values and supports distinct cultures within one society while all participate in common civic life. Assimilation expects minority traits to disappear, and amalgamation blends groups into a new combined culture. Supporting heritage festivals and multiple languages signals preservation, not blending.

questions.q: Consumer drones became common years before laws and norms about filming over private property were established. This gap illustrates:
o: Culture shock
Culture shock is personal disorientation in an unfamiliar culture.
Cultural lag
Correct: nonmaterial culture (laws, norms) trails behind material change (technology).
Cultural diffusion
Diffusion is spread of a trait between cultures, not a delay within one.
Cultural relativism
Relativism concerns judging practices by their own cultural context.
questions.x: Ogburn's cultural lag is the delay between change in material culture, such as new technology, and the adjustment of nonmaterial culture, such as laws, norms and values. Drones spread before rules about their use existed. Cultural diffusion concerns traits spreading between societies, not this internal mismatch.

questions.q: Researchers track an immigrant group across three generations. Host-language fluency rises steadily, and intermarriage with the majority group increases from 5% to 40%. These data most directly indicate:
o: Growing multiculturalism
Rising intermarriage and language shift point to blending into the majority, not preserved distinctness.
Increasing residential segregation
Higher intermarriage implies more, not less, contact.
Stronger transmission of the heritage culture
Rising host-language fluency and intermarriage signal weakening, not stronger, heritage transmission.
Increasing assimilation
Correct: language shift and intermarriage are classic markers of assimilation.
questions.x: Assimilation is commonly measured by markers such as adopting the host language, residential integration and intermarriage with the majority group. Rising fluency and intermarriage across generations show the group blending into the mainstream. Multiculturalism would instead show distinct heritage practices being maintained.

questions.q: Some second-generation immigrants absorb the norms of a disadvantaged segment of society and experience downward mobility, while others keep strong ethnic ties and move up. This pattern is described by:
o: Straight-line assimilation
Straight-line models predict uniform progress toward the mainstream.
Segmented assimilation
Correct: outcomes depend on which segment of society the group assimilates into.
Cultural pluralism
Pluralism describes groups coexisting distinctly, not divergent mobility paths.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation describes cultures blending into a new composite.
questions.x: Segmented assimilation theory says immigrants and their children assimilate into different parts of society, with different results. Some move upward into the middle class, some assimilate into disadvantaged groups and move downward, and some rise while keeping strong ethnic ties. Straight-line assimilation wrongly predicts one uniform path toward the mainstream.

questions.q: Heavy television viewers estimate their chance of being a victim of violent crime as much higher than light viewers do, even after controlling for neighborhood crime rates. Which theory best explains this?
o: Agenda-setting theory
Agenda-setting concerns which issues seem important, not distorted beliefs about real-world risk.
Two-step flow model
That model says media effects pass through opinion leaders.
Uses and gratifications theory
That theory explains media choice, not changes in worldview.
Cultivation theory
Correct: long-term heavy exposure shapes beliefs to match the media world.
questions.note: Cultivation's 'mean world syndrome'.
questions.x: Cultivation theory argues that heavy, long-term media exposure leads people to see the real world as resembling the media world. Because TV overrepresents violence, heavy viewers overestimate crime risk, sometimes called mean world syndrome. Agenda-setting concerns which issues seem important, not distorted estimates of real-world danger.

questions.q: A survey of 2,000 teens finds a correlation of r = 0.25 between weekly hours of violent video games and self-reported aggression. Which conclusion is justified?
o: Violent games cause aggression in most teens
A correlational survey cannot establish causation.
The two are positively associated, but causation cannot be inferred
Correct: the link may reflect reverse causation or a third variable.
Aggressive teens are drawn to violent games, not the reverse
The data cannot determine the direction of the relationship either way.
The relationship is too weak to have any meaning
A modest correlation in a large sample is still a real association.
questions.x: A correlation of 0.25 shows a modest positive association, but survey data cannot establish causation. Games could cause aggression, aggressive teens could prefer violent games, or a third factor could drive both. Claiming either specific direction overreaches, and in a sample of 2,000, a correlation of 0.25 is a real, if modest, association.

questions.q: A teen learns techniques for shoplifting and justifications for it, such as 'big stores can afford it', from his closest friends. Which theory best explains his behavior?
o: Labeling theory
Labeling theory focuses on reactions to deviance, not on how it is learned.
Strain theory
Strain theory focuses on the gap between goals and means.
Differential association theory
Correct: deviance is learned through interaction with intimate others.
Social control theory
Control theory asks why people conform, emphasizing social bonds.
questions.x: Sutherland's differential association theory says deviance is learned through interaction with intimate others, who teach both techniques and attitudes or justifications favorable to breaking rules. Learning shoplifting methods and rationalizations from close friends fits exactly. Labeling theory instead focuses on how others' reactions shape later deviance.

questions.q: After being publicly branded a 'delinquent' by his school, a boy begins to see himself that way and commits more serious offenses. This progression is called:
o: Primary deviance
Primary deviance is initial rule-breaking that does not shape self-identity.
Anomie
Anomie is a societal breakdown of norms.
Differential association
That theory concerns learning deviance from close others, not the effect of a label.
Secondary deviance
Correct: the deviant label is internalized and leads to further deviance.
questions.x: Labeling theory distinguishes primary deviance, initial rule-breaking that does not affect identity, from secondary deviance, which follows when a person accepts a deviant label and it becomes part of their self-concept. Being branded delinquent and then committing more serious offenses reflects secondary deviance driven by the label.

questions.q: In Goffman's classification, stigma attached to a person's ethnicity, nationality or religion is called:
o: Abomination of the body
This refers to physical deformities.
Blemish of individual character
This refers to perceived character flaws, such as addiction or imprisonment.
Courtesy stigma
Courtesy stigma falls on those associated with a stigmatized person.
Tribal stigma
Correct: tribal stigma is tied to group identity passed through lineage.
questions.x: Goffman described three types of stigma: abominations of the body (physical differences), blemishes of individual character (such as addiction or a prison record) and tribal stigma (race, nationality or religion, passed through lineage). Courtesy stigma is a separate idea in which stigma spreads to people associated with a stigmatized person.

questions.q: A man with schizophrenia comes to believe the stereotype that people like him are incompetent, and he stops applying for jobs. This is an example of:
o: Courtesy stigma
Courtesy stigma falls on associates, such as family, not the person himself.
Public stigma
Public stigma is the general population's endorsement of stereotypes.
Self-stigma
Correct: he has internalized the stereotype, lowering self-esteem and effort.
Structural stigma
Structural stigma lives in institutional policies, not personal beliefs.
questions.x: Self-stigma occurs when a person internalizes public stereotypes about their own group and applies them to themselves, lowering self-esteem and motivation. This can cause a why-try effect, like giving up on job applications. Public stigma is the general population's endorsement of the stereotype, not the person's own acceptance of it.

questions.q: Relatives of people with substance use disorders report being avoided by neighbors because of their family member's addiction. This is best described as:
o: Tribal stigma
Tribal stigma attaches to race, nation or religion.
Courtesy stigma
Correct: courtesy (associative) stigma is applied to those connected to a stigmatized person.
Self-stigma
Self-stigma is internalizing stereotypes about oneself.
Secondary deviance
Secondary deviance is the labeled person's own further rule-breaking.
questions.x: Courtesy (associative) stigma is disapproval directed at people because of their connection to a stigmatized person, such as family members of someone with an addiction. The relatives have no discrediting trait themselves. Tribal stigma differs because it attaches to one's own race, nation or religion.

questions.q: A nurse washes her hands far more often than her coworkers, who tease her for it, even though her practice reduces infections. Sociologically, her behavior is best described as:
o: Normative, because it is beneficial
Normative means matching group expectations, which she does not.
Not deviant, because it breaks no formal rule
Deviance includes violations of informal norms.
Deviant, because it departs from the group's norms
Correct: deviance is defined by departure from norms, not by harm.
Criminal, because it breaks workplace expectations
Crime requires violating formal law.
questions.note: Deviance can be positive; it is defined relative to group norms.
questions.x: Sociologically, deviance means departing from the norms of a group, whether or not the act is harmful or beneficial. Her coworkers' teasing shows she violates their informal norm, so she is deviant in that context. This is sometimes called positive deviance; it is not criminal, since no law is broken.

questions.q: First-time juvenile offenders are randomly assigned to formal court processing or to an informal diversion program. Those formally processed later reoffend more often. Which theory do these results most directly support?
o: Strain theory
Strain theory concerns blocked opportunities, which were not manipulated.
Functionalism
Functionalism does not predict that official processing increases reoffending.
Social control theory
Control theory focuses on bonds, which the design did not measure.
Labeling theory
Correct: official labeling as an offender appears to promote further deviance.
questions.x: Labeling theory predicts that formally labeling someone as an offender can push them toward a deviant identity and further deviance. Random assignment means the formal-processing group differed only in the label-producing treatment, so higher reoffending supports labeling theory. Strain theory would require blocked opportunities to be manipulated.

questions.q: A theory of crowd behavior holds that in ambiguous situations, crowd members collectively develop new norms that define what behavior is appropriate. This is:
o: Contagion theory
Contagion theory says emotions spread irrationally through a crowd, overwhelming individuals.
Convergence theory
Convergence theory says crowds gather people who already share dispositions.
Value-added theory
Value-added theory lists the conditions required for collective behavior to occur.
Emergent-norm theory
Correct: crowds create new, situation-specific norms through interaction.
questions.x: Emergent-norm theory says that in ambiguous situations, crowd members interact and collectively create new norms that define appropriate behavior for that situation. Crowd behavior is thus seen as rule-governed, not irrational. Contagion theory instead claims emotion spreads uncontrollably and overrides individual reasoning.

questions.q: A researcher argues that violent protest crowds are not created by the crowd itself but form because people who already hold similar grievances and dispositions gather together. This view is:
o: Contagion theory
Contagion theory says the crowd itself transforms individuals.
Emergent-norm theory
Emergent-norm theory says new norms develop within the crowd.
Convergence theory
Correct: crowd behavior reflects like-minded individuals converging.
Diffusion of responsibility
This explains reduced helping, not why crowds form.
questions.x: Convergence theory argues that crowd behavior reflects the preexisting attitudes and dispositions of the people who choose to gather; like-minded individuals converge. The crowd does not create their behavior. Contagion theory says the opposite, that the crowd itself transforms individuals.

questions.q: Investigators study an outbreak of headaches and fainting in a school. Which finding would most support a psychogenic rather than a toxic cause?
o: Elevated levels of a solvent in affected students' blood
This points to a real chemical exposure.
Symptom severity rising with proximity to an air vent
A dose-response with location suggests an environmental toxin.
All affected students having been in a single room
Shared location is consistent with a toxic source.
Symptoms spreading along friendship networks, including to other buildings
Correct: spread by social ties rather than location suggests psychogenic illness.
questions.x: Toxic exposures follow physical patterns, such as measurable chemicals in the body or symptoms worse near a source. Psychogenic illness spreads through social contact and observation, so it follows friendship ties, even across locations that share no air supply. Spread through social networks rather than physical proximity points to a psychogenic cause.

questions.q: A study finds parents in closely supervised jobs stress obedience in their children, while parents in self-directed jobs stress independence, even after controlling for income. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Work conditions shape the values parents pass on to children
Correct: occupational experience links the workplace to family socialization.
Children's personalities determine their parents' jobs
Reverse causation is implausible and not tested.
Income fully explains differences in parenting values
Income was controlled, and the difference remained.
Peer groups are the main source of children's values
Peers were not measured.
questions.x: Kohn's work showed that parents' job conditions shape the values they emphasize to children: closely supervised work encourages valuing obedience, while self-directed work encourages valuing independence. Because income was controlled, it cannot fully explain the difference. This links the workplace to family socialization.

questions.q: An immigrant speaks the host language and follows host customs at work while keeping her heritage religion, language and cuisine at home. In Berry's acculturation model, this strategy is:
o: Assimilation
Assimilation abandons the heritage culture.
Integration
Correct: she maintains her heritage culture while participating in the host culture.
Separation
Separation maintains the heritage culture while avoiding the host culture.
Marginalization
Marginalization rejects both cultures.
questions.x: Berry's acculturation model crosses two questions: is the heritage culture kept, and is the host culture engaged? Integration means yes to both, as with keeping heritage at home while following host customs at work. Assimilation drops the heritage culture, separation avoids the host culture and marginalization engages neither.

questions.q: Students overestimate how much their peers drink. After a campaign shows that most students actually have fewer than four drinks when they go out, heavy drinking declines. The campaign most likely worked by:
o: Increasing obedience to campus authorities
The campaign shared information about peers, not commands.
Reducing social loafing
Loafing concerns effort on pooled tasks.
Increasing deindividuation
Nothing in the campaign changed anonymity or self-awareness; it changed beliefs about peers.
Correcting a misperceived descriptive norm
Correct: students conform to what they believe peers do, so fixing the belief changes behavior.
questions.x: Descriptive norms are beliefs about what others actually do, and people tend to conform to them. When students overestimate peer drinking, they drink more to match. Correcting the misperception lowers the perceived norm, and behavior follows. This is the social norms approach, not obedience, because no authority issued commands.

questions.q: Most residents adopted a new health app not after seeing its ads but after hearing about it from respected acquaintances who closely followed tech news. This pattern supports the:
o: Cultivation theory
Cultivation concerns long-term exposure shaping worldviews.
Hypodermic needle model
That model predicts direct effects of media on passive audiences.
Two-step flow model
Correct: media influence passes through opinion leaders to others.
Agenda-setting theory
Agenda-setting concerns which issues seem important.
questions.x: The two-step flow model holds that media messages influence opinion leaders first, who then pass them on through personal contact to others. Residents adopting the app after hearing about it from informed acquaintances fits. The hypodermic needle model, which assumes direct effects of media on passive audiences, does not.

questions.q: An archival study finds that crowds watching a person threaten to jump from a building were more likely to jeer and urge the person on when the crowd was large and it was dark. This is best explained by:
o: Social facilitation
Facilitation concerns task performance, not hostile crowd behavior.
Deindividuation
Correct: large size and darkness increase anonymity and reduce restraint.
The bystander effect
The bystander effect explains failure to help, not active jeering.
Group polarization
Polarization requires discussion that intensifies prior attitudes.
questions.x: Large crowds and darkness increase anonymity, which reduces self-awareness and accountability, producing deindividuation and disinhibited behavior such as jeering. The bystander effect explains failure to help, not active hostility. Group polarization would require discussion that intensifies prior attitudes.

questions.q: A student who moves next to a railway stops reacting to passing trains after a few weeks. Which process best describes this?
o: Extinction
Extinction requires a previously conditioned response; reacting to train noise was never conditioned.
Habituation
Correct: a decreased response to a repeated, harmless stimulus is habituation.
Sensitization
Sensitization is an increase in responding, not a decrease.
Stimulus discrimination
Discrimination means responding differently to similar stimuli, not fading response to one.
questions.note: Habituation is a drop in an unlearned response to a repeated stimulus.
questions.x: Habituation is a decline in an unlearned response when a harmless stimulus repeats, like the startle to train noise fading over weeks. Extinction is tempting because responding also drops, but extinction applies only to a response that was first conditioned and then the CS is presented without the UCS. Reacting to a loud noise was innate, never conditioned.

questions.q: For hours after a nearby explosion, a soldier startles strongly at many unrelated quiet sounds. Which process does this illustrate?
o: Sensitization
Correct: an intense stimulus amplified responding to a wide range of later stimuli.
Habituation
Habituation would reduce, not increase, startle responses.
Dishabituation
Dishabituation restores response to one habituated stimulus; it is not a broad increase across many sounds.
Negative reinforcement
No behavior is being strengthened by removal of an aversive stimulus.
questions.note: Sensitization: increased response after an intense or noxious stimulus.
questions.x: Sensitization is a non-associative increase in responding after an intense or noxious stimulus, and it spreads broadly to many stimuli, not just the one that started it. Dishabituation is the tempting alternative, but it restores the response to one specific habituated stimulus; here startle rises to many unrelated sounds after a single traumatic event.

questions.q: Infants view one face until looking time drops, then see either that face again or a new face. Infants look much longer at the new face. What can researchers conclude?
o: Infants prefer the familiar face
They looked longer at the novel face, not the familiar one.
Looking time was operantly reinforced
No consequence followed looking, so no operant contingency existed.
Infants can discriminate between the two faces
Correct: recovery of looking to the new face means infants perceived it as different.
Infants were sensitized to all faces
Looking at the repeated face declined, which is the opposite of sensitization.
questions.note: Habituation–dishabituation paradigms test perceptual discrimination in preverbal infants.
questions.x: In the habituation–dishabituation paradigm, infants look less at a repeated stimulus, and renewed looking to a new one shows they detect the difference. This lets researchers test perception in babies who cannot talk. Sensitization does not fit, because looking to the repeated face fell rather than rose.

questions.q: Which observation best distinguishes habituation from sensory adaptation?
o: A novel stimulus can quickly restore a habituated response
Correct: dishabituation shows the receptors still work, so the decline reflects central learning.
Habituation occurs only in the retina
Habituation is not a receptor-level process confined to one sense organ.
Sensory adaptation can be reversed by a novel stimulus
Sensory adaptation reflects receptor changes and recovers with time, not with novel stimuli elsewhere.
Habituation requires reinforcement
Habituation needs no reinforcement; it occurs from mere repetition.
questions.note: Sensory adaptation happens at receptors; habituation is a learned change in responding.
questions.x: Sensory adaptation is reduced firing of receptors under constant stimulation, while habituation is a central, learned decline in behavioral responding. A novel stimulus can immediately restore a habituated response (dishabituation), showing the sensory pathway still works. Adaptation does not reverse this way; receptors recover only after the stimulus stops for a while.

questions.q: Many chemotherapy patients begin to feel nauseated as soon as they enter the clinic waiting room, before any drug is given. Which explanation fits best?
o: The drug causes nausea through negative reinforcement
Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by removing an aversive stimulus; this is not that.
Patients have habituated to the clinic
Habituation would reduce reactions to the clinic, not create nausea.
Clinic cues have become conditioned stimuli for nausea
Correct: clinic sights and smells were repeatedly paired with drug-induced nausea.
Nausea is an unconditioned response to the waiting room
The waiting room does not naturally cause nausea; the response was learned.
questions.note: Anticipatory nausea is a classic real-world conditioned response.
questions.x: Anticipatory nausea comes from classical conditioning: clinic sights and smells (neutral) were repeatedly paired with chemotherapy (UCS) that causes nausea (UCR), so the clinic alone now triggers nausea (CR). It is not an unconditioned response, because waiting rooms do not naturally cause nausea; the reaction was learned through pairing.

questions.q: A patient's fear of elevators is extinguished during sessions at a clinic, but the fear returns when he enters an elevator at his office, where the fear was learned. What does this renewal effect suggest?
o: Extinction learning is tied to the context where it occurred
Correct: the inhibitory extinction learning did not transfer outside the clinic context.
Extinction permanently erased the original association
If it were erased, fear could not return in the original context.
The office acts as a new unconditioned stimulus
The office does not innately produce fear; it is a context cue.
Fear returned because of sensitization to elevators
Sensitization is a nonassociative increase, not context-specific return of a CR.
questions.note: Extinction is new learning layered on top of the old association.
questions.x: Renewal shows that extinction is new inhibitory learning tied to the context where it happened, while the original fear association stays intact. Moving back to the acquisition context (or any new one) can bring the CR back. If extinction erased the association, fear could not return just because the setting changed, which is why therapists vary exposure settings.

questions.q: After a light reliably predicts food, a tone is repeatedly paired with the light, with no food given. The tone alone now elicits salivation. This is:
o: Stimulus generalization
A tone and a light are not physically similar stimuli.
Higher-order conditioning
Correct: an established CS (light) served as the UCS for conditioning a new CS (tone).
Sensory preconditioning
In sensory preconditioning, the two neutral stimuli are paired before either is linked to food.
Blocking
Blocking prevents learning about a new cue; here the tone was learned.
questions.x: In higher-order (second-order) conditioning, an established CS acts like a UCS for a new neutral stimulus: the light predicts food, the tone is paired with the light, and the tone alone now triggers salivation. Sensory preconditioning involves the same stimuli but in the reverse order, with the two neutral stimuli paired before either is linked to food.

questions.q: Rats first learn that a tone predicts shock. Then a tone-plus-light compound is paired with shock. Tested alone, the light produces little fear. Which phenomenon is this?
o: Overshadowing
Overshadowing occurs when both cues are new and the more salient one dominates.
Latent inhibition
Latent inhibition requires prior exposure to the light alone.
Extinction
The light was never conditioned, so there was nothing to extinguish.
Blocking
Correct: the tone already predicted shock, so the light added no new information and was not learned.
questions.note: Blocking shows conditioning depends on predictive information, not mere pairing.
questions.x: Blocking (Kamin) shows that conditioning depends on surprise and predictive information. Because the tone already fully predicted shock, adding the light gave no new information, so little fear was learned to the light. Overshadowing is the tempting alternative, but it happens when two new cues are trained together and the more salient one wins, with no prior training.

questions.q: Two groups receive the same number of tone–shock pairings, but group 2 also gets many shocks with no tone. Group 2 shows much less fear of the tone. Why?
o: The tone predicts shock less reliably in group 2
Correct: extra unsignaled shocks lower the tone–shock contingency.
Group 2 had fewer tone–shock pairings
Both groups had the same number of pairings.
Group 2 habituated to the tone
Habituation to the tone cannot explain the difference, since tone exposures were equal.
Group 2 learned through observation
No model was involved.
questions.note: Contingency, not just contiguity, drives classical conditioning.
questions.x: Rescorla's work showed that contingency, the degree to which the CS predicts the UCS, matters more than the number of pairings. When many shocks occur without the tone, the tone adds little predictive information, so less fear is learned. Explanations based on pairing counts fail, because both groups had equal tone–shock pairings.

questions.q: A therapist teaches a client deep relaxation, then gradually presents images of spiders from least to most frightening while the client stays relaxed. This technique is:
o: Flooding
Flooding exposes the client to the most feared stimulus at full intensity right away.
Aversive conditioning
Aversive conditioning pairs an unwanted behavior with an unpleasant stimulus.
Token economy
A token economy uses secondary reinforcers for target behaviors.
Systematic desensitization
Correct: relaxation is paired with a graded fear hierarchy, a form of counterconditioning.
questions.x: Systematic desensitization is counterconditioning: the client learns a response incompatible with fear (relaxation) and then moves gradually up a fear hierarchy, so feared cues become linked with calm. Flooding also uses exposure, but it starts at full intensity with no gradual steps or relaxation training, relying on extinction instead.

questions.q: Long-term heroin users face higher overdose risk when they inject a usual dose in an unfamiliar setting. Which explanation is best supported by conditioning research?
o: The new setting acts as an unconditioned stimulus for overdose
A setting cannot innately cause overdose; its effect is learned.
Familiar cues normally trigger a compensatory response that is missing
Correct: usual drug cues elicit a conditioned response opposing the drug, raising tolerance in that context.
Tolerance is purely pharmacological and unaffected by setting
Context-dependent overdose shows tolerance has a learned component.
Users generalize tolerance more strongly to novel settings
The problem is weaker tolerance in novel settings, not stronger.
questions.note: Conditioned compensatory responses explain context-specific tolerance.
questions.x: Siegel's work shows drug tolerance is partly conditioned: cues that reliably come before a drug trigger a compensatory response that opposes the drug's effects. In an unfamiliar setting this learned response is missing, so the usual dose acts more strongly and can be fatal. This rules out purely pharmacological tolerance, which would not depend on the setting.

questions.q: In a conditioning study, a control group gets the same number of tones and shocks, but at random, unpaired times. What is the main purpose of this group?
o: To measure spontaneous recovery
Spontaneous recovery requires prior extinction and a rest interval.
To increase the sample size of the paired group
A control group is a comparison, not added participants for the experimental condition.
To provide more conditioning trials
The goal is a comparison condition without contingency, not more learning.
To rule out responses due to mere exposure rather than association
Correct: if only the paired group responds to the tone, learning reflects the CS–UCS association.
questions.x: A truly random (unpaired) control gets the same CS and UCS exposure without any predictive relationship. If only the paired group responds to the tone, the response reflects a learned CS–UCS association, not pseudoconditioning or sensitization caused by shock exposure alone. The control is a comparison condition; it does not add trials or participants.

questions.q: Dogs are first exposed to a tone many times with nothing following it. Later, they take longer than naive dogs to learn that the tone predicts food. This is:
o: Blocking
Blocking requires another cue already predicting the UCS.
Latent learning
Latent learning is unexpressed learning revealed when reinforcement appears.
Latent inhibition
Correct: preexposure to a CS alone slows later conditioning to it.
Spontaneous recovery
Nothing was conditioned and then extinguished.
questions.note: Trap: latent inhibition (classical) is not latent learning (Tolman).
questions.x: Latent inhibition is slower conditioning after a CS has been presented alone many times; the animal learns that the stimulus predicts nothing. Latent learning sounds similar but is Tolman's idea of learning that happens without reinforcement and shows up only when a reward is introduced. Blocking needs a second cue that already predicts the UCS.

questions.q: A pigeon is conditioned to a 1,000 Hz tone, then tested with 600, 800, 1,000, 1,200 and 1,400 Hz tones. Which response pattern is most likely?
o: Equal responding to all five tones
That would be complete generalization, which is unusual after training on one tone.
Responding only at 1,000 Hz and none to others
Some generalization to nearby tones is expected without discrimination training.
Strongest responding at 600 and 1,400 Hz
Responding falls, not rises, with distance from the trained tone.
Peak at 1,000 Hz, declining as frequency moves away
Correct: a generalization gradient peaks at the trained stimulus.
questions.x: A generalization gradient shows that responding is highest to the trained stimulus and declines steadily as test stimuli become less similar. Some response to nearby frequencies is expected unless discrimination training has narrowed it. Responding only at 1,000 Hz would require such training, and a flat response pattern would mean no stimulus control at all.

questions.q: After a conditioned response is extinguished, re-pairing the CS and UCS restores the response in far fewer trials than the original learning took. What does this suggest?
o: The UCS has become more intense
The UCS was unchanged; faster learning reflects retained association.
The original association was not fully erased
Correct: rapid reacquisition (savings) means some of the original learning remained.
Extinction strengthened the association
Extinction reduces responding; it does not strengthen the CS–UCS link.
The response is now an unconditioned reflex
It still depends on the CS–UCS pairing, so it remains conditioned.
questions.x: Savings, or rapid reacquisition, means relearning after extinction is faster than the original learning. This shows the original CS–UCS association survives extinction, which adds new inhibitory learning rather than erasing the old link. It fits with spontaneous recovery and renewal, which also show the original memory remains.

questions.q: In general, which condition produces the fastest habituation?
o: A weak stimulus presented at short intervals
Correct: habituation is faster with lower intensity and more frequent presentation.
An intense stimulus presented at long intervals
Intense stimuli and long gaps slow habituation.
An intense stimulus presented at short intervals
Strong stimuli can produce sensitization rather than fast habituation.
A weak stimulus presented at long intervals
Long intervals allow recovery between presentations, slowing habituation.
questions.x: Habituation develops fastest with weak stimuli presented at short intervals. Intense stimuli resist habituation and can cause sensitization, while long gaps between presentations allow partial recovery, slowing the decline. A strong stimulus presented often is the tempting choice, but intensity tends to keep responding high.

questions.q: Rats pressing a lever for food stop pressing whenever a tone that previously preceded shock is played. Researchers use this drop in pressing mainly to measure:
o: Negative punishment of lever pressing
Shock was never contingent on pressing, so this is not punishment.
Extinction of lever pressing
Food is still delivered for pressing; suppression occurs only during the tone.
Habituation to the food reward
Pressing resumes when the tone ends, so food value is unchanged.
A classically conditioned fear response to the tone
Correct: conditioned suppression indexes fear elicited by the CS.
questions.note: Conditioned suppression combines operant baseline with a classical CS.
questions.x: Conditioned suppression measures classical fear: an ongoing operant behavior, like lever pressing for food, is suppressed when a CS previously paired with shock is presented, and the size of the drop indexes fear. It is not punishment, because shock never depended on pressing, and food reinforcement continues throughout.

questions.q: A cumulative record shows almost no responding right after each reinforcer, then steadily accelerating responding until the next one, repeating in a scalloped pattern. Which schedule produced it?
o: Variable interval
VI produces a steady, moderate rate without scallops.
Fixed interval
Correct: the FI scallop reflects anticipation of reinforcement at a predictable time.
Variable ratio
VR produces high, steady responding without long pauses.
Continuous reinforcement
Continuous reinforcement does not produce the time-based scallop.
questions.x: A fixed interval schedule produces the scallop: after each reinforcer the animal pauses, because no response can pay off for a while, then responds faster as the predictable reward time nears. Variable schedules remove predictability, so they produce steady responding without scallops. Fixed ratio schedules produce a pause followed by a burst at a high, constant rate, not gradual acceleration.

questions.q: Compared with partial reinforcement, continuous reinforcement typically leads to:
o: Slower acquisition but slower extinction
Continuous reinforcement speeds acquisition.
Faster acquisition and slower extinction
Behavior learned under continuous reinforcement extinguishes relatively fast.
Slower acquisition and faster extinction
Acquisition is faster, not slower, with continuous reinforcement.
Faster acquisition but faster extinction
Correct: every-response reinforcement teaches quickly, but its absence is noticed quickly.
questions.x: Continuous reinforcement makes the behavior–consequence link easy to detect, so learning is fast, but when rewards stop the change is obvious and extinction is quick. Partial reinforcement teaches more slowly yet makes behavior more persistent, because unrewarded responses were normal during training. The best practice is to start continuous and then thin to partial.

questions.q: A rat on an FR-50 schedule pauses after each pellet, then responds rapidly. Which change would most likely lengthen the post-reinforcement pause?
o: Increasing the requirement to FR-100
Correct: larger ratio requirements produce longer post-reinforcement pauses.
Decreasing the requirement to FR-10
Smaller ratios shorten the pause.
Switching to a variable ratio with a mean of 50
Variable ratios largely eliminate predictable pauses.
Switching to continuous reinforcement
Reinforcing every press removes the pause almost entirely.
questions.x: On fixed ratio schedules, the post-reinforcement pause grows as the ratio requirement grows, since a large block of work lies ahead. Raising FR-50 to FR-100 lengthens the pause. Switching to a variable ratio has the opposite effect, because any press could pay off and there is no predictable stretch of unreinforced work to delay.

questions.q: Group A rats get food for every lever press; group B gets food for about one in four presses. Food is then stopped for both groups. What is the most likely result?
o: Group A keeps pressing longer than group B
Continuously reinforced behavior extinguishes faster.
Both groups stop at the same time
Reinforcement history strongly affects resistance to extinction.
Group B keeps pressing longer than group A
Correct: the partial reinforcement extinction effect makes intermittent reinforcement more persistent.
Group B stops immediately
Group B is used to unreinforced presses, so it persists.
questions.x: The partial reinforcement extinction effect means intermittently reinforced behavior keeps going longer after rewards stop. Group B was used to many unrewarded presses, so the start of extinction is hard to detect. Group A, reinforced for every press, notices the change immediately and quits sooner, even though continuous reinforcement produced faster initial learning.

questions.q: A therapist teaches a child to wash hands as a linked sequence: wet hands, apply soap, rinse, dry, with finishing each step serving as the cue for the next. This is best described as:
o: Shaping
Shaping refines one target behavior through successive approximations.
Latent learning
Latent learning occurs without reinforcement and appears later.
Insight learning
Insight is sudden problem solution, not trained sequences.
Chaining
Correct: distinct behaviors are linked so each completed step signals the next.
questions.note: Shaping builds one behavior; chaining links several.
questions.x: Chaining teaches a complex skill as a sequence of separate behaviors, where completing each step acts as a cue for, and a conditioned reinforcer of, the next. Shaping is the tempting mix-up: it gradually refines one behavior through successive approximations, while chaining links several distinct behaviors in order.

questions.q: A woman with social anxiety declines every invitation and never feels anxious at parties. Why is such avoidance behavior especially resistant to extinction?
o: Avoidance is maintained by positive punishment
Avoidance is maintained by negative reinforcement (relief), not punishment.
She never learns that parties would not have been harmful
Correct: avoidance prevents exposure, so the feared outcome is never disconfirmed.
Avoidance responses are unconditioned reflexes
Declining invitations is a learned operant behavior.
Each avoided party adds a pleasant stimulus
Relief comes from removing anticipated anxiety, which is negative reinforcement.
questions.x: Avoidance is maintained by negative reinforcement: each avoided situation brings relief from expected anxiety. Because she never enters the situation, she never discovers that it is safe, so the fear is never extinguished. This is why exposure-based therapy is used. Avoidance is a learned operant behavior, not a reflex and not punishment.

questions.q: Dogs given inescapable shocks later fail to jump a low barrier to escape shock, even though escape is now possible. This is best explained by:
o: Stimulus discrimination
The dogs failed to act, not to tell stimuli apart.
Extinction of the escape response
The escape response was never learned, so it could not be extinguished.
Learned helplessness
Correct: experience with uncontrollable events leads to a belief that responding is futile.
Habituation to shock
Shock remained aversive; the dogs did not stop reacting to it.
questions.note: Learned helplessness is a cognitive model of depression.
questions.x: Learned helplessness (Seligman) occurs when experience with uncontrollable aversive events teaches an organism that its actions do not matter, so it stops trying even when control becomes possible. It is a cognitive and motivational deficit, not habituation, because the shock still distresses the animal. It has been used as a model for some forms of depression.

questions.q: Behaviorists often advise pairing punishment of an unwanted behavior with reinforcement of an alternative behavior. Why?
o: Punishment always strengthens the unwanted behavior
Punishment, by definition, decreases the behavior it follows.
Reinforcement and punishment cannot be used separately
Each can be used alone; combining them is simply more effective.
Punishment is a form of classical conditioning
Punishment is an operant procedure.
Punishment shows what not to do but not what to do instead
Correct: reinforcing a replacement behavior gives the learner a rewarded option.
questions.x: Punishment can suppress a behavior, but it does not teach an appropriate replacement and can cause fear, aggression or avoidance of the person who punishes. Reinforcing an alternative behavior gives the learner a rewarded way to meet the same need. Punishment, by definition, reduces the behavior it follows, so it does not strengthen the unwanted act.

questions.q: A pigeon receives food every 15 seconds no matter what it does. It soon begins turning in circles before each delivery. This behavior is best explained by:
o: Instinctive drift toward feeding behaviors
Turning in circles is not a natural food-related behavior drifting back.
Shaping by the experimenter
No one deliberately reinforced successive approximations.
Classical conditioning of turning to a tone
No tone or CS was used; the behavior was strengthened by chance pairings with food.
Accidental reinforcement of whatever preceded food
Correct: food happening to follow turning strengthened it, producing superstitious behavior.
questions.x: Skinner's superstition experiment showed that response-independent rewards can strengthen whatever behavior happens to come just before them. A chance pairing of turning with food made turning more likely, so it was more often followed by food again. This is accidental operant reinforcement, not shaping, because no one chose which behavior to reward.

questions.q: Prisoners can shorten their sentences by following rules, and rule-following increases. Which operant process best describes this?
o: Negative reinforcement
Correct: removing an aversive stimulus (time in prison) increases rule-following.
Positive reinforcement
Nothing pleasant is added; time served is taken away.
Negative punishment
Behavior increased, so this is reinforcement.
Positive punishment
No aversive stimulus is added, and behavior increased.
questions.x: Negative reinforcement strengthens a behavior by removing an aversive stimulus. Following rules removes time from an unpleasant prison sentence, and rule-following increases. The tempting answer is positive reinforcement because early release feels like a reward, but the consequence is taking away part of something unpleasant rather than adding something.

questions.q: A student gets detention each time he is late, yet his lateness does not decrease. In behavioral terms, detention is:
o: Positive punishment
Without a decrease in lateness, it does not meet the definition of punishment.
Negative punishment
Nothing is removed, and the behavior did not decline.
Not functioning as a punisher for lateness
Correct: punishers are defined by decreasing behavior, which did not happen.
Negative reinforcement
Lateness did not increase, and nothing aversive was removed.
questions.note: Consequences are defined by their effect on behavior, not intent.
questions.x: Consequences are defined by their effect on behavior, not by intent. A punisher must decrease the behavior it follows; if lateness continues, detention is not functioning as a punisher for this student, and it may even be reinforcing for him. Labeling detention as positive punishment assumes it works, but the data show it does not.

questions.q: Researchers record a child's on-task behavior at baseline, while tokens are given for on-task work, and after tokens are withdrawn. Which pattern best shows the tokens are reinforcers?
o: Behavior rises steadily across all three phases
A steady rise could reflect maturation or practice, not the tokens.
Behavior is unchanged across all three phases
No change means tokens did not reinforce on-task work.
Behavior rises with tokens and falls when they are withdrawn
Correct: changes that track the intervention in a reversal design show a functional relation.
Behavior falls with tokens and rises when withdrawn
That would suggest tokens act as punishers.
questions.x: An ABA reversal design tests whether an intervention causes behavior change: if behavior rises when tokens are introduced and falls when they are withdrawn, the change follows the intervention. A steady rise across phases could reflect practice, maturation or time, so it cannot show the tokens are responsible. Reversal is what supports a causal conclusion.

questions.q: A lab switches a rat from FR-20 to VR-20, keeping the average number of presses per pellet the same. Which change in responding is most expected?
o: Overall response rate drops sharply
VR schedules sustain high response rates.
Post-reinforcement pauses become shorter or disappear
Correct: since the next reinforcer could come at any press, the rat has less reason to pause.
A scalloped pattern appears
Scallops are typical of fixed interval schedules.
Behavior becomes less resistant to extinction
Variable ratio behavior is more, not less, resistant to extinction.
questions.x: Post-reinforcement pauses occur on fixed ratio schedules because the animal knows a set block of unreinforced work comes next. On variable ratio schedules, any response might be reinforced, so pausing wastes opportunities and pauses shrink or disappear, giving a high steady rate. Scallops belong to fixed interval schedules, not ratio schedules.

questions.q: Children who love to draw are paid for each drawing for two weeks. After payments stop, they draw less than they did before payments began. This illustrates:
o: Spontaneous recovery
Drawing fell below baseline instead of returning.
The Premack principle
Premack concerns using preferred activities as reinforcers.
Learned helplessness
They had control over outcomes; this concerns motivation, not helplessness.
The overjustification effect
Correct: external rewards shifted their reason for drawing away from intrinsic interest.
questions.x: The overjustification effect occurs when external rewards for an already enjoyable activity shift a person's reason for doing it from interest to reward. When the rewards stop, the activity can fall below its original level. It is not the Premack principle, which uses a preferred activity to reinforce a less preferred one rather than rewarding the preferred activity itself.

questions.q: A raccoon trained to drop coins into a box for food begins rubbing the coins together and dipping them instead, even though this delays food. This is:
o: Instinctive drift
Correct: innate food-handling behavior intrudes on the trained response.
Extinction burst
Food was still available for dropping coins; this is not a response to removed reinforcement.
Stimulus generalization
No new similar stimuli are involved.
Shaping
The behavior drifted away from, not toward, the target.
questions.note: Biological constraints limit what operant conditioning can produce.
questions.x: Instinctive drift, reported by the Brelands, is the tendency of trained behaviors to slide back toward innate, species-typical patterns. Raccoons naturally rub and wash food, so coins associated with food draw that behavior even though it delays reward. This shows biological constraints on operant learning; it is not an extinction burst, because reinforcement was still available.

questions.q: Rats quickly learn to run away to avoid shock but learn very slowly to press a lever to avoid the same shock. This difference best reflects:
o: A failure of negative reinforcement
Both responses can be negatively reinforced; they differ in how easily they are learned.
Stimulus discrimination between lever and runway
The difference concerns the responses, not stimulus discrimination.
The rats' lack of motor ability to press levers
Rats easily press levers for food, so motor ability is not the issue.
Biological constraints favoring species-typical defense responses
Correct: responses resembling natural defensive reactions are easier to condition for avoidance.
questions.x: Bolles proposed that animals learn avoidance most easily when the required response resembles a species-specific defense reaction, such as fleeing, freezing or fighting. Running fits a rat's natural defenses, while lever pressing does not, even though rats press levers easily for food. This is a biological constraint on learning, not a motor limit.

questions.q: Children who saw a model punished for hitting a toy imitated less than children who saw the model rewarded. When all children were then offered a treat to show what the model did, both groups imitated equally well. What does this show?
o: Learning occurred even when performance was suppressed
Correct: vicarious punishment reduced performance, not acquisition.
Vicarious punishment prevented learning
The punished-model group reproduced the behavior once given an incentive.
Observational learning requires direct reinforcement
Children learned without being reinforced themselves.
Treats caused the children to learn the behavior
The treat came after observation and only revealed what was already learned.
questions.note: Learning and performance are separable in social cognitive theory.
questions.x: Bandura's Bobo doll work separated acquisition from performance. Seeing the model punished reduced imitation, but once an incentive was offered, children in every condition reproduced the aggression equally well, so all had learned it. Vicarious punishment affected whether they chose to perform the behavior, not whether they learned it.

questions.q: fMRI studies show overlapping human brain activation when people perform an action and when they watch it. Why is this weaker evidence for mirror neurons than monkey single-cell recordings?
o: fMRI cannot detect activity in the frontal lobe
fMRI measures activity throughout the brain.
fMRI cannot show that the same neuron responds in both conditions
Correct: a voxel holds many thousands of neurons, so overlap may reflect separate cells.
fMRI measures electrical spikes too slowly to detect any activity
fMRI measures blood-oxygen signals, not spikes; slowness is not the key problem.
Humans do not imitate others' actions
Humans imitate extensively.
questions.x: Single-cell recordings can show that one neuron fires during both doing and watching, which defines a mirror neuron. fMRI measures blood-oxygen changes averaged over voxels that each contain many neurons, so overlapping activation could come from separate populations of cells that happen to be close together. That limit on spatial resolution, not regional coverage, is the key weakness.

questions.q: A voter changes her opinion after carefully evaluating the evidence and logic in a detailed policy proposal. According to the elaboration likelihood model, she was persuaded via the:
o: Peripheral route
The peripheral route relies on superficial cues like attractiveness.
Heuristic route of mere exposure
Mere exposure involves repeated presentation, not argument evaluation.
Central route
Correct: thoughtful evaluation of argument quality is central-route processing.
Foot-in-the-door route
That is a compliance technique, not an ELM route.
questions.x: The elaboration likelihood model describes two routes. The central route involves careful thought about the arguments and requires both motivation and ability; the peripheral route relies on surface cues such as attractiveness or the number of arguments. Attitudes formed centrally tend to last longer, resist change, and predict behavior better, which fits a voter who studied the evidence.

questions.q: Students hear strong or weak arguments for a new exam policy said to begin either at their own school next year or at a distant school in ten years. Which result does the ELM predict?
o: Argument strength matters more for the distant policy
Low relevance reduces elaboration, so argument quality matters less.
Argument strength matters more when the policy affects them next year
Correct: high personal relevance increases elaboration, making argument quality decisive.
Argument strength matters equally in both conditions
The ELM predicts relevance moderates the effect of argument quality.
Weak arguments persuade best when relevance is high
Under high elaboration, weak arguments are easily rejected.
questions.x: This design mirrors classic ELM studies: personal relevance increases motivation to elaborate, so under high relevance strong arguments persuade and weak ones backfire. Under low relevance, people process less, and argument quality has a smaller effect, while peripheral cues matter more. Relevance therefore moderates how much argument strength matters.

questions.q: Participants paid 2 dollars to tell others a dull task was fun later rated it more enjoyable than participants paid 50 dollars. This best supports:
o: Cognitive dissonance theory
Correct: low pay gave insufficient justification, so attitudes shifted to match the behavior.
Positive reinforcement of enjoyment
Larger rewards would then predict more liking, the opposite result.
The sleeper effect
The sleeper effect concerns forgetting a message source.
The overjustification effect
Overjustification lowers interest in an already enjoyable activity; this task was dull.
questions.x: Cognitive dissonance theory holds that inconsistent cognitions cause discomfort, which people reduce by changing an attitude. Paid only 2 dollars for lying, participants lacked enough outside justification, so they decided the task really was fun. Those paid 50 dollars could explain the lie by the money. Reinforcement theory predicts the reverse, more liking with bigger pay.

questions.q: A man who seldom thinks about recycling notices he has been recycling every day and concludes that he must care about the environment. Which theory best explains his conclusion?
o: Cognitive dissonance theory
Dissonance requires discomfort from conflicting cognitions, which is not described.
Self-perception theory
Correct: with weak prior attitudes, people infer attitudes from their own behavior.
Elaboration likelihood model
ELM concerns persuasive messages, not inferring attitudes from one's own actions.
Reciprocal determinism
That describes mutual influence among person, behavior and environment, not attitude inference.
questions.x: Bem's self-perception theory states that when attitudes are weak or unclear, people infer them by observing their own behavior, much as an outside observer would. Dissonance theory is the tempting choice, but it involves discomfort from a conflict between an existing attitude and behavior, and this man had no strong prior attitude to conflict with.

questions.q: Mild distraction during a speech with weak arguments can increase persuasion. What is the most likely reason?
o: It increases the listener's motivation to elaborate
Distraction lowers ability to elaborate, not motivation.
It makes the source seem more expert
Distraction does not change perceived expertise.
It disrupts the listener's ability to generate counterarguments
Correct: reduced elaboration keeps listeners from noticing and refuting flaws.
It strengthens the arguments themselves
The arguments are unchanged; only processing is affected.
questions.x: In the ELM, distraction lowers ability to elaborate. With weak arguments, careful listeners would generate counterarguments and reject the message, so mild distraction can increase persuasion by blocking that critique. With strong arguments distraction has the reverse effect and lowers persuasion, since listeners can no longer appreciate the good points.

questions.q: Lab-raised monkeys watching edited videos learn to fear snakes after seeing a model monkey react fearfully to them, but do not learn to fear flowers from the same fearful reactions. What does this suggest?
o: Monkeys cannot learn by observation
They did learn fear of snakes by observation.
Observational fear learning is shaped by biological preparedness
Correct: some fears are acquired from models far more readily than others.
Flowers are unconditioned stimuli for fear
Flowers do not innately cause fear, and none was learned.
Fear of snakes is fully innate in lab-raised monkeys
They acquired the fear only after watching the model.
questions.x: Mineka's monkey studies showed that observational fear learning is shaped by biological preparedness: lab-raised monkeys quickly acquired fear of snakes from models but not fear of flowers, even with identical fearful reactions. The fear was learned, since it appeared only after watching, but evolution made some stimuli far easier to link with fear.

questions.q: A student expects that studying will lead to good grades but doubts she can make herself study effectively. In social cognitive terms, she has:
o: Low outcome expectancy but high self-efficacy
She does believe studying leads to good grades.
High outcome expectancy but low self-efficacy
Correct: she believes the behavior works but doubts her ability to perform it.
An external locus of control
