She attributes grades to her own studying, an internal factor.
Learned helplessness about grades
She thinks grades are controllable through studying.
questions.x: Bandura separated outcome expectancy (believing a behavior will produce a result) from self-efficacy (believing one can carry out the behavior). This student believes studying works but doubts she can make herself do it, so outcome expectancy is high and self-efficacy is low. Locus of control does not apply, because she attributes grades to her own studying, an internal factor.

questions.q: According to the ELM, when can a model's attractiveness act as a central-route argument rather than a peripheral cue?
o: Whenever the audience is distracted
Distraction reduces elaboration, making attractiveness a peripheral cue.
When the audience has low need for cognition
Low need for cognition favors peripheral processing.
Never; attractiveness is always peripheral
ELM holds that one variable can play different roles depending on context.
When attractiveness is directly relevant to the product's claims
Correct: for a skin-care product, visible results can count as evidence.
questions.note: A variable's role in the ELM depends on context.
questions.x: The ELM proposes that one variable can play several roles: it can act as a peripheral cue, as an argument, or by changing how much people elaborate. Attractiveness is usually a peripheral cue, but for a beauty product a model's clear skin can serve as evidence for the claim, so careful processors treat it as an argument. Its role depends on context.

questions.q: To test source credibility, researchers give participants the same essay attributed either to a Nobel-winning scientist or to a high school student, then measure agreement. What is the independent variable?
o: The attributed author of the essay
Correct: the researchers manipulate only who supposedly wrote the essay.
Participants' level of agreement
Agreement is the measured dependent variable.
The content of the essay
The essay is held constant across conditions.
Participants' prior education
This is a participant variable, not the manipulated factor.
questions.x: The independent variable is the factor researchers deliberately manipulate, here the attributed author, which varies credibility while the essay content stays the same. Agreement is the dependent variable, the outcome measured. Holding the essay constant means any difference in agreement can be attributed to perceived source credibility.

questions.q: Which term refers to the full set of beliefs and knowledge a person holds about who they are?
o: Self-concept
Correct: self-concept is the overall cognitive picture of oneself.
Self-esteem
Self-esteem is the evaluative judgment of worth, not the full set of self-beliefs.
Self-efficacy
Self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to succeed at specific tasks.
Identity foreclosure
Foreclosure is a Marcia status of commitment without exploration.
questions.note: Concept = what I think I am; esteem = how I feel about it.
questions.x: Self-concept is the whole cognitive picture of who you are: your traits, roles, values and beliefs about yourself. Self-esteem is narrower, the emotional judgment of how good or worthy that self is. Think of self-concept as the description and self-esteem as the grade you give it.

questions.q: A person's overall evaluation of their own worth is best described as:
o: Self-schema
A self-schema is an organized belief about oneself in a domain, not a worth judgment.
Self-esteem
Correct: self-esteem is the affective, evaluative side of the self.
Self-efficacy
Self-efficacy concerns confidence in task performance, not global worth.
Locus of control
Locus of control concerns where one places causes of outcomes.
questions.x: Self-esteem is the evaluative, feeling-based part of the self: how much you like and value yourself overall. A self-schema is a belief about yourself in one domain, and self-efficacy is confidence about succeeding at particular tasks. Only self-esteem is a global judgment of worth.

questions.q: After failing her driving test, Maya says the examiner was unfair and the route was unusually difficult. Her explanation best reflects:
o: An internal locus of control
Internals credit their own effort or skill for outcomes.
High self-efficacy
She makes no claim about her ability to succeed next time.
An external locus of control
Correct: she attributes the outcome to forces outside herself.
Identity achievement
Identity achievement is a Marcia status, unrelated to attributions.
questions.x: Locus of control (Rotter) describes where a person places the causes of outcomes: inside (effort, ability) or outside (luck, others, circumstances). Blaming the examiner and route places the cause outside Maya. Self-efficacy is a forward-looking belief about her capability, which she never states.

questions.q: According to Bandura, which source most strongly builds self-efficacy?
o: Mastery experiences
Correct: personal successes are the most powerful source of efficacy beliefs.
Vicarious experiences
Watching similar others succeed helps, but less than one's own successes.
Verbal persuasion
Encouragement from others is a weaker, more fragile source.
Physiological states
Interpreting arousal affects efficacy but is the least robust source.
questions.x: Bandura named four sources of self-efficacy: mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion and physiological or emotional states. Mastery is strongest because one's own successes are direct, hard-to-dispute evidence of capability. Watching others succeed helps, but less than doing it yourself.

questions.q: Dogs exposed to inescapable shocks later fail to escape shocks that they could easily avoid. This phenomenon is best termed:
o: Operant extinction
Extinction is loss of a response when reinforcement stops.
Habituation
Habituation is reduced response to a repeated harmless stimulus.
Learned helplessness
Correct: perceived lack of control leads to passivity even when control is possible.
Social facilitation
Social facilitation concerns performance in the presence of others.
questions.note: Learned helplessness links to an external locus of control and depression.
questions.x: Learned helplessness (Seligman) occurs when repeated uncontrollable bad events teach an organism that its actions do not matter, so it stops trying even after escape becomes possible. It is a learned expectation of no control, not a weakened response from lost reinforcement as in extinction.

questions.q: An adult who is excessively orderly, rigid and stingy would, according to Freud, most likely be fixated at which stage?
o: Anal
Correct: anal-retentive traits are tied to conflict over toilet training.
Oral
Oral fixation shows as dependency or oral habits like smoking.
Phallic
Phallic fixation involves Oedipal issues and vanity.
Genital
The genital stage is the mature endpoint, not a fixation point.
questions.x: Freud tied the anal stage to the battle over toilet training. Harsh or rigid training was said to produce an anal-retentive adult who is orderly, stubborn and stingy, while overly lax training produced messiness. Oral fixation, by contrast, shows up as dependency and mouth-centered habits.

questions.q: In Freud's theory, a period from about age 6 to puberty in which sexual impulses are dormant is called the:
o: Genital stage
The genital stage begins at puberty with mature sexual interest.
Phallic stage
The phallic stage involves the Oedipal conflict at ages 3 to 6.
Latency stage
Correct: libido is suppressed and energy goes toward school and friendships.
Anal stage
The anal stage centers on toilet training in toddlerhood.
questions.x: Freud's latency stage spans roughly age 6 to puberty, when sexual impulses are repressed and energy is redirected into schoolwork, hobbies and same-sex friendships. It follows resolution of the phallic Oedipal conflict and ends when puberty reawakens sexual drives in the genital stage.

questions.q: A college student has explored several majors and religious views but has not yet committed to any. Which of Marcia's identity statuses fits best?
o: Foreclosure
Foreclosure is commitment without exploration.
Diffusion
Diffusion lacks both exploration and commitment.
Moratorium
Correct: active exploration without commitment.
Achievement
Achievement requires commitment after exploration.
questions.x: Marcia classified identity by two questions: has the person explored alternatives, and have they committed? Moratorium is active exploration with no commitment yet, often a normal phase in college. Achievement would require committing after exploring, which this student has not done.

questions.q: Marcia's four identity statuses are defined by crossing which two dimensions?
o: Autonomy and intimacy
These are Erikson stage themes, not Marcia's axes.
Exploration and commitment
Correct: presence or absence of each yields the four statuses.
Assimilation and accommodation
These are Piaget's cognitive processes.
Conformity and obedience
These are social influence concepts.
questions.note: Diffusion (−/−), foreclosure (−explore/+commit), moratorium (+/−), achievement (+/+).
questions.x: Marcia built his four identity statuses by crossing exploration (crisis) with commitment: diffusion (neither), foreclosure (commitment only), moratorium (exploration only) and achievement (both). Autonomy and intimacy are Erikson stage themes, not the axes of Marcia's model.

questions.q: A physician breaks a hospital rule to save a patient, arguing that preserving human life outweighs any rule. Which Kohlberg stage is this?
o: Law and order
Stage 4 would uphold the rule.
Universal ethical principles
Correct: stage 6 follows self-chosen principles even against rules.
Good interpersonal relationships
Stage 3 reasons from approval of others.
Obedience and punishment
Stage 1 reasons from avoiding punishment.
questions.x: Kohlberg's postconventional level judges laws by deeper principles. At stage 6, people follow self-chosen universal ethical principles, such as the value of human life, even when they conflict with rules. A stage 4 thinker would hold that the hospital rule must be obeyed to maintain order.

questions.q: Carol Gilligan criticized Kohlberg's theory mainly because it:
o: Ignored cognitive development entirely
Kohlberg's theory is explicitly cognitive-developmental.
Overemphasized unconscious drives
That critique fits Freud, not Kohlberg.
Was based on male samples and stressed justice over care
Correct: she argued it undervalued a care-based ethic.
Proposed too few stages
Her objection was about bias, not the number of stages.
questions.x: Kohlberg built his stages largely from interviews with boys and men and scored justice-based reasoning highest. Gilligan argued this undervalued an ethic of care, which emphasizes relationships and responsibility and which she found more often in women. Her critique concerned bias, not stage count.

questions.q: Researchers score moral development by the justification participants give for their answer to a dilemma, not by whether they answer yes or no. This reflects Kohlberg's view that:
o: Moral behavior directly predicts moral reasoning
Kohlberg measured reasoning, not behavior.
Children are amoral until adolescence
Children reason at preconventional levels.
Culture determines the order of stages
Kohlberg claimed a universal, fixed order.
The reasoning, not the decision, indicates the stage
Correct: the same choice can be justified at different stages.
questions.x: Kohlberg classified moral development by the structure of reasoning, not the choice made. In the Heinz dilemma, 'steal the drug' can be justified by fear of blame, by duty to family, or by the value of life, which are different stages. So the answer alone cannot place someone in a stage.

questions.q: A tutor gives a student detailed hints on early problems, then gradually removes them as the student gains skill. This is called:
o: Assimilation
Assimilation is fitting new information into existing schemas.
Scaffolding
Correct: temporary support within the ZPD that is withdrawn as competence grows.
Shaping
Shaping reinforces successive approximations of a behavior.
Accommodation
Accommodation is changing schemas to fit new information.
questions.x: Scaffolding is temporary, adjustable support from a more skilled helper that is withdrawn as the learner becomes competent, keeping the task within the zone of proximal development. Shaping is an operant technique that reinforces successive approximations, not a fading of instructional hints.

questions.q: A child playing soccer anticipates what teammates and opponents will do and follows the rules of the game. This best reflects Mead's concept of the:
o: Significant other in the play stage
The play stage involves one specific role at a time.
Imitation in the preparatory stage
This child understands roles, not mere mimicry.
Generalized other in the game stage
Correct: grasping the whole group's expectations at once marks the game stage.
Looking-glass self
That is Cooley's idea about imagined judgments.
questions.x: In Mead's game stage, children grasp the expectations of everyone in an organized activity at once and can anticipate how each role fits together. This internalized sense of the group's or society's expectations is the generalized other. The play stage involves only one specific role at a time.

questions.q: A toddler copies his father's shaving motions without understanding what shaving is for. Which of Mead's stages does this represent?
o: Game stage
The game stage involves understanding multiple roles and rules.
Play stage
The play stage involves taking on roles with some understanding.
Generalized-other stage
This is not a stage name; the generalized other arises in the game stage.
Preparatory stage
Correct: pure imitation without understanding marks the preparatory stage.
questions.x: Mead's preparatory stage is the earliest, when young children simply imitate others' actions without grasping their meaning. Mimicking shaving motions with no idea of its purpose fits this. In the play stage children understand and act out roles, which requires more comprehension.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of Cooley's looking-glass self?
o: Imagining how we appear to others
This is the first component.
Directly learning others' true opinions of us
Correct: the process relies on imagined, not verified, judgments.
Imagining how others judge that appearance
This is the second component.
Developing a self-feeling such as pride or shame
This is the third component.
questions.x: Cooley's looking-glass self has three parts: imagining how we appear to others, imagining their judgment of that appearance, and developing a self-feeling such as pride or shame. The process depends on our perceptions of others' views, which may be wrong, not on learning their actual opinions.

questions.q: Participants rated their own intelligence after viewing profiles of either highly accomplished peers or average peers. Those who viewed the accomplished peers rated themselves lower. This best illustrates:
o: Downward social comparison
Comparing to worse-off others tends to raise self-ratings.
Upward social comparison
Correct: comparison with better-off others lowered self-evaluations.
Self-verification
That is seeking feedback that confirms existing self-views.
Cognitive dissonance
No conflicting cognitions or behaviors are involved.
questions.x: Social comparison theory (Festinger) says we evaluate ourselves by comparing with others. Upward comparison with better-off others tends to lower self-evaluation, while downward comparison with worse-off others tends to raise it. Viewing accomplished peers lowered self-ratings, so this is upward comparison.

questions.q: According to self-discrepancy theory, a gap between one's actual self and ought self is most associated with:
o: Depression and dejection
Those follow an actual vs. ideal self gap.
Pride
Discrepancies produce negative, not positive, emotions.
Apathy
The theory links discrepancies to specific distress, not apathy.
Anxiety and guilt
Correct: falling short of duties and obligations produces agitation.
questions.note: Ideal gap → sadness; ought gap → anxiety.
questions.x: Higgins's self-discrepancy theory distinguishes the ideal self (hopes) from the ought self (duties). Falling short of the ideal self produces dejection-related emotions like sadness, while falling short of the ought self produces agitation-related emotions like anxiety and guilt.

questions.q: A child sorts toys into 'for boys' and 'for girls' and avoids those labeled for the other gender. This child is relying on a:
o: Gender schema
Correct: a cognitive framework organizing the world by gender.
Sexual orientation
Orientation concerns attraction, not toy categorization.
Gender dysphoria
Dysphoria is distress about incongruent gender identity.
Androgynous identity
Androgyny means high levels of both masculine and feminine traits.
questions.x: Gender schema theory (Bem) proposes that children build mental frameworks that sort people, objects and behaviors by gender, then use them to guide their own choices. Labeling toys as 'for boys' or 'for girls' and avoiding the other category reflects such a schema, not attraction or distress.

questions.q: When asked to complete 'I am ___' twenty times, participants from Japan listed more social roles and group memberships than U.S. participants. This best supports the idea that:
o: Individualist cultures foster interdependent selves
Individualist cultures foster independent, trait-based selves.
Collectivist cultures foster interdependent self-construals
Correct: self is defined more by relationships and roles.
Self-esteem is higher in collectivist cultures
The study measured self-descriptions, not self-esteem.
Self-concept is unaffected by culture
The cultural difference contradicts this.
questions.x: Markus and Kitayama distinguished independent self-construals, which define the self by personal traits and are common in individualist cultures, from interdependent self-construals, which define the self by relationships and roles and are common in collectivist cultures such as Japan.

questions.q: Children who saw a model punished for aggression imitated less, but when later offered rewards to imitate, they reproduced the aggression as well as children who saw the model rewarded. This shows that:
o: Learning can occur without being performed
Correct: they had learned the behavior; consequences affected performance.
Punishing a model erases what observers learned
The rewarded test showed the learning was intact.
Imitation requires direct reinforcement of the observer
They learned without being reinforced themselves.
Modeling works only when the model is a peer
The model was an adult.
questions.note: Bandura: acquisition vs. performance.
questions.x: Bandura distinguished acquiring a behavior from performing it. Seeing a model punished suppressed imitation, but offering rewards revealed the children had learned the aggression just as well. Vicarious consequences change motivation to perform, not whether learning occurred.

questions.q: Researchers measure locus of control, then give participants an unsolvable puzzle described as either skill-based or chance-based. Theory predicts which group will persist longest?
o: Internals in the skill condition
Correct: they believe effort determines success on skill tasks.
Externals in the skill condition
Externals expect outcomes to depend little on effort.
Internals in the chance condition
Effort cannot help on a chance task, even for internals.
Externals in the chance condition
Both their disposition and the framing discourage effort.
questions.x: Persistence depends on expecting effort to pay off. Internals believe outcomes reflect their effort, and a skill framing reinforces that belief, so they keep working longest on an unsolvable puzzle. When a task is framed as chance, effort seems pointless even to internals.

questions.q: Before an exam, a student stays out late so that if he does poorly he can blame fatigue rather than lack of ability. This strategy is best described as:
o: Self-verification
Self-verification is seeking feedback that confirms existing self-views, not creating excuses.
Learned helplessness
He is acting strategically, not passively giving up after uncontrollable failure.
Downward social comparison
He is not comparing himself with worse-off others.
Self-handicapping
Correct: creating an obstacle in advance lets failure be blamed on it, protecting self-esteem.
questions.note: Self-handicapping protects self-esteem at the cost of performance.
questions.x: Self-handicapping means creating an obstacle before a performance so that a failure can be blamed on that obstacle rather than on lack of ability. It protects self-esteem at the cost of actual performance. Self-verification is different: it means seeking feedback that confirms existing self-views.

questions.q: Attributing one's successes to ability but one's failures to bad luck mainly serves to:
o: Increase accuracy of self-knowledge
The bias distorts, rather than sharpens, self-knowledge.
Protect self-esteem
Correct: the self-serving bias keeps self-evaluations positive.
Raise self-discrepancy
It reduces, not raises, felt gaps between selves.
Strengthen an external locus of control overall
Successes are credited internally, so it is not a general external orientation.
questions.x: The self-serving bias attributes successes to internal causes like ability and failures to external causes like luck. This pattern protects and enhances self-esteem rather than improving accuracy. Because successes are still credited internally, it is not a general external locus of control.

questions.q: Teachers were told that randomly chosen students were about to 'bloom' intellectually, and those students later showed larger test gains. This best illustrates:
o: Self-fulfilling prophecy
Correct: others' expectations changed behavior and outcomes to match.
Stereotype threat
No negative group stereotype was activated in the students.
Halo effect
Gains appeared on objective tests, not just subjective ratings.
Regression to the mean
Random selection rules out choosing students with extreme scores.
questions.x: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when an expectation leads people to act in ways that make it come true. In the Pygmalion study, teachers' raised expectations for randomly chosen students apparently changed how they treated them. Random selection rules out regression to the mean.

questions.q: Identity theory proposes that a person's many identities are arranged in a hierarchy of salience. The most salient identity is the one that:
o: Is most likely to be enacted across situations
Correct: higher salience means a higher chance of being invoked.
Was assigned at birth
Salience depends on commitment, not on being ascribed.
Is suppressed under stress
Salient identities tend to guide behavior, not vanish.
Is determined only by others' perceptions
Salience reflects one's own commitment to the identity.
questions.x: Identity theory (Stryker) says each person holds many identities ranked in a salience hierarchy. Salience is the likelihood an identity will be invoked across situations, and it rises with commitment to the relationships tied to that identity. Salient identities guide behavior rather than being suppressed.

questions.q: Participants assigned to groups by a coin flip still give more rewards to members of their own group. This finding best supports the claim that:
o: Competition over scarce resources is needed for bias
No real conflict existed between the groups.
Prior friendships drive in-group favoritism
Participants were strangers assigned at random.
People default to equal allocation
They favored their own group.
Mere categorization is enough to produce in-group favoritism
Correct: the minimal group paradigm shows bias from trivial grouping.
questions.x: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm assigned people to groups on trivial or random grounds, with no history, interaction or competition, yet participants still favored their own group. This shows that mere categorization is enough to produce in-group bias, contrary to the idea that real conflict is required.

questions.q: People with negative self-views sometimes prefer friends who see them negatively over friends who see them positively. This is best explained by:
o: Self-verification
Correct: people seek feedback that confirms their existing self-concept.
Self-enhancement
Self-enhancement would favor positive feedback.
Self-handicapping
That creates excuses before performance.
Downward social comparison
That involves comparing with worse-off others.
questions.x: Self-verification theory (Swann) proposes that people seek feedback confirming their existing self-views because consistency feels predictable and controllable, even when the self-view is negative. Self-enhancement predicts the opposite, a preference for positive feedback regardless of self-view.

questions.q: A 5-year-old talks aloud to herself while working through a puzzle. Vygotsky viewed this private speech as:
o: Egocentric speech with no function
That was Piaget's interpretation.
A sign of language delay
Private speech is normal at this age.
A self-regulation tool that later becomes inner speech
Correct: social speech is internalized to guide thought and action.
Mere imitation of parents with no cognitive role
Vygotsky saw it as cognitively important.
questions.x: Vygotsky saw private speech as a tool children use to guide and regulate their own thinking and actions. Speech starts as social exchange, becomes audible self-talk, and is gradually internalized as silent inner speech. Piaget instead treated it as egocentric speech with little function.

questions.q: A key difference between Erikson's and Freud's developmental theories is that Erikson:
o: Emphasized social conflicts spanning the entire lifespan
Correct: Erikson extended development through old age and stressed social relationships.
Rejected stage models of development
Erikson proposed eight stages.
Focused only on childhood sexuality
That describes Freud more closely.
Denied that development involves conflicts
Each Erikson stage is defined by a conflict.
questions.x: Freud's five psychosexual stages end at puberty and focus on sexual drives. Erikson kept a stage model with a conflict at each stage, but stressed social relationships and extended development across the whole lifespan in eight stages, through old age.

questions.q: Successful resolution of Erikson's identity vs. role confusion stage yields which virtue?
o: Hope
Hope comes from trust vs. mistrust.
Fidelity
Correct: fidelity, the ability to stay loyal to commitments, follows identity resolution.
Wisdom
Wisdom comes from integrity vs. despair.
Competence
Competence comes from industry vs. inferiority.
questions.x: Each Erikson stage yields a virtue when resolved: hope (trust), will (autonomy), purpose (initiative), competence (industry), fidelity (identity), love (intimacy), care (generativity) and wisdom (integrity). Fidelity means staying loyal to chosen values and commitments.

questions.q: A citizen argues that an unjust law should be changed through democratic means because laws are agreements meant to serve the common good. Which Kohlberg stage fits best?
o: Law and order
Stage 4 treats laws as fixed duties to uphold.
Good interpersonal relationships
Stage 3 reasons from others' approval.
Social contract
Correct: stage 5 sees laws as changeable agreements for the public good.
Obedience and punishment
Stage 1 reasons from avoiding punishment.
questions.x: Kohlberg's stage 5, social contract, views laws as agreements that serve the common good and that can be changed by democratic means when they fail to. Stage 4 sees laws as fixed duties that maintain order. Stage 6 would appeal to universal principles that may justify disobedience.

questions.q: Researchers find that people in some collectivist societies rarely score at Kohlberg's postconventional stages, yet show sophisticated community-centered moral reasoning. This most directly challenges:
o: The universality of Kohlberg's scoring criteria
Correct: it suggests the stages reflect Western, individualist values.
The order of Erikson's stages
Erikson's theory is not about moral reasoning.
Vygotsky's zone of proximal development
The ZPD concerns guided learning.
Freud's latency stage
Latency concerns psychosexual development.
questions.x: Kohlberg claimed his stages were universal, but his highest stages reflect Western, individualist ideals of rights and justice. Findings that people in collectivist cultures reason in sophisticated community-centered ways yet rarely score as postconventional suggest cultural bias in the scoring.

questions.q: A family abandons its native language and customs in order to fully adopt the host country's culture. This acculturation strategy is:
o: Integration
Integration retains the heritage culture.
Separation
Separation retains the heritage culture and rejects the host.
Assimilation
Correct: the heritage culture is replaced by the host culture.
Multiculturalism
That describes a society valuing many cultures, not this family's choice.
questions.x: In Berry's model, assimilation means giving up the heritage culture and fully adopting the host culture. Integration and separation both keep the heritage culture, differing in whether the host culture is also adopted. Multiculturalism describes a society's policy, not an individual's strategy.

questions.q: In a study, adults watching the same crying infant described it as 'angry' when told it was a boy and 'scared' when told it was a girl. This best illustrates:
o: Biological sex differences in emotion
The infant was identical in both conditions.
Gender constancy in infants
Gender constancy develops in early childhood, not infancy.
The infant's temperament
Temperament was held constant across conditions.
Adults' gender expectations shaping how a child is perceived
Correct: gender socialization begins with others' expectations.
questions.x: In the 'Baby X' design, adults saw the same infant behavior but interpreted it differently depending on the gender label. Because the infant was identical, the difference must come from adults' gender expectations, showing gender socialization begins with how others perceive a child.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy says he will turn into a girl if he grows his hair long. He has not yet developed:
o: Gender constancy
Correct: understanding that gender is stable across appearance changes.
Object permanence
He knows objects persist; this concerns gender stability.
Sexual orientation
Orientation concerns attraction, not gender stability.
Gender expression
He clearly expresses gender; he misunderstands its permanence.
questions.x: Gender constancy is the understanding that one's gender stays the same despite changes in appearance or activities, usually achieved around ages 5 to 7. A 3-year-old who thinks long hair would turn him into a girl lacks it. Gender expression concerns outward presentation, which he already shows.

questions.q: Among cardiac patients with similar disease severity, those with higher exercise self-efficacy attended more rehab sessions. What most limits causal conclusions?
o: Patients were randomly assigned
They were not, and random assignment would strengthen causal claims.
The study was double-blind
Blinding would not weaken causal inference.
Self-efficacy was measured, not manipulated
Correct: a correlational design cannot rule out confounds or reverse causation.
The sample was too homogeneous in severity
Matching on severity controls a confound; it does not limit causality.
questions.x: The study observed naturally occurring self-efficacy and attendance, so it is correlational. Without manipulating self-efficacy, a third variable such as motivation or social support could drive both, or attending rehab could raise efficacy. Matching on severity controls one confound but not all.

questions.q: Researchers find that global self-esteem correlates only weakly with exam scores, whereas academic self-efficacy correlates more strongly. Which explanation fits best?
o: Self-esteem is unrelated to the self-concept
Self-esteem is the evaluative part of the self-concept.
Self-efficacy is the same construct as self-esteem
The different correlations suggest distinct constructs.
Task-specific beliefs predict task-specific outcomes better than global worth
Correct: efficacy is tied to the domain being measured.
High self-esteem causes poor exam performance
A weak positive correlation does not imply harm.
questions.x: Specific attitudes predict specific outcomes better than global ones. Academic self-efficacy is tied to the very domain being tested, while global self-esteem is a broad sense of worth that is only loosely linked to any single performance. Different correlations mean distinct constructs.

questions.q: A teen deliberately adopts styles and opinions opposite to those of a clique he dislikes. For him, that clique serves as a:
o: Primary group
A primary group involves close, enduring personal ties.
In-group
He does not identify as a member.
Secondary group
Secondary groups are large, impersonal and goal-oriented.
Negative reference group
Correct: a group whose norms one defines oneself against.
questions.x: A reference group can work in either direction. A positive reference group sets standards to emulate, while a negative reference group is one whose norms a person deliberately rejects to define who they are not. He neither belongs to nor emulates the clique, so it is a negative reference group.

questions.q: Adolescents' self-ratings of competence correlated more strongly with what they believed their parents thought of them than with parents' actual ratings. This best supports:
o: Cooley's looking-glass self
Correct: perceived, not actual, appraisals shape self-views.
Bandura's reciprocal determinism
The finding concerns imagined appraisals, not interacting factors.
Marcia's identity statuses
No exploration or commitment was measured.
Rotter's locus of control
No attributions of control were measured.
questions.x: Cooley's looking-glass self predicts self-views track imagined appraisals, what we think others think of us, rather than their actual opinions. The finding that teens' self-ratings matched perceived parental views more than parents' real ratings supports exactly this.

questions.q: Piaget held that development must precede learning. Vygotsky instead held that:
o: Development must be complete before any learning
That is close to Piaget's view.
Development is fixed by genetics alone
Vygotsky emphasized social and cultural influences.
Learning through social interaction leads development
Correct: guided learning in the ZPD pulls development forward.
Only adolescents can learn from peers
Vygotsky applied his ideas across childhood.
questions.x: Piaget held that children must reach a developmental stage before they can learn related concepts. Vygotsky reversed this: learning through guided social interaction within the zone of proximal development pulls development forward, so instruction should aim slightly ahead of current ability.

questions.q: In attribution theory, explaining a behavior by pointing to a person's traits, abilities or character is called what?
o: A situational attribution
Situational attributions point to external circumstances, not traits.
A stable-external attribution
External causes are situational, so this cannot describe a trait-based explanation.
A self-serving attribution
Self-serving bias is a pattern across outcomes, not the label for any trait explanation.
A dispositional attribution
Correct: dispositional (internal) attributions locate the cause inside the person.
questions.note: Dispositional = internal; situational = external.
questions.x: Attribution theory sorts explanations of behavior by where the cause is located. A dispositional (internal) attribution places it inside the person: traits, abilities, effort or character. A situational (external) attribution places it in circumstances. Self-serving bias is not a type of attribution but a pattern of choosing internal causes for success and external causes for failure.

questions.q: Kelley's covariation model predicts a situational attribution when a behavior shows which combination of consensus, distinctiveness and consistency?
o: Low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency
This pattern points to the person, a dispositional attribution.
High consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency
Correct: everyone does it, only in this situation, reliably, so the situation is the cause.
High consensus, low distinctiveness, low consistency
Low consistency suggests a fluke or transient circumstance, not a clear situational cause.
Low consensus, high distinctiveness, low consistency
Low consistency undermines any stable attribution.
questions.note: Trap: low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency = dispositional.
questions.x: Kelley's covariation model uses three cues. High consensus (others act the same way), high distinctiveness (the person acts this way only toward this stimulus) and high consistency (it happens reliably) point to the situation or stimulus. Low consensus and low distinctiveness with high consistency point to the person. Low consistency suggests a passing circumstance rather than a stable cause.

questions.q: Mateo laughs loudly at every comedian, while few other audience members laugh at tonight's act, and he always laughs this way. By Kelley's model, observers will most likely attribute his laughter to what?
o: Something about the comedian
A stimulus attribution needs high consensus and high distinctiveness.
Something about Mateo
Correct: low consensus, low distinctiveness and high consistency yield a person attribution.
A temporary circumstance
Transient-circumstance attributions follow low consistency, but his laughter is consistent.
The audience's mood that night
Low consensus means the rest of the audience is not reacting the same way.
questions.x: Mateo laughs at every comedian (low distinctiveness), few others laugh at this act (low consensus), and he always does it (high consistency). That combination tells observers the behavior comes from Mateo himself. A stimulus attribution to the comedian would require that most people laugh at this act and that Mateo laughs at this act but not others.

questions.q: Researchers have participants read an essay they are told was assigned to the writer by a coin flip. Participants still rate the writer's true attitude as matching the essay. What does this most directly demonstrate?
o: Actor-observer bias
Actor-observer bias needs a comparison of self versus other explanations.
Cognitive dissonance
Dissonance concerns one's own inconsistent cognitions, not judging another's essay.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation is shown to change the writer's actual behavior.
Correspondence bias
Correct: people infer an attitude matching behavior even when the behavior was externally forced.
questions.note: Correspondence bias is another name for the fundamental attribution error.
questions.x: In this classic design, observers know the essay position was imposed, yet they still infer the writer holds that attitude. Inferring a disposition that corresponds to behavior despite obvious situational constraints is the correspondence bias, another name for the fundamental attribution error. Actor-observer bias would require comparing how people explain their own behavior versus others'.

questions.q: The self-serving bias is generally thought to serve which psychological function?
o: Reducing cognitive load during social judgments
Load reduction explains heuristics like stereotyping, not motivated self-attributions.
Protecting and enhancing self-esteem
Correct: taking credit for success and deflecting blame for failure preserves self-worth.
Increasing accuracy of self-assessment
The bias distorts self-assessment rather than improving it.
Strengthening in-group cohesion
That is closer to the group-serving bias, not the individual self-serving bias.
questions.x: The self-serving bias is usually explained as motivated reasoning that protects and enhances self-esteem: credit for success boosts self-worth and blaming circumstances for failure shields it. Because it distorts reality, it reduces rather than increases accuracy. Cognitive shortcuts that save effort, such as heuristics, are a different, cold-cognition explanation for bias.

questions.q: Researchers find that participants who score high on belief in a just world rate an innocent victim of random violence as less likable after learning the perpetrator was never caught. Which explanation best fits?
o: Unresolved crimes trigger stereotype threat in observers
Stereotype threat affects members of stereotyped groups during performance.
Participants are showing the self-serving bias
The outcome is not about the participants' own success or failure.
The halo effect reverses when a crime is unsolved
The halo effect is trait spreading, unrelated to justice concerns.
Derogating the victim restores the belief that the world is fair
Correct: if justice cannot be restored, devaluing the victim makes the outcome seem deserved.
questions.note: Just-world beliefs are strongest when victims' suffering cannot be fixed.
questions.x: When an injustice cannot be corrected, for example because the perpetrator is never caught, people with strong just-world beliefs face a threat to the idea that the world is fair. Derogating the victim resolves it: if the victim is less worthy, the outcome seems less unjust. The self-serving bias does not apply because the participants' own successes or failures are not at stake.

questions.q: Compared with people from individualist cultures, people from collectivist cultures are on average more likely to do what when explaining others' behavior?
o: Rely exclusively on dispositional traits
No group relies only on traits; a stronger dispositional emphasis is typical of individualist cultures.
Show a stronger self-serving bias
Self-serving bias tends to be weaker, not stronger, in collectivist samples.
Ignore social roles and relationships
Collectivist thinking emphasizes roles and relationships.
Weigh situational and contextual factors
Correct: collectivist cultures emphasize context and roles, reducing the FAE.
questions.x: Collectivist cultures emphasize interdependence, roles and relationships, so people there more readily consider situational and contextual causes of others' behavior and show a weaker fundamental attribution error. Individualist cultures emphasize the autonomous self and lean toward dispositional explanations. No culture relies exclusively on traits, and self-serving bias also tends to be weaker in collectivist samples.

questions.q: A content analysis compared English-language American newspapers and Chinese-language newspapers covering the same murders. The American papers emphasized the killer's personality, while the Chinese-language papers emphasized circumstances and relationships. This finding best supports which claim?
o: The fundamental attribution error is biologically fixed
Cross-cultural variation argues against a fixed, invariant bias.
East Asian writers show a stronger actor-observer bias
Both sets of reports explained another person's behavior; no self-versus-other comparison was made.
The fundamental attribution error is shaped by culture
Correct: dispositional emphasis varied with cultural background, so the bias is not universal in strength.
American writers show stronger stereotype threat
Stereotype threat concerns performance, not newspaper explanations.
questions.x: If the fundamental attribution error were a fixed, universal feature of cognition, coverage of the same events should show similar dispositional emphasis everywhere. Instead, American reports stressed personality while Chinese-language reports stressed context, showing that culture shapes how strongly people favor trait explanations. Actor-observer bias is ruled out because no one compared explanations of their own behavior.

questions.q: A landlord privately dislikes a certain ethnic group but rents to its members on equal terms because of fair-housing laws. This landlord shows what?
o: Prejudice without discrimination
Correct: a negative attitude is present, but treatment is equal.
Discrimination without prejudice
There is a negative attitude, and no unequal treatment occurs.
Institutional discrimination
Institutional discrimination is embedded in policies; none disadvantages the group here.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is experienced by the stereotyped, not the holder of prejudice.
questions.x: Prejudice (an attitude) and discrimination (a behavior) do not always go together. This landlord holds a negative attitude but treats tenants equally because the law constrains behavior, which is prejudice without discrimination. The reverse case, discrimination without prejudice, occurs when unequal treatment comes from rules or pressure rather than personal dislike.

questions.q: A company that holds no negative views of any group requires applicants to have graduated from a few private schools that historically excluded certain minorities. The resulting hiring disparity best exemplifies what?
o: Individual prejudice
The stem specifies that decision makers hold no negative attitudes.
Stereotype threat
No one is underperforming due to a stereotype reminder.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation is shaping applicants' behavior here.
Institutional discrimination
Correct: a neutral-seeming policy produces unequal outcomes without individual prejudice.
questions.note: Discrimination can exist without prejudice when it is built into rules.
questions.x: Institutional discrimination occurs when policies, practices or structures produce unequal outcomes for groups, even when no individual decision maker holds prejudiced attitudes. Requiring degrees from schools that historically excluded minorities carries past exclusion forward. Individual prejudice is ruled out by the stem, which specifies that the company holds no negative views.

questions.q: Which result would most strongly support the claim that stereotype threat works partly by consuming working memory?
o: Threatened participants report liking the test less
Liking is not a measure of working memory.
Non-stereotyped participants score equally in both conditions
This shows the effect is group-specific, not how it works.
Threatened participants spend more time on the first question
Time spent does not directly measure working memory capacity.
Threatened participants show lower working memory span, which statistically accounts for their lower scores
Correct: a mediator that explains the effect supports the proposed mechanism.
questions.note: Mechanism questions need a mediator, not just the main effect.
questions.x: Testing a mechanism requires showing a mediator: the proposed process must change with the manipulation and must statistically account for the effect on the outcome. Lower working memory span that explains the score drop does exactly that. Showing that only stereotyped groups are affected, or that people dislike the test, confirms the effect exists but not how it operates.

questions.q: Researchers randomly label some students as 'expected bloomers' and tell their teachers. At year's end, labeled students show larger gains. Why is random assignment of the label essential to the conclusion?
o: It guarantees that teachers will not discover the deception
Randomization does not affect whether the deception is detected.
It ensures differences in gains are due to teacher expectations rather than preexisting student ability
Correct: randomization rules out the labels simply tracking real differences.
It makes the sample representative of all schools
Representativeness comes from random sampling, not random assignment.
It eliminates the need for a control group
The unlabeled students serve as the control group.
questions.note: Random assignment = internal validity; random sampling = external validity.
questions.x: Random assignment makes the labeled and unlabeled students equivalent on average in ability and motivation, so a later difference in gains can be attributed to the manipulated teacher expectation. This protects internal validity. Random sampling is the tempting confusion: it concerns whether the sample represents the population, which affects external validity, not causal inference.

questions.q: In a summer camp study, two groups of boys became hostile while competing for prizes. Hostility dropped most when they had to cooperate to fix the camp's broken water supply. Which concept explains the reduction?
o: Superordinate goals
Correct: shared goals requiring both groups' cooperation reduce intergroup conflict.
Mere contact
Simple contact during competition had not reduced hostility.
Deindividuation
Deindividuation increases, not reduces, antisocial group behavior.
Social loafing
Social loafing is reduced individual effort in groups.
questions.note: Contact helps most with equal status and shared goals.
questions.x: In the Robbers Cave study, competition created intergroup hostility, and simple contact such as shared meals did not reduce it. Hostility dropped when the groups faced superordinate goals, problems that neither group could solve alone and that required cooperation. Mere contact is the tempting answer, but contact helps only under conditions like shared goals and equal status.

questions.q: Students told a guest lecturer was 'rather cold' rated him less favorably and asked fewer questions than students told he was 'very warm,' though all saw the same lecture. What does the difference in questions suggest?
o: Impressions can influence behavior toward the target, not just ratings
Correct: expectations changed how students interacted with him.
The lecturer gave different lectures to each group
The stem states all students saw the same lecture.
Students showed the self-serving bias
Students were not explaining their own outcomes.
Warm and cold are peripheral traits
The large effect shows they act as central traits.
questions.x: Because everyone saw the same lecture, the only difference was the label. Students expecting a cold lecturer both rated him lower and asked fewer questions, showing that impressions shape actual behavior toward a person, not just private judgments. This behavioral effect is the first step of a self-fulfilling prophecy, since the target may respond to the reduced engagement.

questions.q: A manager sees an employee yawning and assumes he is lazy, never considering that he worked a night shift. What would most reduce this error?
o: Relying on first impressions
First impressions often drive the error rather than correct it.
Increasing cognitive load while judging
Load makes people rely more on dispositional shortcuts.
Considering situational explanations before judging
Correct: deliberate attention to context counters the fundamental attribution error.
Observing the employee for less time
Less information tends to increase reliance on trait inferences.
questions.x: The manager commits the fundamental attribution error by inferring a trait (laziness) while ignoring an obvious situational cause (a night shift). Deliberately generating situational explanations counteracts this, because correcting a trait inference requires effortful thought. Distraction, less information or reliance on first impressions all increase dependence on quick trait judgments.

questions.q: Participants judge a speaker's anxiety while silently memorizing a long number or not. Those memorizing rely more on the speaker's visible fidgeting and ignore a stressful topic. Which model best explains this?
o: A purely situational model of attribution
The results show more, not less, dispositional reliance.
A two-step model: automatic trait inference followed by effortful situational correction
Correct: cognitive load blocks the effortful correction step.
The just-world hypothesis
No fairness judgment about outcomes is made.
Social facilitation theory
Social facilitation concerns performance in front of others.
questions.note: Load makes the FAE worse: correction for situation takes effort.
questions.x: Two-step models of attribution propose that people automatically infer a trait from behavior and then, if they have the cognitive resources, effortfully correct for situational causes. Memorizing a number consumes those resources, so participants stop at the trait inference and ignore the stressful topic. The results show greater dispositional reliance, ruling out a purely situational account.

questions.q: Primacy usually dominates impression formation. Under which condition is a recency effect most likely instead?
o: All information is presented rapidly in one session
Rapid single presentation typically favors primacy.
The perceiver is distracted during the later information
Distraction during later information would reduce its impact.
A long delay separates the two sets of information and judgment follows the second set
Correct: delay weakens the first information, so the most recent dominates.
The first information is especially vivid
Vivid early information strengthens primacy.
questions.x: Primacy usually wins because early information shapes how later information is interpreted. When a long delay separates the first and second sets and the judgment is made right after the second, the earlier information has faded from memory, so the most recent information dominates. Distraction during the later information would weaken it, which favors primacy rather than recency.

questions.q: According to Weiner's attribution model, a student who attributes failure to low ability rather than low effort is most likely to do what?
o: Expect future failure and feel less motivated
Correct: ability is stable and uncontrollable, so failure seems likely to repeat.
Study harder for the next exam
That follows an unstable, controllable attribution such as effort.
Blame the teacher for unfair grading
That is an external attribution, not low ability.
Expect future success because luck will change
That follows a luck attribution.
questions.note: Stability of the cause predicts expectations for the future.
questions.x: In Weiner's model, stability predicts expectations about the future. Low ability is internal, stable and uncontrollable, so the student expects failure to repeat and loses motivation, a pattern linked to learned helplessness. Attributing failure to low effort, which is unstable and controllable, instead predicts working harder next time.

questions.q: When an out-group member performs a positive act, prejudiced observers often say it was luck or an exception. Which bias does this describe?
o: Self-serving bias
Self-serving bias concerns one's own outcomes, not out-group members'.
Ultimate attribution error
Correct: out-group positives are explained away situationally, negatives attributed to disposition.
False consensus effect
False consensus is overestimating agreement with one's views.
Recency effect
No order of information is involved.
questions.x: The ultimate attribution error applies attribution bias to whole groups. Negative acts by out-group members are attributed to disposition, while positive acts are explained away as luck, special circumstances or exceptions. This lets prejudiced beliefs survive disconfirming evidence. Self-serving bias is similar in structure but concerns explanations of one's own outcomes.

questions.q: Participants randomly assigned to watch either a frightening or a neutral film clip then rate the same set of ambiguous faces. Those who saw the frightening clip rate the faces as more hostile. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The faces in the frightening condition were objectively more hostile
The same ambiguous faces were used in both conditions.
Frightening films cause permanent hostility
A single short session cannot show permanent effects.
The perceiver's emotional state can bias social perception
Correct: random assignment to clips links mood to face ratings.
Perceivers in the neutral condition showed stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect, not a rating of faces.
questions.x: Because participants were randomly assigned and rated the same faces, the only systematic difference was the clip, which altered their emotional state. Mood therefore biased how they interpreted ambiguous social cues, showing that the perceiver's internal state shapes social perception. A single brief session cannot support claims about permanent effects.

questions.q: Perceiving a relationship between two variables, such as a minority group and a rare behavior, when none exists is called what?
o: Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is seeking supporting evidence for existing beliefs.
Base-rate fallacy
The base-rate fallacy ignores prior probabilities in judgments.
Illusory correlation
Correct: distinctive pairings seem related even when they are not.
Belief perseverance
Belief perseverance is clinging to beliefs after they are discredited.
questions.x: An illusory correlation is perceiving a relationship between two variables that are unrelated or only weakly related. It is especially likely when two distinctive or rare things co-occur, such as a minority group and an uncommon behavior, because those pairings are memorable. Confirmation bias can maintain such beliefs, but it describes selective search for supporting evidence, not the perception of a link itself.

questions.q: Participants read statements about two groups. Group A is described in twice as many statements as Group B, and in both groups undesirable behaviors are a minority of statements in the same proportion. Participants rate Group B more negatively. What best explains this?
o: Group B actually showed more undesirable behaviors per member
The proportions were identical.
Pairing a minority group with infrequent behaviors creates an illusory correlation
Correct: two distinctive things co-occurring stand out and seem linked.
Participants showed out-group homogeneity for Group A
No in-group/out-group distinction was established.
Participants showed a recency effect
Information order was not manipulated.
questions.note: Distinctiveness-based illusory correlation helps explain how stereotypes form.
questions.x: This is the distinctiveness-based illusory correlation. Statements about the smaller group are rarer, and undesirable behaviors are rarer, so their co-occurrence is doubly distinctive and better remembered. Participants then overestimate how often Group B acted badly although the proportions were identical. Option A is ruled out by design, which held the proportion of undesirable behavior constant.

questions.q: When a prejudiced person meets a friendly, competent member of a disliked group, he labels her 'an exception' and keeps his stereotype. This process is called what?
o: Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect on the stereotyped person.
Superordinate goal formation
Superordinate goals reduce conflict through cooperation.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation is changing the target's behavior.
Subtyping
Correct: disconfirming members are placed in a special subcategory so the stereotype survives.
questions.x: Subtyping places stereotype-disconfirming individuals into a separate subcategory, such as 'the exception,' so the overall stereotype remains intact. It is a major reason stereotypes resist change after contact with individual counterexamples. Changing stereotypes works better when disconfirming information is spread across many typical group members rather than concentrated in a few.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that dominant groups promote stereotypes of subordinate groups because those beliefs justify unequal access to wealth and status. Which processes does this argument emphasize as sources of prejudice?
o: Power, prestige and class
Correct: prejudice is seen as maintaining existing hierarchies.
Individual cognitive limitations
The argument focuses on group interests, not mental shortcuts.
Random variation in personality
The argument is structural, not about individual personality.
Biological threat detection
The argument is about social hierarchy, not evolved fear.
questions.x: Conflict and structural perspectives hold that prejudice serves dominant groups by justifying unequal access to resources: stereotypes rationalize hierarchies of power, prestige and class. This places the origin of prejudice in social structure and group interests. Cognitive limitations are a valid source of stereotyping, but they are an individual-level explanation that the argument does not emphasize.

questions.q: A man diagnosed with depression begins to believe he is weak and worthless because of his diagnosis, and stops seeking help. This illustrates what?
o: Public stigma
Public stigma is others' negative attitudes, not his own internalization.
Stereotype lift
Stereotype lift is improved performance from comparison with a stereotyped out-group.
Courtesy stigma
Courtesy stigma affects people associated with a stigmatized person.
Self-stigma
Correct: the person internalizes negative societal views about his condition.
questions.x: Self-stigma occurs when a person internalizes society's negative stereotypes about a condition and applies them to himself, lowering self-esteem and reducing help seeking. Public stigma is the tempting alternative, but it refers to the general public's negative attitudes, not the person's own internalization. Courtesy stigma affects those associated with the stigmatized person.

questions.q: A researcher finds that patients who strongly endorse negative beliefs about mental illness skip more therapy appointments. Which conclusion is justified by this finding alone?
o: Negative beliefs cause patients to skip appointments
Correlation alone cannot establish causation.
Endorsement of these beliefs is associated with missing appointments
Correct: a correlational finding supports only an association.
Skipping appointments causes negative beliefs
Reverse causation cannot be confirmed either.
Stigma has no effect on treatment
The data show an association, contradicting no relationship.
questions.x: This is a correlational finding: belief endorsement and missed appointments were measured, not manipulated. Correlation supports an association but not the direction of causation, since beliefs might cause missed sessions, missed sessions might reinforce beliefs, or a third variable such as symptom severity might drive both. Concluding that beliefs cause skipping is the tempting overreach.

questions.q: A person scores low on a self-report prejudice scale but shows strong automatic bias on a reaction-time test. What does this pattern best suggest?
o: Explicit and implicit attitudes can diverge
Correct: conscious self-reports and automatic associations are distinct.
The self-report scale measured implicit bias
Self-report scales measure explicit attitudes.
The person must be lying on the questionnaire
Implicit bias can exist without awareness, so lying is not required.
Reaction-time tests cannot detect bias
The test did detect a bias in this case.
questions.x: Explicit attitudes are consciously endorsed and measured by self-report, while implicit attitudes are automatic associations measured indirectly, such as by reaction times. The two can diverge, so a person can sincerely report low prejudice and still show automatic bias. Lying is the tempting explanation, but implicit associations can exist without awareness, so no deception is required.

questions.q: A person who sincerely endorses equality avoids an out-group member only in ambiguous situations where a nonracial excuse is available. This pattern is best described as what?
o: Overt discrimination
Overt discrimination is open and does not depend on available excuses.
Institutional discrimination
Institutional discrimination arises from policies, not individual avoidance.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is understanding practices in context.
Aversive racism
Correct: egalitarian self-image coexists with subtle bias that appears when it can be justified.
questions.x: Aversive racism describes people who sincerely hold egalitarian values yet harbor unacknowledged negative feelings. Their bias appears mainly when behavior can be attributed to a nonracial reason, which protects their egalitarian self-image. Overt discrimination is open and does not depend on such excuses, and institutional discrimination comes from policies rather than individual avoidance.

questions.q: Which element is required for an outcome to count as a self-fulfilling prophecy rather than an accurate prediction?
o: The expectation must be negative
Self-fulfilling prophecies can be positive or negative.
The expectation itself causes behavior that produces the outcome
Correct: the prediction must play a causal role in making itself true.
The target must know about the expectation
Targets often never learn the expectation.
The expectation must be based on a stereotype
Any expectation, stereotyped or not, can be self-fulfilling.
questions.x: A self-fulfilling prophecy requires that the expectation causally produces its own confirmation, usually by changing the expecter's behavior, which then changes the target's behavior. An accurate prediction merely forecasts what would have happened anyway. Expectations can be positive or negative, and the target need not know about them.

questions.q: White male math majors told that a test compares their scores with Asian students' scores perform worse than controls. What does this suggest about stereotype threat?
o: It only affects historically disadvantaged groups
This result shows a non-disadvantaged group affected.
It depends on actual differences in math ability
The groups were not shown to differ in true ability.
It only occurs on verbal tests
The test here was a math test.
It can affect any group facing an unfavorable comparison stereotype
Correct: even high-status groups are vulnerable when a relevant stereotype applies.
questions.x: Stereotype threat is not limited to historically disadvantaged groups. Highly skilled white male math students performed worse when told they were being compared with Asian students, a group stereotyped as better at math. Any group can be affected when a negative comparison stereotype becomes relevant, showing the effect is driven by the situation rather than by true ability differences.

questions.q: Non-stereotyped participants sometimes perform slightly better when a negative stereotype about an out-group is made salient. This is called what?
o: Stereotype threat
Threat lowers performance of the stereotyped group.
Social loafing
Social loafing is reduced effort in groups.
Stereotype lift
Correct: downward comparison with a stereotyped out-group boosts performance.
Golem effect
The Golem effect is lowered performance from low expectations.
questions.x: Stereotype lift is a small performance boost in members of a non-stereotyped group when a negative stereotype about an out-group is made salient, likely from favorable downward comparison. It is the mirror image of stereotype threat, which lowers the performance of the stereotyped group. Both depend on the stereotype being relevant to the task.

questions.q: A critic argues that strict cultural relativism makes it impossible to condemn practices that cause serious harm. Which position responds most directly to this critique?
o: Cultural relativism as a research method need not imply that all practices are morally acceptable
Correct: methodological relativism (understanding) differs from moral relativism (approval).
Ethnocentrism is the only defensible alternative
Rejecting extreme relativism does not require judging everything by one's own culture.
Harmful practices do not exist in any culture
This denies the premise rather than addressing the critique.
Cultural relativism requires adopting other cultures' practices
Relativism concerns understanding, not adoption.
questions.x: Methodological cultural relativism is a research stance: understanding a practice within its cultural context before judging it. It does not require moral relativism, the view that no practice can be judged wrong. Separating understanding from approval answers the critique without retreating to ethnocentrism, which would judge everything by one's own culture.

questions.q: One explanation for the actor-observer bias is perceptual salience. Which finding best supports this account?
o: Actors know more about their own past behavior than observers do
That supports an informational account, not salience.
Observers make more dispositional attributions for liked targets
Liking is a motivational factor, not visual salience.
When actors watch a video of themselves from the observer's viewpoint, they make more dispositional self-attributions
Correct: changing visual perspective changes attributions, showing the role of what is salient.
Actors make more self-serving attributions after failure
That describes self-serving bias.
questions.x: The perceptual salience account says actors explain their behavior situationally because the situation fills their visual field, while observers see the actor as most salient. Storms showed that when actors watched a video from the observer's viewpoint, their self-attributions became more dispositional. The informational account, that actors know more about their own history, is a different explanation.

questions.q: In a study, participants randomly assigned to write trivia questions stumped others assigned to answer them. Observers then rated the question writers as more knowledgeable. Why is this an example of the fundamental attribution error?
o: Question writers truly knew more than answerers
Roles were randomly assigned, so knowledge should not differ systematically.
Observers ignored the role advantage of writing questions from one's own knowledge
Correct: the situation, not greater intelligence, produced the apparent difference.
Observers attributed the result to the difficulty of the questions
That would be a situational attribution, the opposite of the FAE.
Answerers credited their own failures to bad luck
That is self-serving bias, and the stem concerns observers.
questions.x: Question writers drew on their own idiosyncratic knowledge, a built-in role advantage, so their apparent superiority came from the situation. Because roles were randomly assigned, the groups did not differ in actual knowledge. Observers who rated writers as more knowledgeable attributed a situational advantage to disposition, the fundamental attribution error.

questions.q: Jurors who see themselves as similar to an accident victim assign the victim less blame than jurors who see themselves as dissimilar. This best illustrates what?
o: Just-world hypothesis
The just-world view predicts more victim blame, regardless of similarity.
Out-group homogeneity
No perception of group sameness is measured.
Stereotype threat
Jurors are not performing in a stereotyped domain.
Defensive attribution
Correct: blaming a similar victim would imply one could be blamed too.
questions.x: Defensive attribution is assigning blame in a way that protects oneself from the idea of being blamed or harmed in a similar situation. Jurors who see themselves as similar to the victim blame the victim less, because blaming someone like themselves would imply they could be blamed too. Just-world reasoning predicts victim blaming generally and does not explain the role of similarity.

questions.q: American and Chinese participants view an animated fish swimming ahead of a group. Americans more often say the lead fish is leading by its own choice; Chinese participants more often say the group is pushing or chasing it. What does this best illustrate?
o: Cultural differences in visual acuity
Both groups saw the same display; interpretation differed, not acuity.
Cultural differences in emphasis on context in explaining behavior
Correct: holistic thinkers attend to the group and situation.
Stereotype threat in the Japanese participants
No stereotype about performance was activated.
A primacy effect in the American participants
No order of information was manipulated.
questions.x: Both groups saw the same display, so the difference lies in interpretation. Americans, from an individualist culture, explained the lead fish's movement by its internal dispositions; Chinese participants, from a more collectivist culture, attended to the group as a contextual cause. This parallels the weaker fundamental attribution error found in cultures that emphasize context and relationships.

questions.q: An orchestra begins auditioning musicians behind a screen so judges hear but cannot see them. The share of women advancing rises, while the applicant pool is unchanged. What does this finding most strongly suggest?
o: Women improved as musicians once screens were introduced
The screen changed what judges knew, not how well people played.
Evaluators' knowledge of gender had biased earlier decisions
Correct: removing gender cues changed outcomes for equal performances.
Screens produced stereotype threat in men
No stereotype about performance was activated in men.
Women's applications fell after screens were introduced
The stem states the applicant pool did not change, so the rise is not about who applied.
questions.x: A screen hides the performer's identity without changing the sound. If women advance more often once judges cannot see them, while the applicant pool is the same, then knowing the performer's gender was influencing earlier evaluations. This is a classic blind-evaluation logic for detecting bias. The tempting alternative, that women played better, is ruled out because the screen changes only what judges know.

questions.q: A study finds that patients from a minority group receive less pain medication than majority-group patients with identical documented pain scores. Which additional finding would best indicate the disparity reflects provider bias?
o: Minority patients report pain more often
Pain scores were already identical.
Providers with stronger implicit bias scores show larger treatment gaps
Correct: linking individual bias to the size of the gap supports a bias explanation.
Majority patients have more insurance coverage
That suggests a structural confound, not provider bias.
The hospital has a diverse staff
Staff diversity alone does not test whether bias drives the gap.
questions.x: Showing that provider bias drives a disparity requires linking a measure of bias to the outcome. If providers with stronger implicit bias show larger treatment gaps, the gap tracks the proposed cause, supporting the bias explanation. Insurance differences are tempting, but they point to a structural confound rather than to the providers' own biases.

questions.q: According to the stereotype content model, a group seen as highly competent but low in warmth is most likely to elicit what?
o: Pity
Pity is elicited by groups seen as warm but incompetent.
Contempt
Contempt is elicited by groups seen as low on both dimensions.
Admiration
Admiration is reserved for groups high on both dimensions.
Envy
Correct: high competence and low warmth produce envious prejudice.
questions.x: In the stereotype content model, high-competence, low-warmth groups are seen as capable but cold or threatening, eliciting envy, a mix of resentment and grudging respect. Warm but incompetent groups elicit pity, groups low on both elicit contempt, and groups high on both elicit admiration. Envious prejudice can turn into hostility during social instability.

questions.q: Two rival departments are encouraged to see themselves as one company team. Bias between them decreases. Which model best explains this?
o: Common in-group identity model
Correct: recategorizing 'us' and 'them' as 'we' reduces intergroup bias.
Realistic conflict theory
That explains how conflict arises from competition, not how recategorization reduces it.
Frustration-aggression hypothesis
That explains scapegoating, not bias reduction.
Implicit personality theory
That concerns beliefs about which traits co-occur.
questions.x: The common in-group identity model proposes that intergroup bias decreases when members of different groups recategorize themselves into one inclusive group, turning 'us and them' into 'we.' In-group favoritism then extends to former out-group members. Realistic conflict theory is tempting because it concerns rivalry, but it explains how conflict arises rather than how recategorization reduces bias.

questions.q: People judge a likable in-group member more favorably than a similar out-group member, but judge an unlikable in-group member more harshly than a similar out-group member. This is called what?
o: Out-group homogeneity
That concerns perceived sameness of out-group members.
Ultimate attribution error
That concerns explaining out-group behavior, not punishing in-group deviants.
Group polarization
That concerns attitude extremity after discussion.
Black sheep effect
Correct: deviant in-group members are derogated to protect the group's image.
questions.x: The black sheep effect is the tendency to judge likable in-group members more favorably but unlikable in-group members more harshly than comparable out-group members. Derogating deviant in-group members protects the group's positive image, consistent with social identity theory. The ultimate attribution error concerns explaining out-group behavior, not punishing in-group deviants.

questions.q: In a resource allocation task, participants choose between giving both groups more points or giving their own group fewer points but a larger margin over the other group. Many choose the larger margin. What does this suggest?
o: Participants were motivated purely by self-interest
Self-interest would favor the higher absolute payoff.
Participants showed cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is unrelated to point allocation.
Participants were trying to be fair
Fairness would favor equal allocation.
In-group favoritism can center on relative advantage rather than absolute gain
Correct: maximizing difference matters more than maximizing the in-group's own total.
questions.x: In Tajfel's allocation matrices, many participants chose options that maximized the difference between groups even when this cost their own group points. This shows that in-group favoritism can center on relative standing rather than absolute gain, consistent with social identity theory's emphasis on positive distinctiveness. Pure self-interest would choose the option giving the in-group the most points.

questions.q: Participants rate essays paired with a photo of either an attractive or an unattractive author. Essays from the 'attractive' author receive higher quality ratings. Which change would best strengthen the conclusion that attractiveness caused the difference?
o: Using the same essay across photo conditions with random assignment
Correct: identical essays and random assignment isolate the photo as the cause.
Letting participants choose which essay to read
Self-selection would introduce confounds.
Using different essays for each photo
Different essays would confound quality with photo condition.
Telling participants the hypothesis beforehand
This would create demand characteristics.
questions.x: To show that the photo causes higher ratings, everything except the photo must be identical. Using the same essay in both conditions removes essay quality as a confound, and random assignment equalizes participant differences between conditions.
