Using different essays for each photo is the tempting error because it confounds quality with attractiveness.

questions.q: In a simulation, participants must quickly 'shoot' armed targets and not unarmed ones. They mistakenly shoot unarmed Black targets more often than unarmed White targets. Which conclusion is most justified?
o: Participants hold conscious hostility toward Black people
Errors under time pressure do not demonstrate conscious attitudes.
Automatic stereotypic associations can bias rapid decisions
Correct: time pressure reveals implicit associations in behavior.
Black targets held objects that looked more like weapons
Object images were controlled across target race.
The bias would increase with more time to decide
More deliberation time typically reduces such errors.
questions.x: Shooter-bias studies show that, under time pressure, participants more often mistakenly shoot unarmed Black targets than unarmed White targets. Because objects were controlled, the difference reflects automatic stereotypic associations influencing fast decisions, which appear even in people who do not hold conscious hostility. More time to deliberate usually reduces these errors, allowing controlled processing to correct the automatic response.

questions.q: A researcher claims stereotype threat lowers scores because of anxiety. In an experiment, threat lowers scores but self-reported anxiety does not differ between conditions. What is the best interpretation?
o: Stereotype threat does not exist
The threat condition still lowered scores.
Anxiety is proven to be irrelevant in every case
One null result on self-report cannot rule out anxiety universally.
Self-reported anxiety does not appear to mediate the effect in this study
Correct: the proposed mediator did not differ, so another mechanism may be at work.
The independent variable was not manipulated
Scores differed, showing the manipulation had an effect.
questions.x: A mediator explains how an independent variable affects an outcome, so it should differ between conditions and account for the effect. Here the threat lowered scores but self-reported anxiety did not differ, so self-reported anxiety does not appear to mediate the effect in this study. Other mechanisms, such as reduced working memory, may be involved, and a single null result does not rule out anxiety entirely.

questions.q: A coach who prizes physical toughness judges other people mainly on how tough they seem and pays little attention to their kindness. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: The fundamental attribution error
The FAE concerns trait versus situation explanations, not which traits are noticed.
Out-group homogeneity
No group membership comparison is involved.
Stereotype threat
No one's performance is impaired by a stereotype.
Our self-schemas shape the dimensions we use to judge others
Correct: traits central to one's self-concept guide perceptions of others.
questions.x: Self-schemas are organized beliefs about oneself, and traits central to a person's self-concept become the dimensions they use to perceive others. A coach who values toughness notices and judges others mainly on toughness while overlooking other qualities. The fundamental attribution error is tempting, but it concerns explaining behavior by traits versus situations, not which traits a perceiver attends to.

questions.q: Satisfied couples tend to attribute a partner's thoughtful gift to the partner's caring nature, and a forgotten anniversary to a busy week. This pattern is best described as what?
o: Distress-maintaining attributions
Those attribute negatives to the partner's character.
Fundamental attribution error
The FAE would attribute the forgotten anniversary to disposition.
Self-serving bias
The attributions concern the partner's behavior, not one's own outcomes.
Relationship-enhancing attributions
Correct: positives are internal and stable, negatives external and temporary.
questions.x: Happy couples tend to make relationship-enhancing attributions: a partner's positive acts are explained by internal, stable traits, while negative acts are explained by external, temporary circumstances. Distressed couples show the reverse, distress-maintaining pattern. The fundamental attribution error would predict blaming the forgotten anniversary on the partner's character, which these couples avoid.

questions.q: A woman completes residency and becomes a board-certified surgeon. Her status as surgeon is best described as:
o: Achieved
Correct: it was earned through her own effort and training.
Ascribed
Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth or involuntarily, such as race or age.
Master
Nothing indicates this status dominates all others in how people see her.
Primary
Primary describes a type of group, not a type of status.
questions.x: An achieved status is a position a person gains through her own effort, choices or merit, like earning a degree and board certification. An ascribed status is assigned without effort, at birth or by circumstance, such as age, race or royal birth. Master status is not a separate type of acquisition; it describes any status that dominates how others see someone, and nothing here suggests that.

questions.q: A man released from prison finds that employers focus only on his criminal record and overlook his degree and work history. His ex-offender status is functioning as a:
o: Role set
A role set is the cluster of roles tied to one status, not a dominant label.
Ascribed status
A criminal record results from his own actions, so it is not ascribed.
Reference group
A reference group is a standard for self-evaluation, not a status.
Master status
Correct: one status overshadows all others and shapes every interaction.
questions.x: A master status is the one status that overrides all others and shapes how people interpret everything about a person. Here the ex-offender label eclipses his education and job history, so employers react to it alone. It is tempting to call it ascribed because it feels imposed, but it stems from his own actions, so it is achieved; what makes it master is its dominance, not how it was acquired.

questions.q: A professor teaches lectures, advises graduate students and serves on hiring committees. These multiple behaviors attached to her single position are called her:
o: Status set
A status set is all the statuses a person holds, not roles within one status.
Role set
Correct: a role set is all the roles linked to one status.
Role strain
Role strain is tension within a role; the stem describes no tension.
Master status
A master status dominates identity; nothing here describes domination.
questions.x: A status is a position; the bundle of roles, or expected behaviors, attached to that one position is its role set. A professor's single status brings teaching, advising and committee roles. The status set is different: it is all the statuses one person holds at once, such as professor, mother and citizen. Role strain would require tension among these roles, which the stem does not describe.

questions.q: A child born into a royal family is called a prince from birth. His royal status is:
o: Achieved
Achieved statuses require effort or choice by the person.
Instrumental
Instrumental describes goal-directed group ties, not status types.
Ascribed
Correct: he did nothing to earn it; it was assigned at birth.
Exited
Role exit refers to leaving a role, which has not occurred.
questions.x: Ascribed statuses are assigned to a person involuntarily, usually at birth, regardless of effort or ability; royal title, sex and ethnicity are classic examples. Achieved statuses, by contrast, are earned or chosen. Because the prince did nothing to obtain his title, it is ascribed, even though he will later be expected to perform the duties that come with it.

questions.q: A woman is a respected physician but a member of a group that faces discrimination, and patients sometimes question her authority. Which concept best captures the mismatch?
o: Status inconsistency
Correct: her statuses carry conflicting levels of prestige, producing contradictory treatment.
Role exit
She has not left any role.
Role strain
Role strain is competing demands inside one role, not unequal prestige across statuses.
Achieved master status
Her physician status is achieved, but the problem is the clash between statuses.
questions.note: Status inconsistency: a person ranks high on one status and low on another.
questions.x: Status inconsistency occurs when a person holds statuses ranked very differently in prestige, so others respond to her in contradictory ways. Her high-prestige profession clashes with a stigmatized group membership, and some patients react to the lower-ranked status. Role strain is tempting, but strain is about competing demands within one role, not mismatched prestige between two statuses.

questions.q: A first-year resident is told by attendings to see patients faster and by patients to spend more time with them. This is best classified as:
o: Role conflict
Role conflict requires clashing demands from two different statuses.
Role strain
Correct: both expectations attach to the single status of resident.
Role exit
Nothing suggests the resident is leaving the role.
Role reversal
Role reversal means trading positions with another person.
questions.note: Trap: multiple audiences can still create strain within one role.
questions.x: Role strain is tension among the expectations attached to one status. Speed demanded by attendings and time demanded by patients are both expectations of being a resident, so this is strain. Role conflict is tempting because two audiences are involved, but conflict requires the demands to come from two different statuses the person holds.

questions.q: According to Ebaugh's model of role exit, which stage immediately follows a person's first doubts about a role?
o: The turning point
The turning point comes after alternatives have been considered.
Creating the ex-role
Building an ex-role identity is the final stage.
Anticipatory socialization
This is a general socialization concept, not a named Ebaugh stage.
Searching for alternatives
Correct: after doubts, the person weighs other possible roles.
questions.note: Ebaugh: first doubts → alternatives → turning point → creating ex-role.
questions.x: Ebaugh described role exit as four stages: first doubts about the role, a search for alternatives, a turning point where the person decides to leave, and creating an ex-role identity. Weighing alternatives therefore comes right after the first doubts. The turning point is tempting but comes later, once alternatives have been considered and a decision is made.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a primary group?
o: A company's accounting department
Workplace departments are typically secondary, task-focused groups.
A semester-long lecture class
Classes are impersonal, temporary and goal-oriented, so secondary.
A close-knit family
Correct: primary groups are small, intimate, long-lasting and expressive.
A national professional association
Large formal associations are secondary groups.
questions.x: Primary groups are small, intimate, long-lasting and valued for the relationships themselves (expressive), with family and close friends as the model. Secondary groups are larger or impersonal, formed to accomplish tasks (instrumental), and often temporary. Departments, classes and professional associations bring people together for goals, not for intimacy, so they are secondary.

questions.q: Researchers randomly label participants as "overestimators" or "underestimators" of dot counts. Participants then give more money to anonymous members of their own label. This best demonstrates:
o: In-group favoritism even with trivial group criteria
Correct: the minimal group paradigm shows mere categorization produces bias.
Realistic conflict over scarce resources
Groups never competed, so conflict over resources does not explain it.
Reference group comparison
Participants were allocating rewards, not evaluating themselves.
Primary group loyalty
These arbitrary groups have no intimacy or history.
questions.x: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm showed that assigning people to groups on trivial or even random criteria is enough to produce in-group favoritism in reward allocation. No competition, history or contact was needed. Realistic conflict theory is the tempting alternative, but it explains bias through competition for scarce resources, which was absent here.

questions.q: A college junior hoping to attend medical school models her study habits after current medical students she admires. The medical students serve as her:
o: Primary group
She has no intimate, enduring relationship with them.
Out-group
An out-group is a group she does not belong to or identify with; she admires and emulates these students.
Reference group
Correct: a reference group provides standards a person uses to evaluate themselves.
Dyad
A dyad is a two-person group, not a source of standards.
questions.x: A reference group is any group whose standards a person uses to evaluate herself and guide her behavior, whether or not she belongs to it. Aspiring students often adopt the habits of the profession they hope to join, a form of anticipatory socialization. Primary group is wrong because she has no intimate, lasting tie to these students.

questions.q: Two roommates who keep arguing invite a third friend to move in. Compared with the dyad, the new triad is more likely to:
o: Collapse if any one person leaves
Losing one member of a triad leaves a dyad, so the group survives.
Become more intimate
Adding members generally reduces intimacy.
Allow one member to mediate or join a coalition
Correct: a third person can act as mediator or create two-against-one alliances.
Eliminate all conflict
Triads add new conflict possibilities, such as exclusion.
questions.x: Adding a third member creates a triad, which is more stable than a dyad because it survives the loss of one person, and it introduces new dynamics. The third person can mediate disputes between the other two or join one of them in a coalition. Intimacy usually drops as attention is divided, and new conflicts such as exclusion become possible.

questions.q: A team grows from 4 members to 6. How does the number of possible one-to-one relationships change?
o: From 4 to 6
This counts members, not pairwise relationships.
From 12 to 30
Using n(n − 1) double-counts each pair.
From 8 to 12
Doubling the member count does not give the number of pairs.
From 6 to 15
Correct: n(n − 1)/2 gives 4·3/2 = 6 and 6·5/2 = 15.
questions.note: Relationships grow much faster than members: n(n − 1)/2.
questions.x: The number of possible pairwise relationships in a group of n people is n(n − 1)/2, because each person can pair with n − 1 others and each pair is counted twice. For 4 members that is 4·3/2 = 6; for 6 members it is 6·5/2 = 15. Forgetting to divide by 2 gives 12 and 30, the most tempting error.

questions.q: In a hospital's communication map, one nurse is the only link between the ICU staff and the pharmacy staff. Removing her would most likely:
o: Increase the density of each cluster
Density within clusters is unaffected by removing a between-cluster link.
Have no effect because weak ties are unimportant
Bridging ties are often the most important for information flow.
Merge the two clusters into one
Removing the only connection separates rather than merges them.
Cut the flow of information between the two clusters
Correct: she is a bridge across a structural hole, so losing her disconnects the clusters.
questions.x: A bridge is a tie that is the only link between two otherwise separate clusters; it spans what network theorists call a structural hole. Removing it disconnects the clusters, so information can no longer pass between them. Density within each cluster is unchanged, which is why the density option is a distractor.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy?
o: Hiring based on family connections
Weber's model calls for hiring by technical qualifications.
Flexible, informal decision-making
Bureaucracies rely on formal, standardized procedures.
A clear hierarchy of authority with written rules
Correct: Weber emphasized hierarchy, rules, division of labor and impersonality.
Emotional ties among all members
Bureaucracy stresses impersonal relationships.
questions.x: Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy has a hierarchy of authority, written rules and procedures, specialized division of labor, impersonal relationships and hiring or promotion based on technical qualifications. These features aim at efficiency and predictability. Hiring through family connections and informal, emotional decision-making are exactly what the model tries to eliminate.

questions.q: A grassroots patient-advocacy group founded on equal voting gradually comes to be run by a few long-serving leaders who control decisions. This illustrates:
o: The iron law of oligarchy
Correct: Michels argued organizations tend toward rule by a small elite.
McDonaldization
McDonaldization concerns efficiency and standardization, not elite rule.
Bureaucratic ritualism
Ritualism is rigid rule-following, not concentration of power.
The strength of weak ties
That concept concerns information flow in networks.
questions.x: Michels' iron law of oligarchy states that organizations, even democratic ones, tend to be taken over by a small group of leaders because of the need for coordination, expertise and control of communication. An egalitarian group drifting into rule by a few long-serving leaders is the textbook case. McDonaldization is about efficiency and standardization, not who holds power.

questions.q: A clinic judges physicians mainly by the number of patients seen per hour rather than by quality of care. Which dimension of McDonaldization does this reflect?
o: Predictability
Predictability means standardized, uniform experiences.
Control
Control refers to replacing human judgment with technology or rules.
Efficiency
Efficiency is the fastest means to an end, not measurement of quantity.
Calculability
Correct: calculability emphasizes quantifiable output over quality.
questions.x: Ritzer's McDonaldization has four dimensions: efficiency, calculability, predictability and control. Calculability means emphasizing what can be counted, valuing quantity over quality. Judging physicians by patients per hour rather than care quality is calculability; efficiency is tempting, but efficiency concerns the fastest method to a goal, while this stem is about measuring and valuing quantity.

questions.q: A pharmacy chain installs automated dispensing machines that limit what pharmacists can do and dictate each step. Which McDonaldization dimension is most emphasized?
o: Calculability
No emphasis on counting or quantity is described.
Predictability
Uniform outcomes may follow, but the key feature is constraining workers.
Control
Correct: nonhuman technology constrains workers' discretion.
Efficiency
Speed is not the focus; dictating worker behavior is.
questions.x: In McDonaldization, control means replacing human judgment with nonhuman technology, scripts or rules that dictate how work is done. Machines that constrain pharmacists' discretion and specify each step exemplify control. Predictability is tempting because uniform output may follow, but the stem stresses limiting workers' choices, which is the core of control.

questions.q: A hospital volunteer program that people join because they value its mission is, in Etzioni's typology, a:
o: Coercive organization
Coercive organizations, like prisons, involve involuntary membership.
Normative organization
Correct: normative organizations attract members through shared values.
Utilitarian organization
Utilitarian organizations offer pay or material reward.
Primary group
A volunteer program is a formal organization, not a primary group.
questions.x: Etzioni classified formal organizations by why people join: normative (voluntary) organizations attract members who share their values or goals, coercive organizations hold members involuntarily, and utilitarian organizations offer pay or material reward. Volunteers who join for the mission and receive no pay belong to a normative organization.

questions.q: In Goffman's dramaturgical approach, a physician's white coat, stethoscope and office décor that help convey competence are part of the:
o: Front
Correct: the front includes setting, appearance and manner that define the performance.
Back stage
Back stage is where performers relax away from the audience.
Audience
The audience is the people observing the performance.
Role set
A role set is the roles tied to a status, not props.
questions.x: Goffman's dramaturgy treats social life as theater. The front is the part of the performance that defines the situation for the audience: the setting (office décor), appearance (white coat, stethoscope) and manner. These props communicate competence. Back stage is where performers relax out of the audience's view, which is the opposite of what these props do.

questions.q: After a difficult shift, nurses joke and complain freely in a staff room patients cannot enter. In Goffman's terms, the staff room is:
o: Front stage
Front stage is where the performance is given to an audience.
Back stage
Correct: back stage is where performers drop their public role.
A reference group
A reference group is a standard of comparison, not a setting.
A total institution
A total institution controls all aspects of residents' lives.
questions.x: In Goffman's dramaturgy, front stage is where people perform for an audience according to role expectations, and back stage is where they can drop the performance and act more freely. A staff room that patients cannot enter is back stage, where nurses joke and vent. A total institution, such as a prison, controls all aspects of residents' lives and does not fit.

questions.q: A job applicant who privately dislikes teamwork describes herself as a passionate collaborator because the company values it. Which self is she presenting?
o: Tactical self
Correct: the tactical self is who others expect us to be.
Authentic self
The authentic self is who she believes she truly is.
Ideal self
The ideal self is who she would like to become, not who the employer expects.
Looking-glass self
That is Cooley's idea of self formed from imagined judgments.
questions.x: Impression management frameworks distinguish the authentic self (who we believe we really are), the ideal self (who we want to be) and the tactical self (who we present to match others' expectations). Presenting as a passionate collaborator because the company values it is the tactical self. The ideal self is tempting, but she does not aspire to this trait; she adopts it for the audience.

questions.q: Two Deaf colleagues discuss a project in American Sign Language. Their exchange is best classified as:
o: Nonverbal communication
Trap: verbal means using language, not using the voice.
Verbal communication
Correct: sign languages use words and grammar, so they are verbal.
Paralanguage
Paralanguage refers to vocal qualities like tone and pitch.
Animal signaling
ASL is a full human language.
questions.note: Verbal = language-based, whether spoken, written or signed.
questions.x: Verbal communication means communication through language, with words and grammar, whether spoken, written or signed. American Sign Language is a complete natural language, so a conversation in ASL is verbal. The trap is equating verbal with vocal; gestures that are not part of a language, like a shrug, are nonverbal.

questions.q: Participants from two cultures watch a disgusting film alone and show similar facial expressions, but when an authority figure is present, one group masks its expressions. This best supports:
o: Facial expressions are entirely learned
The similar expressions when alone argue against purely learned expressions.
Disgust is not a basic emotion
Both groups showed disgust, consistent with a basic emotion.
Paralanguage varies by culture
The study measured faces, not vocal cues.
Universal basic expressions modified by cultural display rules
Correct: expressions are shared, but norms govern when they are shown.
questions.x: Research by Ekman and colleagues found that basic emotional expressions are largely universal, but cultural display rules govern when it is appropriate to show them. When alone, both groups showed similar expressions; with an authority present, one group masked them. The similarity when alone rules out the idea that expressions are entirely learned.

questions.q: A hand gesture meaning "OK" in one country is considered offensive in another. This shows that gestures, unlike basic facial expressions of emotion, are:
o: Universally understood
The example shows different meanings across cultures.
A form of paralanguage
Paralanguage refers to vocal qualities, not hand movements.
Largely culturally specific
Correct: many gestures have meanings learned within a culture.
Controlled by display rules for emotion
Display rules govern emotional expression, not symbolic gestures.
questions.x: Basic facial expressions of emotion are recognized fairly consistently across cultures, but gestures are largely learned symbols whose meanings vary from culture to culture. The same hand sign can mean approval in one place and be insulting in another. Display rules are tempting but they regulate when emotions are expressed, not what symbolic gestures mean.

questions.q: Gazelles that spot a predator sometimes leap high in place (stotting), wasting energy instead of fleeing. The best evolutionary explanation is that stotting:
o: Is an accident with no function
Persistent costly behavior usually signals adaptive value.
Lures predators toward kin
This would reduce inclusive fitness.
Is a costly, honest signal that the gazelle is fit and hard to catch
Correct: only healthy animals can afford the display, so predators may abandon pursuit.
Is a pheromone release
Stotting is a visual display, not a chemical signal.
questions.note: Handicap principle: costly signals are hard to fake.
questions.x: Zahavi's handicap principle holds that signals which are costly to produce are honest, because only individuals in good condition can afford them. A stotting gazelle advertises to the predator that it is fit and would be hard to catch, so the predator does better chasing a weaker target. Calling it an accident ignores that a costly behavior persisting in a population usually has adaptive value.

questions.q: Participants who were told a partner liked them later rated the partner more favorably than participants given no such information, even though the partner's behavior was identical. This illustrates:
o: Mere exposure
Exposure time was the same in both conditions.
Proximity
Physical distance was not manipulated.
The matching hypothesis
Attractiveness levels were not compared.
Reciprocity of liking
Correct: we tend to like people who like us.
questions.x: Reciprocity of liking is the tendency to like people who we believe like us. Since the partner's behavior was identical across conditions, only the belief about being liked differed, and it raised ratings. Mere exposure and proximity are ruled out because time with the partner and physical distance were the same in both groups.

questions.q: Men who met a female interviewer on a high, swaying bridge were more likely to call her later than men who met her on a stable bridge. Which explanation best fits?
o: They misattributed fear-related arousal to attraction
Correct: physiological arousal from the bridge was labeled as attraction.
Mere exposure to the interviewer increased liking
Exposure time was similar in both conditions.
Proximity differed between groups
Both groups met the interviewer face to face.
The stable bridge produced more arousal
The high bridge produced more arousal.
questions.x: In the Dutton and Aron bridge study, men on the frightening suspension bridge experienced physiological arousal and misattributed it to attraction to the interviewer, making them more likely to call her. This fits the two-factor view that emotion depends on arousal plus a cognitive label. The stable bridge produced less arousal, which is why that group showed less interest.

questions.q: Children who watched an adult hit an inflatable doll later hit the doll more than children who watched a calm adult. This finding supports:
o: Catharsis reducing aggression
Watching aggression increased, not reduced, aggression.
Observational learning of aggression
Correct: children imitated the modeled behavior.
Frustration-aggression theory
No frustration manipulation produced the difference.
Instinctive aggression independent of learning
Group differences came from what children observed.
questions.x: Bandura's Bobo doll studies showed that children who watched an adult model hit an inflatable doll were more likely to imitate that aggression, demonstrating observational learning. The catharsis idea predicts the reverse, that watching aggression would drain aggressive impulses, which the data contradict. Because the groups differed only in what they saw, learning, not instinct, explains the difference.

questions.q: Which biological profile is most associated with increased impulsive aggression?
o: Low serotonin activity and reduced prefrontal cortex control
Correct: weak prefrontal inhibition and low serotonin are linked to impulsive aggression.
High serotonin and enhanced prefrontal activity
These are associated with better impulse control.
Low testosterone and a smaller amygdala response
Lower testosterone and amygdala reactivity are linked to less aggression.
High oxytocin alone
Oxytocin is mainly linked to bonding.
questions.x: Impulsive aggression is associated with low serotonin activity and weak prefrontal cortex control over emotional responses, often alongside high amygdala reactivity and higher testosterone. The prefrontal cortex normally inhibits impulses that the amygdala generates. Low testosterone and reduced amygdala response point toward less aggression, not more.

questions.q: Angered participants gave more electric shocks to a confederate when a rifle lay on a nearby table than when a badminton racket did. This best illustrates:
o: Catharsis
No venting occurred, and aggression increased.
Instrumental aggression
The shocks served no other goal.
The weapons effect, in which aggressive cues prime aggression
Correct: weapons act as cues that activate aggressive thoughts.
Social facilitation
The presence of others was not manipulated.
questions.x: Berkowitz and LePage found that angered participants delivered more shocks when a rifle was nearby than when a badminton racket was, the weapons effect. Weapons act as aggressive cues that prime aggressive thoughts and make aggression more likely in people who are already aroused. Catharsis would predict less aggression, the opposite of what occurred.

questions.q: A survey finds that teens who play more violent video games report more aggressive behavior. Which additional study would best test whether the games cause aggression?
o: Surveying more teens about their gaming habits
A larger correlational sample still cannot establish causation.
Randomly assigning teens to play violent or nonviolent games and then measuring aggression
Correct: random assignment controls confounds and permits causal inference.
Asking aggressive teens why they like violent games
Self-reports of preferences cannot show causation.
Measuring parents' attitudes toward video games
This adds a variable but not experimental control.
questions.x: Correlational surveys cannot show causation because third variables or reverse causation could explain the link, for example aggressive teens choosing violent games. Randomly assigning participants to play violent or nonviolent games makes the groups equivalent on average, so a difference in aggression can be attributed to the games. Simply enlarging the survey sample does not fix the design problem.

questions.q: In the Strange Situation, an infant is upset when the mother leaves, greets her warmly when she returns and is quickly soothed. This infant is classified as:
o: Avoidant
Avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver on return.
Ambivalent
Ambivalent infants are hard to soothe and resist comfort.
Disorganized
Disorganized infants show confused, contradictory behavior.
Securely attached
Correct: secure infants use the caregiver as a secure base and are easily comforted.
questions.x: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, securely attached infants use the caregiver as a secure base, show distress at separation, greet the caregiver on return and are soothed quickly. Ambivalent infants are also distressed, but they resist comfort and are hard to soothe, and avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver on reunion.

questions.q: An infant freezes, approaches the caregiver while looking away, and shows no consistent strategy for seeking comfort. This pattern is most strongly associated with:
o: Secure attachment linked to sensitive care
Secure infants show a coherent comfort-seeking strategy.
Disorganized attachment linked to frightening or abusive care
Correct: disorganized attachment often follows maltreatment.
Avoidant attachment linked to rejecting care
Avoidant infants show a consistent strategy of avoidance.
Ambivalent attachment linked to inconsistent care
Ambivalent infants show a consistent, if anxious, strategy.
questions.x: Disorganized attachment is marked by contradictory, confused behavior, such as freezing or approaching while looking away, with no consistent strategy for getting comfort. It is most strongly linked to frightening or abusive caregiving, where the caregiver is both the source of fear and of comfort. Ambivalent infants, though anxious, still show a consistent strategy.

questions.q: Infant monkeys raised with a wire mother that provided milk and a cloth mother that provided none spent most of their time clinging to the cloth mother. This finding most directly challenged the idea that:
o: Attachment forms mainly because caregivers provide food
Correct: contact comfort, not feeding, drove attachment.
Infants need any contact at all
The monkeys strongly sought contact.
Attachment is influenced by touch
The results support the importance of touch.
Monkeys can form attachments
The monkeys clearly formed attachments.
questions.x: Harlow's experiments showed that infant monkeys preferred a cloth surrogate that provided contact comfort over a wire surrogate that provided milk. This challenged the view that attachment forms mainly because caregivers satisfy hunger. The results support, rather than challenge, the importance of touch in attachment.

questions.q: Newly hatched goslings follow the first moving object they see during a brief period after hatching. This phenomenon demonstrates:
o: Operant conditioning
No reinforcement shapes the behavior.
Kin selection
The goslings follow any moving object, not specifically kin.
Imprinting during a critical period
Correct: the attachment forms only within a limited developmental window.
Secure attachment
Imprinting is a rapid, fixed process rather than a Strange Situation classification.
questions.x: Imprinting, studied by Lorenz, is a rapid form of learning in which young animals form an attachment to the first moving object they see, but only during a brief critical period after hatching. It does not require reinforcement, which rules out operant conditioning. Goslings will follow a person or even an object, showing the attachment is not specific to kin.

questions.q: According to Hamilton's rule (rB > C), helping a full sibling (r = 0.5) is favored by natural selection when the benefit to the sibling is:
o: Greater than the cost to the helper
This would apply only if r = 1, as in identical twins.
Greater than twice the cost to the helper
Correct: 0.5 × B > C means B > 2C.
Greater than half the cost to the helper
This reverses the relationship between r and B.
Greater than four times the cost
This corresponds to r = 0.25, such as a half sibling.
questions.note: Hamilton's rule: the more distant the relative, the larger B must be.
questions.x: Hamilton's rule says helping is favored when rB > C, where r is relatedness, B the benefit to the recipient and C the cost to the helper. For full siblings, r = 0.5, so 0.5B > C, meaning B > 2C. The more distant the relative, the larger the benefit must be; for a half sibling (r = 0.25), B must exceed 4C.

questions.q: Vampire bats regurgitate blood to roost-mates who failed to feed, and they share most often with bats that previously shared with them. This best illustrates:
o: Reciprocal altruism
Correct: helping is exchanged over time between individuals who interact repeatedly.
Kin selection only
Sharing tracks past help, not just relatedness.
Instrumental aggression
No aggression occurs.
Imprinting
Imprinting is early attachment, not food sharing.
questions.x: Reciprocal altruism, proposed by Trivers, is helping a non-relative at a cost with the expectation that the favor will be returned later; it works among individuals who interact repeatedly and can recognize each other. Vampire bats preferentially share blood with those who shared with them before. Kin selection alone cannot explain sharing that tracks past help rather than relatedness.

questions.q: Participants who felt high empathy for a struggling student helped her even when they could easily leave without helping. Low-empathy participants helped mainly when leaving was difficult. These results best support:
o: The negative-state relief model
That model predicts helping to relieve one's own distress, which easy escape would also do.
The empathy-altruism hypothesis
Correct: empathic concern produced helping even when escape was easy.
Kin selection
The student was not related to participants.
The frustration-aggression hypothesis
This explains aggression, not helping.
questions.x: Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis predicts that empathic concern produces genuinely altruistic helping, so high-empathy people help even when escape is easy. Low-empathy people help mainly when escape is hard, consistent with egoistic motives like reducing their own discomfort. The egoistic account is the tempting one, but it predicts that easy escape would reduce helping for everyone.

questions.q: In a hawk-dove model, a population of all doves can be invaded by a hawk mutant, and a population of all hawks can be invaded by doves. What does game theory predict?
o: All doves at equilibrium
An all-dove population is invaded by hawks.
All hawks at equilibrium
An all-hawk population is invaded by doves.
A stable mix of hawk and dove strategies
Correct: when neither pure strategy resists invasion, a mixed equilibrium is evolutionarily stable.
Extinction of both strategies
Invasion produces a mix, not extinction.
questions.x: An evolutionarily stable strategy is one that cannot be invaded by an alternative strategy. In the hawk-dove game, hawks do well in a population of doves and doves do well among hawks, so neither pure strategy is stable. The predicted outcome is a stable mixture of hawks and doves, with frequencies set by the costs of fighting and the value of the resource.

questions.q: Researchers find that social support predicts better health among people facing major life stressors but has little effect among people with low stress. These data best support:
o: The direct (main) effect hypothesis
A main effect would predict benefits at all stress levels.
The frustration-aggression hypothesis
This hypothesis concerns aggression, not health.
The buffering hypothesis
Correct: support protects mainly by cushioning the effects of stress.
The iron law of oligarchy
This concerns organizational power.
questions.note: Buffering = an interaction; main effect = benefit regardless of stress.
questions.x: The buffering hypothesis states that social support protects health mainly by cushioning the effects of stress, so its benefits show up chiefly among people under high stress. That is an interaction between stress and support. The direct (main) effect hypothesis instead predicts that support improves health at all stress levels, which these data contradict.

questions.q: Studies comparing perceived and received social support usually find that well-being is more strongly predicted by:
o: Received support, counted as the number of helping acts
Received support relates less consistently to well-being.
Perceived support, the belief that help is available
Correct: perceived availability shows stronger links to well-being than actual help received.
Network size alone
Size matters less than perceived quality.
The number of secondary groups a person belongs to
Group count is a weak proxy for support.
questions.x: Perceived social support, the belief that help would be available if needed, is generally a stronger and more consistent predictor of well-being than received support, the actual helping acts counted. Receiving lots of help can even signal that someone is struggling, which muddies its link to well-being. Network size and group counts are weaker proxies for quality.

questions.q: In pipefish, males carry and nourish the eggs, and females compete for males while males are choosy. This best supports which idea?
o: The sex that invests more in offspring tends to be choosier
Correct: parental investment, not biological sex itself, predicts choosiness.
Males are always the competitive sex
Pipefish show that females can be the competing sex.
Mating behavior is unrelated to parental care
The reversal tracks the reversal in care.
Females always invest more in offspring
Here males invest more.
questions.note: Trivers: higher investment → more selective.
questions.x: Trivers' parental investment theory predicts that the sex investing more in each offspring will be choosier about mates, while the sex investing less competes for access. In most species females invest more, but in pipefish males brood the eggs, and the roles reverse. This shows investment, not sex itself, drives choosiness.

questions.q: A female bird chooses a mate with bright plumage that signals parasite resistance, though he provides no food or nest. She gains:
o: Direct material benefits
Direct benefits include food, territory or care, which he does not provide.
Benefits from kin selection
Her mate is not her relative.
Indirect genetic benefits for her offspring
Correct: good genes passed to offspring are indirect benefits.
Benefits from reciprocal altruism
No exchange of favors over time is described.
questions.x: Mate choice can yield direct benefits, such as food, territory or parental care for the chooser, or indirect benefits, which are good genes passed to offspring. Bright plumage that signals parasite resistance, from a male that provides nothing else, offers only genetic quality for her young. Direct benefits are ruled out because he provides no resources.

questions.q: A participant reports no negative feelings toward older adults, but on an Implicit Association Test responds faster when pairing "old" with negative words. This result best indicates:
o: Explicit prejudice
She explicitly denies negative attitudes.
Institutional discrimination
No organizational policy is involved.
Individual discrimination
No discriminatory behavior was observed.
Implicit bias that may differ from explicit attitudes
Correct: automatic associations can exist without consciously endorsed prejudice.
questions.x: The Implicit Association Test measures automatic associations by how quickly people pair concepts. Faster pairing of old with negative words indicates an implicit bias, even though she reports no negative feelings. Explicit and implicit attitudes can diverge, and an IAT result does not by itself show discriminatory behavior.

questions.q: A shop owner holds no personal prejudice but refuses to hire members of a minority group because he fears customers will object. In Merton's typology, he is a:
o: All-weather liberal
All-weather liberals neither hold prejudice nor discriminate.
Timid bigot
Timid bigots are prejudiced but do not discriminate.
Active bigot
Active bigots are prejudiced and discriminate.
Fair-weather liberal (unprejudiced discriminator)
Correct: he discriminates without holding prejudice, due to social pressure.
questions.x: Merton cross-classified prejudice and discrimination: the all-weather liberal is unprejudiced and does not discriminate, the fair-weather liberal is unprejudiced but discriminates under social pressure, the timid bigot is prejudiced but does not discriminate, and the active bigot is prejudiced and discriminates. The shop owner discriminates without prejudice, so he is a fair-weather liberal.

questions.q: A company that excluded women for decades now lays off workers by seniority, so women are disproportionately let go. This is best described as:
o: Past-in-present discrimination
Correct: a neutral-seeming practice perpetuates the effects of earlier discrimination.
Individual discrimination
No individual is acting on personal bias now.
Implicit bias
The disparity arises from policy, not automatic associations.
Prejudice
Prejudice is an attitude, not a layoff policy.
questions.x: Past-in-present discrimination occurs when a seemingly neutral practice carries forward the effects of earlier discrimination. Because women were excluded for decades, they have less seniority, so seniority-based layoffs hit them hardest. Individual discrimination is ruled out because no one is acting on bias now; the disparity comes from the policy.

questions.q: A researcher visited many restaurants with a couple from a minority group and was refused service only once, yet most owners later replied by mail that they would refuse such customers. This finding best shows that:
o: Discrimination always follows prejudice
Owners expressed prejudice but mostly did not discriminate.
Institutional discrimination was absent
The study measured individual owners' behavior, not policies.
Stated prejudice does not always predict discriminatory behavior
Correct: attitudes reported by mail did not match actual treatment.
Implicit bias drove the refusals
Implicit associations were not measured.
questions.x: LaPiere's study found that restaurants and hotels almost always served a traveling couple from a minority group, yet most later said by mail that they would refuse such customers. This shows that stated attitudes do not always predict behavior. The finding contradicts the idea that discrimination always follows prejudice.

questions.q: Durkheim compared society to a living organism whose parts each contribute to overall stability. This analogy is central to which perspective?
o: Conflict theory
Conflict theory stresses competition and inequality, not interdependent parts maintaining balance.
Symbolic interactionism
Interactionism studies micro-level meaning-making, not society as an organism.
Functionalism
Correct: functionalism views institutions as interrelated parts that keep society stable.
Rational choice theory
Rational choice focuses on individual cost-benefit decisions, not societal systems.
questions.note: Organism analogy, stability, equilibrium: think functionalism.
questions.x: Functionalism, rooted in Durkheim, treats society like a body: each institution is an organ that performs a function keeping the whole in balance. Conflict theory is the tempting rival because it is also macro-level, but it sees society as groups competing over scarce resources, not parts cooperating toward stability.

questions.q: A hospital's openly stated purpose of diagnosing and treating patients is best described as its:
o: latent function
Latent functions are unrecognized or unintended, not the stated purpose.
latent dysfunction
A dysfunction disrupts stability; treating patients supports it.
social fact
Social facts are external constraints on behavior, not an institution's stated goal.
manifest function
Correct: a manifest function is the intended, recognized purpose of an institution.
questions.x: A manifest function is the openly recognized, intended purpose of an institution, so a hospital's stated mission of diagnosis and treatment is manifest. Latent functions are side effects nobody planned, such as a hospital becoming a major local employer. A stated goal can never be latent, because latent means unrecognized or unintended.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that drug manufacturers shape clinical guidelines to protect profits, even when patients bear higher costs. This argument most reflects:
o: functionalism
Functionalism would emphasize how guidelines promote stability, not exploitation.
conflict theory
Correct: it frames the system as powerful groups advancing their interests at others' expense.
symbolic interactionism
Interactionism would focus on face-to-face meaning, not institutional power.
social exchange theory
Exchange theory examines reciprocal rewards in relationships, not structural domination.
questions.x: Conflict theory explains social arrangements as the result of powerful groups using their resources to protect their interests at the expense of others. Industry shaping guidelines for profit while patients pay more fits that lens directly. Functionalism would instead ask how guidelines keep the health system stable, ignoring who gains and who loses.

questions.q: "If people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences." This statement, the Thomas theorem, is most associated with which perspective?
o: Functionalism
Functionalism examines institutional contributions to stability, not subjective definitions.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory emphasizes material power struggles over subjective definitions.
Rational choice theory
Rational choice assumes objective cost-benefit calculation, not definitions of the situation.
Symbolic interactionism
Correct: it holds that people act on the meanings they assign to situations.
questions.x: The Thomas theorem says people respond to their interpretation of a situation, so a belief can produce real outcomes even when it is false. That focus on subjective meaning guiding action is the core of symbolic interactionism. Rational choice is the trap: it assumes people respond to objective costs and benefits, not to socially constructed definitions.

questions.q: Paper currency has value only because people collectively agree that it does. This best exemplifies which concept?
o: Cultural lag
Cultural lag is nonmaterial culture trailing technological change.
Manifest function
Manifest functions are intended purposes of institutions, not shared agreements about value.
Social constructionism
Correct: money's value is a reality created and sustained by shared agreement.
Social exchange
Exchange theory concerns rewards in relationships, not how meanings become real.
questions.x: Social constructionism holds that many realities, such as money, exist because people collectively agree to treat them as real. Paper money has little intrinsic worth, yet shared agreement gives it purchasing power. Social exchange theory involves trading rewards, which money facilitates, but it does not explain where money's value comes from.

questions.q: A sociologist finds that a country's official racial categories on census forms changed several times over one century. This finding most directly supports the idea that race is:
o: socially constructed
Correct: shifting official categories show race is defined by social agreement, not fixed biology.
a latent function
Latent functions are unintended consequences of institutions, not category definitions.
a cultural universal
A universal would be present in all cultures, not shifting definitions.
a biological constant
Constantly changing categories contradict the idea of a fixed biological basis.
questions.x: If race were a fixed biological category, official classifications would not keep changing. Shifting census categories show that racial boundaries are defined by social and political agreement, a hallmark of social constructionism. Biological variation exists, but the categories societies draw around it are socially created.

questions.q: A student chooses a college major after weighing expected salary against tuition costs and hours of study required. Which theory best explains this decision?
o: Feminist theory
Feminist theory examines gender inequality, not individual cost-benefit decisions.
Symbolic interactionism
Interactionism emphasizes shared meanings rather than calculated payoffs.
Functionalism
Functionalism explains how institutions meet societal needs, not individual choices.
Rational choice theory
Correct: it models people as weighing costs and benefits to maximize advantage.
questions.x: Rational choice theory treats people as calculating actors who weigh costs against benefits and pick the option with the best expected payoff. Comparing salary with tuition and study hours is exactly that calculation. Social exchange theory is related but applies cost-benefit logic to relationships between people, not to an individual's choice of major.

questions.q: Two friends maintain their relationship because each feels that what they receive roughly matches what they give. Which theory best explains this?
o: Conflict theory
Conflict theory analyzes group struggles over resources, not balanced friendships.
Social exchange theory
Correct: relationships persist when perceived rewards balance or exceed costs.
Functionalism
Functionalism focuses on societal stability, not dyadic reward balance.
Feminist theory
Feminist theory focuses on gendered power, which is not described here.
questions.x: Social exchange theory extends cost-benefit reasoning to relationships: people stay in relationships when rewards match or exceed costs. The friends' sense of balanced giving and receiving is a classic exchange explanation. Rational choice is close but focuses on individual decisions generally, whereas exchange theory centers on the interaction between partners.

questions.q: Which perspective centrally examines how gender inequality is built into institutions such as the family and the workplace?
o: Rational choice theory
Rational choice centers on individual cost-benefit decisions.
Feminist theory
Correct: feminist theory analyzes gendered power and inequality in social structures.
Functionalism
Functionalism has historically treated gender roles as functional, not unequal.
Symbolic interactionism
Interactionism studies meanings in interaction but is not centered on gender inequality.
questions.x: Feminist theory examines how gender shapes access to power, resources and opportunity, and how inequality is built into institutions like family and work. It belongs to the conflict family of theories but focuses specifically on gender. Functionalism historically described gender roles as complementary and useful rather than unequal.

questions.q: A study finds that female physicians spend more unpaid time on patients' emotional concerns than male peers. Explaining this as a product of gendered expectations embedded in medicine reflects:
o: functionalism
Functionalism would treat the pattern as serving system needs, not as gendered inequality.
rational choice theory
Rational choice would attribute it to individual payoffs, not structural gender expectations.
social exchange theory
Exchange theory would frame it as a trade of rewards between individuals, not a gendered institutional norm.
feminist theory
Correct: it attributes the disparity to gendered power and expectations in an institution.
questions.note: Feminist theory is a conflict-family perspective focused specifically on gender.
questions.x: Attributing the extra unpaid emotional labor to gendered expectations built into medicine is a feminist analysis, since it locates the cause in institutional gender norms. Rational choice would instead explain the pattern by individual payoffs, and functionalism would ask what need it meets for the system, neither naming gender inequality as the cause.

questions.q: Max Weber broadened Marx's class analysis by arguing that social stratification also rests on:
o: status and party (political power)
Correct: Weber's three dimensions were class, status and party.
mechanical and organic solidarity
These are Durkheim's types of social cohesion.
manifest and latent functions
These are Merton's functionalist concepts.
the sacred and the profane
This is Durkheim's distinction in the study of religion.
questions.note: Weber: class (economic), status (prestige), party (power).
questions.x: Weber argued stratification has three dimensions: class (economic position), status (social prestige or honor) and party (political power). This let him explain cases where wealth and prestige diverge, which Marx's purely economic view could not. Mechanical versus organic solidarity is a Durkheim concept about social cohesion, not stratification.

questions.q: Researchers find that schools funded mainly by local property taxes show outcomes closely tracking neighborhood wealth. A conflict theorist would most likely interpret this as:
o: schools efficiently matching talent to occupations
This is a functionalist sorting interpretation.
students' cost-benefit decisions about effort
This is a rational choice interpretation.
teachers and students negotiating classroom meanings
This is an interactionist interpretation.
the education system reproducing existing class inequality
Correct: conflict theory sees institutions as preserving advantages of the powerful.
questions.x: Conflict theory sees institutions such as schools as tools that help advantaged groups pass on their advantages. When funding follows local property wealth, richer areas get better schools and their children keep their position, reproducing class inequality. The functionalist reading that schools sort talent ignores that outcomes track wealth rather than ability.

questions.q: Historians note that childhood as a protected life stage with distinct needs emerged only in recent centuries. This best illustrates:
o: cultural lag
Cultural lag concerns nonmaterial culture trailing material change.
rational choice theory
Rational choice concerns individual cost-benefit decisions.
latent dysfunction
A latent dysfunction is an unintended harmful consequence of an institution.
social constructionism
Correct: the meaning and boundaries of childhood were created socially and changed over time.
questions.x: Social constructionism holds that categories we treat as natural are created and sustained by social agreement. Childhood as a protected stage emerged only as laws, schooling and family norms changed, showing its meaning was built socially. Cultural lag would require nonmaterial culture trailing a specific material change, which the stem does not describe.

questions.q: In social exchange theory, the partner who is less dependent on a relationship for valued rewards typically:
o: has less power because they invest less
Lower investment and dependence actually confer power.
has equal power because exchanges always balance
Exchanges are often unequal; dependence creates power differences.
holds more power over the relationship
Correct: the principle of least interest says the less dependent partner has more leverage.
exits the relationship immediately
Lower dependence does not require leaving; it shifts power.
questions.note: Principle of least interest: whoever needs the relationship less controls it more.
questions.x: In exchange theory, power comes from dependence: whoever needs the relationship less has more alternatives and more leverage. This is the principle of least interest. It is tempting to think investing less means losing influence, but lower dependence actually lets that partner set the terms.

questions.q: Teachers are told that randomly chosen students are "likely to bloom," and those students later show greater gains. Which perspective best explains this result?
o: Functionalism
Functionalism does not explain how labels shape individual performance.
Symbolic interactionism
Correct: teacher expectations conveyed in interaction create a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Conflict theory
No group struggle over resources is involved in this random labeling.
Social exchange theory
The effect stems from labels and expectations, not reward balancing.
questions.x: In the Pygmalion effect, teachers' expectations shape how they treat students, which changes students' performance: a self-fulfilling prophecy. Because the effect works through labels and meanings conveyed in interaction, it fits symbolic interactionism. No group competition over resources is involved, so conflict theory does not apply.

questions.q: In an economic game, many participants refuse a small but nonzero offer they view as unfair, leaving both players with nothing. This finding most directly challenges which theory?
o: Symbolic interactionism
Interactionism readily allows meanings like fairness to guide action.
Feminist theory
Nothing in the game concerns gender.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory does not predict acceptance of any positive payoff.
Rational choice theory
Correct: a pure payoff maximizer should accept any amount above zero.
questions.note: Fairness norms can override material self-interest.
questions.x: Rational choice assumes people maximize material payoff, so a responder should accept any offer above zero, since something beats nothing. Rejecting unfair offers shows fairness norms and emotions can override self-interest. Interactionism can easily explain the result, because meanings like fairness are exactly what it says guides action.

questions.q: Durkheim's concept of "social facts" refers to:
o: verified statistics collected by governments
Durkheim's concept is broader than official statistics.
individual personality traits that shape behavior
Social facts are external to individuals, not personality traits.
ways of acting and thinking that are external to individuals and constrain them
Correct: norms, laws and values exist beyond individuals and shape their behavior.
meanings people create in face-to-face interaction
That is the focus of symbolic interactionism.
questions.x: Durkheim defined social facts as ways of acting, thinking and feeling that exist outside any individual and constrain behavior, such as laws, norms and religious beliefs. He argued sociology should study them as things in themselves. Meanings created in face-to-face interaction belong to symbolic interactionism, a micro perspective.

questions.q: Analyzing how race, class and gender combine to shape a working-class Black woman's experience of health care reflects which concept?
o: Intersectionality
Correct: it examines how overlapping social identities jointly produce advantage or disadvantage.
Anomie
Anomie is normlessness during social upheaval.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism means judging practices by their own culture's standards.
Organic solidarity
Organic solidarity is cohesion through specialized interdependence.
questions.x: Intersectionality, from Kimberlé Crenshaw, holds that race, class, gender and other identities combine to create distinct experiences of advantage or disadvantage that cannot be understood one category at a time. A working-class Black woman's care reflects all three together. Cultural relativism concerns judging practices within their culture, not overlapping identities.

questions.q: Durkheim argued that industrial societies are held together mainly by interdependence among people performing specialized jobs. He called this:
o: mechanical solidarity
Mechanical solidarity rests on similarity and shared beliefs in simple societies.
false consciousness
This is a Marxist idea about ideology.
the iron cage
This is Weber's image of bureaucratic rationalization.
organic solidarity
Correct: specialized roles make people depend on each other, binding society.
questions.note: Mechanical = sameness (traditional); organic = interdependence (modern).
questions.x: Durkheim said modern societies hold together through organic solidarity: specialized roles make people depend on one another, like organs in a body. Traditional societies rely on mechanical solidarity, cohesion through sameness of beliefs and work. Students often reverse the labels, so tie mechanical to sameness.

questions.q: Everyone in a neighborhood benefits from a park cleanup, yet few residents volunteer. A rational choice theorist would attribute low participation to:
o: latent dysfunction
This functionalist term does not explain individual incentives to abstain.
the free-rider problem
Correct: individuals can enjoy the shared benefit without bearing the cost, so many abstain.
culture shock
Culture shock is disorientation in an unfamiliar culture.
false consciousness
This Marxist idea concerns class ideology, not public goods.
questions.x: A free rider enjoys a shared benefit without paying its cost. Because a clean park helps everyone whether or not they volunteer, a purely self-interested person may let others do the work, so participation is low. This rational choice logic explains why public goods are often underprovided.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes social constructionism from symbolic interactionism?
o: Constructionism emphasizes how shared knowledge and institutions come to seem objective; interactionism emphasizes meanings made in face-to-face encounters.
Correct: constructionism is broader and societal; interactionism centers on micro interaction.
Constructionism is a macro theory of class conflict; interactionism is a theory of stability.
Neither description fits; class conflict and stability belong to other perspectives.
Constructionism denies that meanings exist; interactionism affirms them.
Both perspectives treat meanings as real and consequential.
Constructionism studies rational choices; interactionism studies institutions.
These descriptions match neither perspective.
questions.x: Both perspectives agree meaning is socially created. Social constructionism, from Berger and Luckmann, emphasizes how shared knowledge and institutions come to seem objective and natural across society. Symbolic interactionism focuses on how meanings are made and changed in specific face-to-face interactions.

questions.q: Two people both identify as members of the same faith, but one prays daily and attends services weekly while the other rarely does either. They differ most in:
o: religious affiliation
Their affiliation is the same.
religiosity
Correct: religiosity is the degree of religious belief, practice and commitment.
secularization
Secularization is a society-wide decline in religion's influence.
ecclesia membership
An ecclesia is a state-aligned church type, not a personal measure.
questions.x: Religious affiliation is the group someone identifies with, while religiosity is how intensely they believe and practice, measured by things like prayer and attendance. The two people share an affiliation but differ in religiosity. Secularization is a society-wide decline in religion's influence, not a difference between two individuals.

questions.q: After a charismatic religious founder dies, followers create written rules, offices and procedures for choosing successors. Weber called this process:
o: secularization
Secularization is religion's declining influence in society.
the routinization of charisma
Correct: charismatic authority is transformed into traditional or rational-legal forms.
anomie
Anomie is normlessness, not the institutionalization of authority.
cultural diffusion
Diffusion is the spread of cultural traits between groups.
questions.x: Charismatic authority depends on one exceptional person, so it is unstable and faces a crisis when that leader dies. Weber called its conversion into lasting rules, offices and succession procedures the routinization of charisma, turning it into traditional or rational-legal authority. Secularization is a decline in religion's influence, not this process.

questions.q: C. Wright Mills argued that a small group of top corporate, military and political leaders controls most national decisions. This view contrasts most directly with the pluralist claim that:
o: religion legitimizes state power
Neither model is centered on religion.
the economy determines all other institutions
This is closer to a Marxist claim, not pluralism.
authority rests on tradition
Traditional authority is a Weberian type, not the pluralist claim.
power is spread among many competing interest groups
Correct: pluralism sees no single elite dominating decisions.
questions.x: Mills's power elite model holds that a small, interconnected group of corporate, military and political leaders makes most major decisions. Pluralism counters that power is spread among many competing interest groups, none of which consistently dominates. Saying the economy determines everything is closer to Marx than to the pluralist position.

questions.q: Over a century, most births moved from homes attended by midwives to hospitals run by obstetricians. Feminist critics would most likely argue this change:
o: eliminated all risks associated with childbirth
Feminist critique concerns control and power, not absolute safety claims.
was driven solely by patients' rational cost-benefit choices
This is a rational choice framing, not a feminist one.
shifted control over childbirth from women to a male-dominated profession
Correct: it reframes medicalization as a transfer of authority over women's bodies.
strengthened mechanical solidarity among mothers
Mechanical solidarity is a Durkheimian concept unrelated to this critique.
questions.x: Feminist scholars describe the move from midwife-attended home births to physician-run hospital births as medicalization that shifted authority over childbirth from women, both mothers and midwives, to a then male-dominated profession. The critique is about power and control, not a claim that hospitals made birth risk-free.

questions.q: A physician presents treatment options and their risks, and she and the patient choose together based on the patient's values. This reflects which model of the physician-patient relationship?
o: Shared decision-making
Correct: physician and patient jointly reach decisions using evidence and patient values.
Paternalistic
In paternalism the physician decides what is best with little patient input.
Activity-passivity
This model treats the patient as a passive recipient, as when unconscious.
Sick role exemption
This is a feature of the sick role, not a relationship model.
questions.x: In shared decision-making, the physician supplies evidence about options and risks and the patient contributes values and preferences, and they decide together. The paternalistic model has the physician decide what is best with little input. Szasz and Hollender's activity-passivity model fits cases like an unconscious patient who cannot participate.

questions.q: As two-earner households become the norm, demand rises for daycare and after-school programs. A functionalist would interpret this as:
o: evidence that institutions are independent of one another
The example shows the opposite: institutions are interdependent.
the economy losing all influence over the family
The economic shift is what drives the family change.
proof that social change is always harmful
Functionalists see adaptation, not inevitable harm.
other institutions adjusting to a change in the economy and family
Correct: change in one institution prompts adaptation in related ones.
questions.x: Functionalists see institutions as interdependent parts that adjust to one another to restore balance. When economic change draws both parents into paid work, families have new childcare needs and other institutions adapt with daycare and after-school programs. This adaptation shows interdependence, not institutions acting independently.

questions.q: Ivan Illich argued that modern medicine harms society by making people dependent on professionals to manage ordinary life events such as birth, grief and aging. This critique is known as:
o: social iatrogenesis
Correct: harm arises from the medicalization of everyday life and professional dependence.
clinical iatrogenesis
Clinical iatrogenesis is direct harm from treatment, such as drug side effects.
the sick role
The sick role is Parsons's set of expectations for ill people.
culture lag
Culture lag is nonmaterial culture trailing technology.
questions.x: Illich described three levels of iatrogenesis, harm caused by medicine. Clinical iatrogenesis is direct harm from treatment, such as drug side effects or infections. Social iatrogenesis is the medicalization of everyday life that makes people dependent on professionals for ordinary experiences like birth, grief and aging.

questions.q: The proposal that the structure of a language shapes how its speakers perceive and think about the world is known as:
o: cultural relativism
Cultural relativism concerns judging cultures by their own standards.
the Thomas theorem
The Thomas theorem concerns definitions of situations having real consequences.
the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis
Correct: it proposes linguistic relativity, language influencing thought.
cultural diffusion
Diffusion is the spread of cultural traits between societies.
questions.x: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, or linguistic relativity, proposes that the structure of a language influences how its speakers perceive and think about the world. The strong version, that language determines thought, is largely rejected, while weaker influence has some support. Cultural relativism concerns judging practices within their culture, not language shaping thought.

questions.q: Lactase persistence into adulthood is much more common in populations with long histories of dairy herding. This pattern best illustrates:
o: gene-culture coevolution
Correct: a cultural practice altered selection pressures on a gene.
cultural lag
Cultural lag concerns nonmaterial culture trailing technology.
cultural relativism
Relativism concerns how cultures are evaluated.
cultural diffusion
Diffusion spreads practices between groups but does not explain allele frequencies.
questions.note: Culture can shape genes, and genes can shape culture.
questions.x: Gene-culture coevolution describes how cultural practices change selection pressures on genes, and genes in turn shape culture. Dairy herding made milk available to adults, so alleles for lactase persistence were favored and became common in those populations. Diffusion can spread dairying but cannot by itself change allele frequencies.

questions.q: Surveys show nearly everyone in a country says honesty is important, yet tax evasion is widespread there. This gap illustrates the difference between:
o: material and symbolic culture
Both honesty and tax behavior are nonmaterial; this is not the distinction shown.
folkways and mores
Both elements here concern the same norm, not two norm types.
subculture and counterculture
No subgroup rejecting or modifying values is described.
ideal culture and real culture
Correct: stated values differ from actual behavior.
questions.x: Ideal culture is the values and norms a society says it holds; real culture is how people actually behave. Widespread claims that honesty matters alongside widespread tax evasion show the gap between them. This is not a folkways versus mores contrast, since it compares a stated value with conduct, not two kinds of norms.

questions.q: Sources of cultural change include invention, discovery and diffusion. Scientists' recognition that microorganisms cause many diseases is best classified as:
o: discovery
Correct: discovery is recognizing something that already existed.
invention
Invention creates something new, such as a tool or process.
diffusion
Diffusion is the spread of traits between cultures.
cultural lag
Cultural lag is a gap between types of change, not a source of change.
questions.note: Germs existed already: discovery. The microscope was an invention.
questions.x: Cultural change arises from discovery, invention and diffusion. Discovery is recognizing something that already existed, such as microorganisms causing disease. Invention creates something new, such as the microscope used to see them. Since germs existed before scientists recognized them, germ theory is a discovery.

questions.q: Which statement correctly classifies a physician's white coat?
o: The coat and the trust it signals are both material culture.
Trust and authority are ideas, so they are symbolic culture.
The coat and the trust it signals are both symbolic culture.
The physical coat is an object, so it is material culture.
The coat is a norm, and the trust it signals is a value.
A physical object is not a norm.
The coat is material culture, and the authority it signals is symbolic culture.
Correct: the object is material; the meaning attached to it is symbolic.
questions.x: An object can belong to material culture while the meanings attached to it belong to symbolic culture. A white coat is a physical object, so it is material, while the trust and authority it signals are ideas, so they are symbolic. Lumping both into one category misses that meaning and object are distinct.

questions.q: An observational study finds that adults who attend religious services weekly have lower mortality, and that much of the difference disappears after adjusting for social support. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Attendance causes longer life through belief alone.
Adjusting for social support weakened the link, so belief alone is not supported.
Religion has no relationship to health.
An association was found, so this overstates the result.
Social support is the only possible cause of the association.
Some difference remained, and observational data cannot exclude other factors.
Social networks may partly explain how religious participation relates to health.
Correct: the adjustment suggests social support is one pathway, without proving causation.
questions.note: An attenuated association after adjustment suggests a mediator, not proof of cause.
questions.x: When an association weakens after adjusting for a variable, that variable may partly mediate or confound the link. Lower mortality among attenders shrinking after controlling for social support suggests social networks are one pathway. Since some difference remained and the study is observational, it neither proves causation nor shows social support is the only explanation.

questions.q: A cohort of medical students shows declining empathy scores between year 1 and year 3. Which additional finding would most strengthen a hidden curriculum explanation?
o: The decline is concentrated in clinical rotations with more exposure to cynical role models.
Correct: linking the drop to informal role modeling supports implicit learning as the cause.
Empathy scores also fall among age-matched students in other fields.
This suggests a general age or schooling trend rather than medical training.
Students' formal ethics coursework increased in year 2.
Formal coursework is the explicit curriculum, not the hidden one.
Empathy scores were measured with a new instrument in year 3.
A change in instrument suggests measurement artifact, weakening any explanation.
questions.x: The hidden curriculum predicts empathy loss comes from informal lessons, such as role models' attitudes. Finding the decline concentrated where students meet cynical role models links the drop to that mechanism. A similar decline in age-matched students outside medicine would point instead to a general trend, weakening the explanation.
