questions.q: Across 30 countries, religiosity is lower where national income is higher. A researcher concludes that wealth causes secularization. What is the best critique?
o: Religiosity cannot be measured in surveys.
Religiosity is routinely measured through attendance and belief items.
The sample of countries is too large.
A larger sample generally strengthens, not weakens, an analysis.
Correlational data cannot rule out confounders such as education levels.
Correct: a third variable could drive both income and religiosity.
Wealthier countries have no religious institutions.
This is factually false and irrelevant to the inference.
questions.x: A correlation across countries cannot show causation, because a third variable, such as education or urbanization, could raise income and lower religiosity at the same time. The direction could also run the other way. Sample size and the possibility of measuring religiosity are not the weaknesses here.

questions.q: Over a decade, diagnoses of an attention disorder rose 40%, while community surveys using a fixed symptom checklist found stable symptom levels. This pattern best supports:
o: a true rise in the disorder's underlying prevalence
Stable symptom levels contradict a true increase in the condition.
demedicalization of the condition
Demedicalization would reduce diagnoses, not increase them.
medicalization through broader diagnosis of the same behaviors
Correct: more behaviors are being labeled medical without more symptoms.
cultural lag in diagnostic technology
Nothing indicates nonmaterial culture trailing technology.
questions.x: If diagnoses rise while a fixed symptom measure stays flat, the change is in labeling, not in the underlying condition. That pattern supports medicalization, where broader diagnostic criteria or practices bring more of the same behaviors under medical definitions. A true rise in prevalence would require symptoms to increase too.

questions.q: In a study of couples, both partners who feel they give more than they get and partners who feel they get more than they give report lower satisfaction than partners in balanced relationships. This finding best supports:
o: equity theory, an extension of social exchange theory
Correct: perceived imbalance in either direction produces discomfort.
pure reward maximization
This predicts over-benefited partners should be happiest.
functionalism
Functionalism addresses societal stability, not dyadic fairness.
the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis
This concerns language and thought.
questions.x: Equity theory, an extension of social exchange theory, says people are most satisfied when the ratio of rewards to contributions feels fair. Underbenefited partners feel resentful and overbenefited partners feel guilty, so both report lower satisfaction. Pure reward maximization would predict the overbenefited partner is happiest, which the data contradict.

questions.q: In the 1850s a physician proposed "drapetomania," a supposed mental illness causing enslaved people to flee captivity. This example best illustrates that:
o: diagnoses always reflect objective biological findings
This diagnosis reflected social interests, not biology.
disease categories can reflect prevailing social values and power relations
Correct: the label medicalized resistance in a way that served slaveholders.
the sick role exempts patients from blame
The label was used to justify control, not to exempt anyone.
medicalization reduces the influence of physicians
Medicalization expands, not reduces, medical authority.
questions.x: Drapetomania labeled enslaved people's attempts to escape as a mental illness, turning resistance into a medical problem in a way that served slaveholders. It shows that disease categories can reflect the values and power relations of their time rather than objective biology. Medicalization like this expands medical authority rather than reducing it.

questions.q: Workers who earn a diploma are paid notably more than workers who completed nearly the same coursework but left before graduating. This finding most strongly supports:
o: the view that education pays only by raising job skills
Nearly identical coursework implies similar skills, yet pay differs.
the credentialist view that diplomas signal value beyond skills
Correct: the credential itself is rewarded, not just the learning.
the hidden curriculum's effect on punctuality
The data compare credentials, not implicit lessons.
de facto segregation in schools
Nothing in the finding concerns separation by race or class.
questions.x: If people with almost the same coursework, and so similar skills, earn more simply by holding a diploma, the credential itself is being rewarded. This sheepskin effect supports credentialism, where degrees act as signals beyond the skills they certify. A pure skills view predicts similar pay for similar learning.

questions.q: Researchers find that after a town's main factory closes, divorce rates and school dropout rates both rise over the next five years. This pattern best illustrates that:
o: institutions operate independently of each other
The pattern shows change in one institution affecting others.
the family is the only institution that shapes education
The economic change preceded both effects.
a change in the economy can ripple into family and education
Correct: social institutions are interdependent.
dropout causes factory closures
The timing runs from closure to dropout, not the reverse.
questions.x: Social institutions are interdependent, so change in one spreads to others. A factory closing hits household incomes, which can strain marriages and push teens to leave school to work, raising divorce and dropout rates. The timing, closure first and effects after, also rules out the idea that dropout caused the closure.

questions.q: Why do sociologists distinguish between sex and gender?
o: Sex is socially constructed; gender is fixed by chromosomes
This reverses the two terms.
The two terms are interchangeable in sociological research
Sociologists deliberately separate them because they can vary independently.
Gender refers only to legal status on official documents
Legal markers are one expression of gender, not its definition.
Sex refers to biological traits; gender refers to socially constructed roles and identities
Correct: sex is anatomical and physiological, while gender reflects cultural expectations and self-identity.
questions.note: Sex = biology; gender = social roles, norms and identity.
questions.x: Sex refers to biological attributes such as chromosomes, hormones and anatomy, while gender refers to the roles, norms and identities a society attaches to being a man or woman. Keeping them separate lets researchers see that gender expectations vary across cultures and over time even when biology does not. The tempting reversal gets it backwards: biology is the 'sex' side, culture the 'gender' side.

questions.q: Which observation most strongly supports the view that race is a social construct?
o: People of different races can have different average heights
Group averages in some traits do not show that the categories themselves are biologically defined.
Skin pigmentation is influenced by melanin production
A biological basis for skin color does not make racial categories biological.
Some diseases are more common in certain geographic ancestries
Ancestry-linked variation exists but does not map neatly onto socially defined races.
The racial categories on a national census have been redefined several times over a century
Correct: categories that shift with politics and convention reflect social, not biological, boundaries.
questions.x: A social construct is a category whose boundaries are set by human agreement rather than by nature. If census racial categories are redrawn every few decades, the categories must be tracking politics and convention, not fixed biology. Trait differences such as pigmentation or disease frequency are real biological variation, but they do not show that the racial boxes themselves are natural divisions.

questions.q: In the 19th-century United States, Irish immigrants were often described as a separate, inferior 'race,' a label later dropped as they were absorbed into the category 'white.' This illustrates:
o: Amalgamation
Amalgamation is the blending of groups into a new culture, not the assigning of racial labels.
Racialization
Correct: racial meaning was assigned to a group that had not been defined that way, then later withdrawn.
Symbolic ethnicity
Symbolic ethnicity is a voluntary, low-cost attachment to heritage, not an imposed racial label.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism means judging cultures by their own standards, unrelated to racial labeling.
questions.note: Racialization: attaching racial meaning to a group, often to justify unequal treatment.
questions.x: Racialization is the process of attaching racial meaning to a group that was not previously defined that way, usually to justify unequal treatment. Irish immigrants were labeled a separate inferior race and later folded into 'white,' showing the label was socially assigned and changeable. Amalgamation is tempting because groups mixed, but it describes cultural blending into something new, not the assignment of racial status.

questions.q: A researcher follows everyone born in a city between 1990 and 1994 to study their employment over time. This group is best described as a:
o: Reference group
A reference group is one people compare themselves to, not a sampling unit by birth year.
Birth cohort
Correct: a cohort is a group sharing a defining event in the same time period, here birth years.
Dependent population
Dependents are people under 15 or over 64, not a group defined by birth period.
Primary group
A primary group is a small, intimate group like a family.
questions.x: A cohort is a group of people who share a defining experience during the same time period; a birth cohort shares birth years. Following a cohort over time lets researchers see how a generation's life course unfolds. A reference group is tempting only because it is also a 'group,' but it refers to whom people compare themselves with, not a sampling unit.

questions.q: A 2005 survey finds adults over 60 use social media far less than adults under 30. Following the same people to 2025, researchers find the older group's use barely changed, while the 2005 under-30 group, now middle-aged, still uses it heavily. The 2005 gap mainly reflected a(n):
o: Cohort effect
Correct: the difference tracked the generation people were born into, not their age at the time.
Age effect
If aging caused it, the 2005 younger adults would have reduced their use as they aged.
Period effect
A period effect would shift all age groups together at one point in time.
Hawthorne effect
The Hawthorne effect is behavior change from being observed, unrelated here.
questions.note: Cohort = generation; age = life stage; period = historical moment affecting everyone.
questions.x: A cohort effect is a difference rooted in when people were born, so it travels with a generation as it ages. Here each group kept its habits over 20 years, so the gap reflected generational experience, not age. An age effect would require people to change as they grow older, so the younger group would have cut back by midlife, which did not happen.

questions.q: After a severe economic recession, reported financial anxiety rose sharply among teenagers, middle-aged adults and retirees alike, then fell as the economy recovered. This pattern is best explained as a(n):
o: Cohort effect
A cohort effect would affect one generation and persist as it aged.
Period effect
Correct: one historical event shifted all age groups at the same time.
Age effect
An age effect would appear at a particular life stage regardless of the year.
Selection effect
Selection bias concerns who enters a sample, not a shared historical shift.
questions.x: A period effect is a change caused by a historical event that hits all age groups at roughly the same time, then fades or persists for everyone. A recession raising anxiety in teens, adults and retirees alike, then easing with recovery, fits exactly. A cohort effect would instead mark one generation and follow it through life, not move every age group together.

questions.q: In every generation studied, voter turnout rises as individuals move from their early 20s into their 50s. This consistent pattern is best described as a(n):
o: Age (life-course) effect
Correct: the change accompanies a life stage and repeats across cohorts.
Cohort effect
A cohort effect would distinguish generations, but here all generations follow the same path.
Period effect
A period effect would be tied to a specific year, not to age.
Ecological fallacy
That is an inference error about individuals from group data, not a temporal pattern.
questions.x: An age or life-course effect is a change tied to a life stage that repeats in every generation. Because turnout rises from the 20s to the 50s in each cohort studied, the pattern tracks aging itself, through things like settling down, owning property and community ties. A cohort effect would show generations differing from each other, which is the opposite of what is described.

questions.q: A country records about 120 male births for every 100 female births. The most likely explanation is:
o: Higher male mortality in infancy
Higher male infant mortality would lower, not raise, the ratio of boys.
Emigration of young women
Emigration affects adult sex ratios, not the ratio at birth.
Normal biological variation in human births
Natural variation stays near 105 boys per 100 girls.
Son preference combined with sex-selective practices
Correct: the natural ratio is about 105; large excesses usually reflect sex-selective abortion or neglect.
questions.note: Sex ratio at birth ≈ 105; far above that signals sex selection.
questions.x: Human populations naturally produce about 105 male births per 100 female births. A ratio near 120 is far outside natural variation and is the signature of son preference combined with sex-selective abortion or neglect of girls. Emigration or male infant mortality are tempting, but they change sex ratios after birth, not the ratio at birth itself.

questions.q: Recently arrived immigrants often have better health than native-born residents of similar income, but this advantage fades the longer they stay. This is called the:
o: Brain drain
Brain drain is the emigration of skilled workers, not a health pattern.
Demographic dividend
That is economic growth from a large working-age share.
Healthy immigrant effect
Correct: migrants are often healthier on arrival, with the edge eroding over time.
Epidemiologic transition
That is a society-wide shift from infectious to chronic disease.
questions.x: The healthy immigrant effect describes newly arrived immigrants being healthier than native-born residents of similar income, partly because healthier people are more likely to migrate and pass screening. Over time, acculturation to local diets, stress and discrimination erode the advantage. Brain drain is a migration term too, but it concerns loss of skilled workers, not health.

questions.q: A study finds that U.S.-born children of immigrants have higher obesity rates than their foreign-born parents despite higher incomes. Which explanation best fits this finding?
o: Adoption of the host country's diet and activity patterns through acculturation
Correct: acculturation to less healthy local habits can erode the first generation's health advantage.
Higher income directly causes obesity
Income generally predicts better, not worse, health; something else must explain the reversal.
Selective emigration of the least healthy parents
Migrant selection usually favors healthier people, which would not explain the children's decline.
Genetic drift between generations
One generation is far too short for genetic drift to explain a population trend.
questions.note: The 'immigrant paradox' often reverses with acculturation.
questions.x: Acculturation means adopting the host culture's practices, including diet and activity patterns. Children raised in the host country take up local eating and sedentary habits more fully than their immigrant parents, so the parents' health advantage fades despite rising income. Income is the tempting explanation, but higher income usually predicts better health, so it cannot explain a decline.

questions.q: Lesbian, gay and bisexual adults show higher average rates of depression than heterosexual adults. The minority stress model attributes this mainly to:
o: Chronic stress from stigma, prejudice and discrimination
Correct: the model locates the cause in hostile social conditions, not orientation itself.
An inherent link between orientation and mental illness
The model explicitly rejects orientation itself as the cause.
Lower average income in all sexual-minority groups
Income may contribute, but the model centers on stigma-related stress.
Overreporting of symptoms by survey respondents
The model treats the disparity as real, not as a measurement artifact.
questions.x: The minority stress model holds that stigmatized groups face chronic, additional stressors such as discrimination, rejection, concealment and internalized stigma, and these stressors raise rates of depression and anxiety. The cause lies in hostile social conditions, not in orientation itself. Income may contribute to disparities, but the model's central mechanism is stigma-related stress.

questions.q: A researcher argues that the workplace discrimination faced by Black women cannot be understood by simply adding the effects of racism and sexism. This argument reflects:
o: Cultural capital
Cultural capital concerns non-financial assets such as education and taste.
Social reproduction
Social reproduction is the transmission of inequality across generations.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own standards.
Intersectionality
Correct: overlapping identities create distinct, not merely additive, experiences of disadvantage.
questions.x: Intersectionality holds that social identities such as race, gender and class combine to create distinct experiences of advantage or disadvantage that are not just the sum of each separately. A Black woman may face stereotypes that neither white women nor Black men face. Social reproduction is tempting because it concerns inequality, but it describes transmission across generations, not overlapping identities.

questions.q: Many recent immigrants from one country settle in a single neighborhood with shops, newspapers and places of worship in their native language. This neighborhood is an example of a(n):
o: Gentrified district
Gentrification is the influx of wealthier residents, not immigrant clustering.
Megalopolis
A megalopolis is a chain of merged metropolitan areas.
Ethnic enclave
Correct: a spatial concentration of an ethnic group with its own institutions.
Suburb
A suburb is a residential area outside a city center, not defined by ethnicity.
questions.x: An ethnic enclave is a neighborhood where an ethnic group is concentrated and has built its own businesses, media and institutions, often easing newcomers' adjustment. The defining features are spatial clustering plus group-specific institutions. Gentrification also changes neighborhoods, but it involves wealthier newcomers moving in and raising costs, not immigrant clustering.

questions.q: Over three generations, an immigrant family stops speaking its native language and adopts the customs of the dominant culture until its origins are no longer visible. This process is:
o: Cultural pluralism
Pluralism means groups keep distinct identities while coexisting.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation blends groups into a new culture rather than absorbing one into another.
Assimilation
Correct: a minority group is absorbed into the dominant culture, losing distinct traits.
Segregation
Segregation is physical and social separation of groups.
questions.x: Assimilation is the process by which a minority group gradually adopts the culture of the dominant group, losing its distinctive language and customs, often over several generations. The direction is one-way: A becomes like B. Amalgamation is the tempting alternative, but in amalgamation both groups blend to form a new culture rather than one being absorbed.

questions.q: Two immigrant groups intermarry over generations, and their cuisines and holidays merge into a new tradition that neither group practiced before. This best illustrates:
o: Amalgamation
Correct: groups blend to form a new cultural group, the 'melting pot.'
Assimilation
In assimilation one group adopts the other's culture rather than both forming something new.
Cultural pluralism
Pluralism keeps the groups distinct.
Cultural lag
Cultural lag is the delay of non-material culture behind material change.
questions.note: Assimilation: A + B → B. Amalgamation: A + B → C. Pluralism: A + B → A + B.
questions.x: Amalgamation occurs when groups mix, often through intermarriage, and produce a new culture that differs from each original, the classic 'melting pot.' The new holiday traditions that neither group practiced before mark it as amalgamation. In assimilation one group simply adopts the other's existing culture, so nothing new is created.

questions.q: Historical U.S. laws classified anyone with any known African ancestry as Black, regardless of appearance. This 'one-drop rule' best demonstrates that:
o: Race is reliably determined by ancestry testing
No ancestry fraction biologically defines a race; the cutoff was arbitrary.
Racial categories are fixed across societies
Other societies drew the same lines quite differently.
Racial boundaries were set by social and legal convention
Correct: the rule assigned race by decree, not by any biological threshold.
Physical appearance determines racial identity
The rule ignored appearance entirely.
questions.x: The one-drop rule assigned anyone with any known African ancestry to the Black category, regardless of appearance or proportion of ancestry. Because the threshold was set by law and custom and differed from rules in other societies, it shows racial boundaries are socially constructed. It did not rely on appearance, which rules out the tempting physical-appearance option.

questions.q: Genetic studies show that most human genetic variation occurs among individuals within the same socially defined racial group rather than between groups. This finding:
o: Supports the view that racial categories are not discrete biological groupings
Correct: if most variation lies within groups, the categories capture little genetic structure.
Shows that racial groups are genetically identical
Variation within groups is large; individuals are not identical.
Proves that race has no effect on health
The finding concerns category boundaries; race can still affect health through racism and social conditions.
Shows that ethnicity is purely biological
Ethnicity is cultural, and the finding concerns race.
questions.x: Population genetics shows that most human genetic variation lies among individuals within any socially defined racial group, with relatively little separating the groups. Such categories therefore capture little genetic structure and are not discrete biological units. This does not mean people are genetically identical, nor that race is irrelevant to health, because racism and social conditions still shape health outcomes.

questions.q: Anthropologists find that tasks considered 'women's work' in one society are considered 'men's work' in another. This most directly supports the claim that:
o: Gender roles are socially constructed
Correct: if roles reverse across cultures, they are not dictated by biology.
Sex differences are entirely cultural
Cross-cultural variation in roles says nothing about biological sex itself.
Gender roles are determined by hormones
Hormones would not produce opposite roles in different societies.
All societies divide labor equally
The finding concerns which sex does a task, not equality.
questions.x: If biology dictated which sex performs a task, the same tasks would be assigned to the same sex everywhere. Finding that 'women's work' in one society is 'men's work' in another shows that gender roles are shaped by culture. The tempting overreach is that sex differences are entirely cultural, but the evidence concerns roles, not biological sex itself.

questions.q: A country's fertility falls to replacement level, yet its population keeps growing for several more decades. The most likely reason is:
o: Replacement fertility always produces growth
Replacement fertility leads to stability once the age structure evens out.
A large young cohort is still entering its reproductive years
Correct: population momentum; many parents still produce many births even at 2.1 children each.
Mortality must be rising
Rising mortality would slow growth, not sustain it.
Crude birth rates are unaffected by age structure
Crude rates depend strongly on age structure; that is why growth continues.
questions.note: Population momentum: a young age structure keeps growth going after fertility drops.
questions.x: Population momentum is continued growth after fertility reaches replacement, because a young age structure means many people are entering childbearing ages. Even at about 2.1 children per woman, a large parent generation produces many births while deaths remain relatively few. Growth stops only once the age structure evens out over several decades.

questions.q: In populations with low mortality, replacement-level total fertility is approximately:
o: 1.0 child per woman
That would halve each generation.
2.1 children per woman
Correct: two to replace the parents, plus a little for deaths before reproductive age and the slight male excess at birth.
3.5 children per woman
That would roughly double the population per generation.
2.0 children per woman exactly
Slightly more than 2 is needed because some children die and more boys than girls are born.
questions.x: Replacement-level fertility is the average number of children per woman needed for each generation to replace itself. It is slightly above 2, about 2.1 in low-mortality populations, because some children die before reproducing and slightly more boys than girls are born. It is higher where child mortality is high, which is why exactly 2.0 is the tempting but wrong answer.

questions.q: Country A has excellent health care but a higher crude death rate than Country B, which has poorer health care. The best explanation is that Country A:
o: Has an older age structure
Correct: crude rates ignore age; many elderly people raise deaths per 1,000 even with good care.
Has a higher infant mortality rate
Good health care would make high infant mortality unlikely.
Has a higher birth rate
More births add young people, which tends to lower the crude death rate.
Has more immigration of young workers
Young immigrants would lower the crude death rate.
questions.note: Compare mortality across populations with age-standardized rates.
questions.x: The crude death rate is deaths per 1,000 total population and does not adjust for age. A country with many elderly people will record many deaths per 1,000 even if its health care is excellent, while a young population records few deaths despite poorer care. That is why mortality comparisons use age-standardized rates; a higher birth rate would make the population younger and lower the crude rate.

questions.q: Historians attribute the initial decline in death rates in 18th- and 19th-century Europe mainly to:
o: Better food supply, sanitation and clean water
Correct: public health and nutrition preceded most effective medical treatments.
Widespread use of antibiotics
Antibiotics arrived in the 1940s, long after death rates began falling.
Falling birth rates
Birth rates fell later and do not directly reduce mortality.
Mass vaccination against all major diseases
Only smallpox vaccination existed early; most vaccines came much later.
questions.x: Death rates in Europe began falling in the 18th and 19th centuries, well before effective medical treatments existed. Historians credit improved nutrition and food supply, followed by sanitation and clean water, which reduced infectious disease. Antibiotics are the tempting answer, but they arrived in the 1940s, long after mortality had already declined substantially.

questions.q: Several high-income countries now record more deaths than births each year. Demographers who describe this as a fifth stage of the demographic transition are emphasizing:
o: A return to high birth and death rates
That describes stage 1, not a post-transition stage.
Rapid growth from falling mortality
That is stage 2.
Fertility below replacement leading to natural population decline
Correct: a proposed stage 5 features births falling below deaths.
Stable population with births equal to deaths
That is the classic stage 4 balance, not decline.
questions.x: The classic demographic transition ends in stage 4 with low birth and death rates and little growth. Some demographers add a stage 5 in which fertility falls well below replacement, deaths exceed births, and populations shrink without immigration. The stage 4 option is tempting, but stage 4 implies balance, while the scenario describes natural decline.

questions.q: Which development most directly undermined Malthus's prediction of mass famine in the 20th century?
o: A sharp rise in global birth rates
Higher births would support, not undermine, his fear.
The spread of infectious diseases
Disease is one of his positive checks, consistent with his theory.
Agricultural innovations that greatly increased crop yields
Correct: technology raised food output far faster than Malthus expected.
Rising world population after 1950
Fast growth without mass famine is what challenged him; growth alone does not.
questions.x: Malthus assumed food supply could grow only slowly, but agricultural technology, including mechanization, fertilizers and high-yield crop varieties, raised food output faster than population in most of the world. This broke the link he predicted between population growth and mass famine. Rising population alone does not refute him; growth without the predicted famine does.

questions.q: An environmental scientist argues that rising world population will exhaust fresh water and arable land unless birth rates are reduced. This view is best described as:
o: Demographic transition theory
Transition theory describes stages of birth and death rates, not resource collapse.
World systems theory
World systems theory concerns global economic hierarchy.
Neo-Malthusian
Correct: it updates Malthus by stressing resource limits and calling for lower fertility.
Dependency theory
Dependency theory concerns exploitation of poorer nations by wealthy ones.
questions.x: Neo-Malthusians update Malthus's argument by stressing that population growth threatens finite resources such as water, land and ecosystems, and they often call for lower fertility. The emphasis on resource limits and reducing births identifies the view. Demographic transition theory is tempting because it concerns population, but it describes stages of birth and death rates, not resource collapse.

questions.q: The population pyramid of an oil-rich Gulf state shows far more men than women aged 20 to 45, while children and elderly are evenly split by sex. The best explanation is:
o: Sex-selective abortion
That would skew the youngest ages, which are balanced.
Higher female mortality in adulthood
Mortality would not produce such a sharp, age-limited gap.
Large-scale labor immigration of working-age men
Correct: migration is selective for age and sex, distorting only the working-age bars.
A baby boom 30 years ago
A boom would enlarge both sexes equally.
questions.note: Migration distorts pyramids in the working ages.
questions.x: Migration is selective: labor migrants are mostly young working-age adults, often men. Large inflows of male workers swell only the working-age male bars, leaving children and the elderly balanced by sex. Sex-selective abortion would skew the youngest ages, which are balanced here, so it cannot explain the pattern.

questions.q: A farmer wants to emigrate for higher wages but cannot afford the journey and is barred by the destination country's visa rules. In Lee's model of migration, these barriers are:
o: Push factors
Push factors drive people out of the origin; these block departure instead.
Intervening obstacles
Correct: factors between origin and destination that impede moving.
Pull factors
Pull factors attract migrants to the destination.
Preventive checks
A Malthusian term for birth-lowering behaviors.
questions.note: Lee: push, pull, intervening obstacles, personal factors.
questions.x: Lee's model of migration includes factors at the origin (push), factors at the destination (pull), intervening obstacles between them, and personal factors. Travel cost and restrictive visa rules stand between the farmer's wish to leave and arrival, so they are intervening obstacles. They are not push factors, because push factors encourage leaving rather than block it.

questions.q: A cross-national study finds that countries with higher GDP per capita have lower fertility. A researcher concludes that rising income causes fertility to fall. The strongest criticism is that:
o: The sample includes too many countries
More countries strengthens, not weakens, a cross-national analysis.
Fertility cannot be measured across countries
TFR is routinely compared across countries.
Confounders such as urbanization and women's education may drive both
Correct: correlation in cross-sectional data cannot rule out third variables.
GDP and fertility are positively correlated
The finding is a negative correlation.
questions.x: A cross-sectional correlation between income and fertility cannot establish causation, because other variables such as urbanization, women's education and contraceptive access may drive both. These confounders could create the association even if income itself had no direct effect. More countries in the sample would strengthen, not weaken, the analysis, so sample size is not the problem.

questions.q: As a country develops, the leading causes of death shift from infections and malnutrition to heart disease and cancer. This shift is called the:
o: Epidemiologic transition
Correct: the change in disease patterns accompanying the demographic transition.
Demographic dividend
That concerns age structure and economic growth.
Nutrition transition
That refers to diet shifts, not causes of death overall.
Healthy immigrant effect
That concerns migrant health, not national disease patterns.
questions.x: The epidemiologic transition is the shift in leading causes of death from infectious disease and malnutrition to chronic, degenerative diseases such as heart disease and cancer. It accompanies the demographic transition because more people survive childhood and reach older ages. The nutrition transition is a narrower change in diets and body weight, not in overall causes of death.

questions.q: Life expectancy at birth in a country rose from 40 to 65 years over a few decades. The largest contributor to such a rise is usually:
o: Extending the maximum human lifespan
Maximum lifespan has barely changed.
Better treatment of cancer in the elderly
Late-life gains add relatively few years to the average at birth.
Higher fertility
Life expectancy is calculated from age-specific death rates, so the number of births does not raise it.
Reduced infant and child mortality
Correct: early deaths subtract many years, so preventing them raises the average sharply.
questions.note: Low life expectancy at birth mostly reflects high child mortality, not that adults die at 40.
questions.x: Life expectancy at birth is an average, so deaths in infancy and childhood pull it down sharply because each subtracts many potential years. Reducing infant and child mortality therefore produces the largest gains. Low life expectancy does not mean adults typically die at 40, and better late-life cancer care adds only a few years to the average.

questions.q: In mid-20th-century U.S. cities, many middle-class white families moved to newly built outer suburbs as minority populations in central cities grew. This pattern is known as:
o: Gentrification
Gentrification is the opposite flow, wealthier people moving into the city.
White flight
Correct: racially patterned movement from cities to suburbs.
Chain migration
Chain migration involves networks of relatives, not suburban moves.
Counterurbanization
Counterurbanization is a move to rural areas, not suburbs.
questions.x: White flight describes the mid-20th-century movement of white middle-class families from central cities to suburbs as minority populations in cities grew. It was shaped by racial attitudes and by policies such as discriminatory lending and highway building. Counterurbanization is a move to rural areas, not suburbs, and gentrification is the opposite flow into the city.

questions.q: Interviews show that residents who stayed in a gentrifying neighborhood enjoyed new parks and lower crime yet felt they no longer belonged as familiar shops and churches closed. Researchers would call this:
o: Cultural displacement
Correct: residents lose their sense of place even without physically moving.
Physical displacement
These residents remained in the neighborhood.
Assimilation
They are not adopting a dominant culture by choice.
Relative deprivation
That concerns perceived disadvantage driving collective action, not loss of place.
questions.x: Displacement can be physical, when residents must move out, or cultural, when residents stay but lose their sense of belonging as the shops, institutions and social networks of their community disappear. The residents in this study remained, so their loss is cultural. Physical displacement is tempting because gentrification often involves moving out, but these people did not leave.

questions.q: National surveys report very different percentages of 'gay, lesbian or bisexual' people depending on whether they ask about identity, sexual behavior or attraction. The best explanation is that:
o: Sexual orientation cannot be studied scientifically
Measurement differences call for careful definitions, not abandoning research.
Respondents always answer randomly
Consistent differences by question type are not random.
Sexual orientation changes daily for most people
Orientation is generally stable; the gaps reflect what is measured.
Identity, behavior and attraction overlap but are not identical
Correct: some people report same-sex attraction or behavior without adopting an LGB identity.
questions.x: Sexual orientation has several dimensions: identity (how people label themselves), behavior (with whom they have sex) and attraction (whom they are drawn to). These overlap but do not coincide, so a person may report same-sex attraction or behavior without identifying as gay, lesbian or bisexual. Surveys that measure different dimensions therefore yield different estimates, without implying that orientation is unstable.

questions.q: A country has growing manufacturing and exports some industrial goods, but still relies on foreign investment and buys raw materials cheaply from poorer nations. In world systems theory, it is best classified as:
o: Core
Core nations dominate investment and do not depend on foreign capital in this way.
Semi-periphery
Correct: it is exploited by the core while exploiting the periphery.
Periphery
Periphery nations mainly export raw materials and lack industrial growth.
External area
External areas lie outside the world economy entirely.
questions.x: In world systems theory, semi-periphery nations sit between the core and the periphery: they have growing industry and some economic power, yet depend on core capital. They are exploited by the core while exploiting the periphery for cheap raw materials. Calling it core is tempting because it exports industrial goods, but its reliance on foreign investment marks it as semi-periphery.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that poor nations remain underdeveloped because wealthy nations structure trade and debt to their own advantage. This view is:
o: Dependency theory
Correct: underdevelopment results from exploitative ties to wealthy nations.
Modernization theory
Modernization theory blames internal traditional values and urges adopting Western institutions.
Demographic transition theory
That describes birth and death rate stages.
Malthusian theory
That concerns population outpacing food.
questions.x: Dependency theory argues that poor nations remain underdeveloped because their economies are structured to serve wealthy nations through unequal trade, debt and investment. The cause of poverty lies in external exploitative relationships. Modernization theory is the main contrast, since it blames internal factors such as traditional values and urges poor nations to adopt Western institutions.

questions.q: A newly emerging respiratory virus is detected on five continents within weeks of its first identified case. Which feature of globalization most directly explains this speed?
o: High volume of international air travel
Correct: global transportation networks move infected people across continents within hours.
Rising fertility in low-income countries
Birth rates do not determine how fast a pathogen spreads between continents.
Urban gentrification
Neighborhood change does not explain intercontinental spread.
Cultural homogenization
Shared culture does not transport pathogens.
questions.x: Globalization connects distant places through rapid transportation, especially international air travel, which can move infected people between continents within a day. That is why a new respiratory pathogen can appear worldwide within weeks of its first identified case. Cultural homogenization involves shared tastes and media, which do not physically carry pathogens.

questions.q: A campaign encourages individuals to reduce their meat consumption by one meal per week, without seeking legal or institutional change. Using Aberle's typology, this is a(n):
o: Redemptive movement
Redemptive movements seek radical, total change in individuals.
Alternative movement
Correct: it targets a limited change in individual behavior.
Reform movement
Reform movements target limited change in society or law.
Revolutionary movement
Revolutionary movements seek radical change in society.
questions.note: Aberle: alternative (limited, individual), redemptive (radical, individual), reform (limited, society), revolutionary (radical, society).
questions.x: Aberle classified movements by whom they target (individuals or society) and how much change they seek (limited or radical). Asking individuals to make one modest behavioral change, without seeking institutional change, is an alternative movement. A redemptive movement also targets individuals, but it seeks a total personal transformation, such as a religious conversion.

questions.q: Factory workers whose wages are rising join a protest movement after learning that workers in a neighboring region earn far more. Which theory best explains their participation?
o: Resource mobilization theory
That theory emphasizes resources and organization, not perceived deprivation.
Relative deprivation theory
Correct: discontent comes from comparing one's situation with others or expectations.
Malthusian theory
Malthusian theory concerns population and food.
Rational choice theory of fertility
Fertility decisions are unrelated to protest participation.
questions.x: Relative deprivation theory holds that discontent arises from comparing one's situation with others or with expectations, not from absolute hardship. These workers are gaining, yet they feel deprived compared with better-paid neighbors, which motivates protest. Resource mobilization theory focuses on resources and organization that let movements succeed, not on what creates the grievance.

questions.q: Two movements with equally intense public grievances are compared. One gains funding, trained leaders, and media contacts and wins policy changes; the other does not. Which theory is best supported?
o: Resource mobilization theory
Correct: success depends on resources and organization, not grievance alone.
Relative deprivation theory
Grievances were equal, so deprivation cannot explain the different outcomes.
Mass society theory
That theory emphasizes social isolation driving participation.
Value-added theory of crowds
This theory, based on structural strain and triggering events, does not center on resources.
questions.x: Resource mobilization theory argues that grievances are common, so movement success depends on acquiring resources such as money, leaders, organization and media access. Because grievances were equal in both movements, only the difference in resources can explain their different outcomes. Relative deprivation theory explains why discontent arises, not why some equally aggrieved movements succeed.

questions.q: A grassroots movement opens a national headquarters, hires paid staff and develops formal procedures. In the life cycle of social movements, this stage is:
o: Emergence
Emergence is the early stage of widespread but unorganized discontent.
Coalescence
Coalescence is when discontent becomes focused and leaders emerge, before formalization.
Bureaucratization
Correct: the movement becomes formally organized with staff and rules.
Decline
Decline is when the movement weakens or ends.
questions.note: Stages: emergence → coalescence → bureaucratization → decline.
questions.x: A common model of social movements runs from emergence (unfocused discontent) to coalescence (organized leadership and strategy), then bureaucratization (formal organization with paid staff and procedures), and finally decline. Opening a headquarters and hiring staff mark bureaucratization. Coalescence is the tempting choice, but it involves focusing grievances and leaders, not formal administration.

questions.q: Many residents want cleaner air but stay home from protests, expecting to benefit from any regulations others win. This is called the:
o: Free rider problem
Correct: people enjoy collective gains without contributing effort.
Bystander effect
The bystander effect concerns failing to help in emergencies.
Social loafing
Social loafing is reduced effort within a working group, not abstaining from participation.
Groupthink
Groupthink is poor decision-making from pressure for consensus.
questions.x: The free rider problem arises when people can benefit from a collective good, such as cleaner air, without contributing to the effort that produces it. Because any gains are shared by everyone, each individual has an incentive to let others do the work, which makes mobilization harder. Social loafing is tempting, but it is reduced effort within a group task, not staying out of participation altogether.

questions.q: A study finds that civil rights protests grew fastest in periods when sympathetic politicians gained office and the state's ability to repress protest weakened. This finding best supports:
o: Political process theory
Correct: political opportunities shape when movements emerge and succeed.
Relative deprivation theory
The pattern tracks political openings, not changes in deprivation.
Malthusian theory
Population and food supply are not involved.
Modernization theory
Modernization theory addresses national development.
questions.x: Political process theory argues that movements grow and succeed when political opportunities open, for example through sympathetic officials, divided elites or weakened repression. The study shows protest tracking such openings rather than changes in grievance. Relative deprivation theory would predict protest rising with perceived deprivation, which is not what was measured.

questions.q: Country X and Country Y both have crude birth rates of 20 per 1,000, but X has a total fertility rate of 1.8 and Y has 3.0. The best explanation is that Country X:
o: Has more children per woman
Its TFR is lower, so women have fewer children.
Has higher infant mortality
Infant mortality does not reconcile a lower TFR with an equal crude birth rate.
Has a much older age structure
An older population would lower its crude birth rate.
Has a larger share of women in their reproductive years
Correct: many women of childbearing age raise the crude rate even when each has few children.
questions.note: TFR removes age structure; crude rates do not.
questions.x: The crude birth rate depends both on how many children each woman has and on what share of the population are women of childbearing age. Total fertility rate removes the age-structure effect. If X has fewer children per woman but the same crude birth rate as Y, it must have a larger proportion of women in their reproductive years; an older population would lower, not raise, its crude rate.

questions.q: A study finds a large Black–white gap in hypertension that shrinks substantially after adjusting for neighborhood poverty, chronic stress and access to care. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The disparity is caused mainly by genetic differences between races
The adjustment points toward social, not genetic, explanations.
Social and structural conditions account for much of the disparity
Correct: the gap narrows when social factors are controlled.
Race has no relationship with hypertension
An unadjusted gap was clearly observed.
Access to care is the only cause of the disparity
Several factors were adjusted together, so no single one can be isolated.
questions.x: When a racial disparity shrinks substantially after controlling for social factors such as poverty, stress and access to care, those factors account for much of the gap. This supports social and structural explanations over genetic ones. Because several factors were adjusted together, the study cannot single out access to care as the only cause.

questions.q: Rural villages in a developing country now consist mostly of children, women and older adults, while cities have a surplus of young men. This pattern best demonstrates that:
o: Fertility is higher in cities than in villages
Rural fertility is usually higher, and fertility would not create a male surplus.
Mortality is higher among rural men
Mortality would not explain the urban male surplus.
Migration affects only the destination population
The origin's structure changed as well.
Migration is selective by age and sex
Correct: young adult men migrated disproportionately, reshaping both origin and destination.
questions.x: Migration is selective: migrants are disproportionately young adults, and in many settings men are more likely to move for work. Their departure leaves origin areas with more children, women and elderly people, while destination cities gain young men. Migration therefore reshapes the age and sex structure of both places, not just the destination.
